note: Per-metric explainer. id is the metric name on the dashboard; entries with <k> are written per family (e.g. partial/<k>/frac covers all freshness buckets in one entry).

items.name: Carryover by data source (sampler counts broken out by data source)
items.what: Carryover counted by the sampler per data source. The number of questions left in the pool at the previous step and carried over to this step. For the same family, pro and flash each have about 25 data sources; the dashboard's official explanation covers only the aggregate definition, with no explanation at the dataset level.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. The relationship that can be verified in the data is: most steps satisfy held ≈ accepted count for this step + previous step's carryover, i.e. task pool = newly accepted + accumulated from the previous step. This relationship does not hold at the step right after a restart; the carryover chain is reset.
items.why: This group of numbers shows whom the sampler allocated traffic to. If a data source's accepted count suddenly drops, it could be that the data recipe was changed, or that it was temporarily removed; if you don't look at this layer, you'll only fail to find the cause when the total batch size changes. pro stops reporting counts for cyber after step 15; the corresponding announcement is the removal of the cyber dataset from the next run.
read: This is a count used by the sampler for traffic allocation, not a performance metric. If it changes, look at the data recipe first; do not use it to infer model capability.

Accepted count, held amount, and carryover should be viewed together: if the accepted count is scaling up and held is also rising, it means this data source is accumulating tasks rather than being consumed.
held ≈ accepted count for this step + previous step's carryover holds for most steps, but breaks at the step after a restart; do not treat it as an identity.
The magnitudes of the data sources differ by one to two orders of magnitude; for cross-source comparison use share, not absolute values.
items.observed: pro and flash each have about 25 data sources, all with complete series. Their magnitudes and trends differ greatly: some data sources scale up with training (e.g. the accepted count for code/dataset-yfch rises from 55 to 121), while others are shrinking. The table below lists the first and last values and the mean for each data source; for the broken chains at the restart steps, there are 3 in pro and 3 in flash.
traps: The dashboard has no official explanation for the num_accepted/{step,held,carryover} family. The reading here is derived by literally translating the tag names and then verifying with rolling relationships in the data; it is not an official definition.
held = accepted count for this step + previous step's carryover is not an identity; the step after a restart breaks it; do not use it to validate data.
The counts summed at the dataset layer are systematically 10%~18% higher than dynsam/agentic/num_accepted/step; the two layers use different definitions, so do not cross-validate them.

sources.quote: During the training process, we maintain an easy data pool, where problems with perfect pass rates are stored. When performing rollouts, there is a probability α (10% in our experiments) to sample data from this easy data pool.

sources.note: Public materials state that full-score questions are stored in a pool and then resampled proportionally; this is the mechanistic background for the existence of the “carryover” count, but the interface does not give its exact definition.

sources.quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts.
sources.topic: Dynamic sampling: discard all-correct/all-wrong (zero-advantage) groups
sources.note: This is the mechanistic origin of this group's 75 num_accepted/* entries: the accepted count equals the number that pass after filtering by 'neither all-correct nor all-wrong within the group', so it fluctuates with the question difficulty/composition at the same step, and does not track avg@n.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: A zero advantage results in zero policy gradients, shrinking the magnitude and increasing the noise sensitivity of the batch gradient, thereby degrading sample efficiency.
sources.topic: Why zero-advantage groups must be discarded
sources.note: It gives the motivation for discarding: the advantage of all-correct/all-wrong groups is identically zero and the gradient contribution is zero, so “a smaller accepted count” directly means this step's effective gradient quantity decreases, rather than a pure compute-accounting matter.

sources.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (Dr. GRPO)
sources.quote: Dr. GRPO introduces simple yet significant modifications to address the biases in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), by removing the length and std normalization terms.
sources.topic: Within-group standard deviation normalization is a bias term.
sources.note: The accepted count is a joint product of dynamic sampling and within-group normalization; the article explains that the scale of the advantage depends on the within-group reward variance, so changes in the accepted count are mixed with the variance composition of “which problems are accepted,” and cannot be attributed solely to problem difficulty.

items.name: Accepted problem count for this step (agentic harness)
items.what: The agentic problem count “accepted” into the training batch at this step. The dashboard has no official explanation for this tag (there is no num_accepted among the 22 entries); from the naming and same-family data, all that can be inferred is: it is the subset of problems in dynamic sampling that are accepted and actually enter training. Alongside it are also three tags under each dataset, dynsam/<source>/<dataset>/num_accepted/{step,held,carryover} (the other 75 entries in this group).
items.how: There is no official definition. Several things can be confirmed: first, at every step it is far smaller than dynsam/num_measurable (pro ratios 1.63~2.04, flash 1.51~2.06), and the two are highly synchronized (correlation coefficients pro 0.958, flash 0.925); second, the sum of num_accepted/step across the 25 datasets is 10%~18% higher than it (pro 1.10~1.18× per step, flash 1.10~1.13×), indicating that the dataset layer and this harness layer do not use the same accounting definition; third, although it and train/harness/*/training/rollouts (the number of rollouts per harness in the training batch) are both on the order of twenty thousand, one is a problem count and the other is a sequence count, so they cannot be directly aligned.
items.why: It is “the sample size from which this step actually learns”: the more accepted, the more effective information in the gradient; if the accepted count halves, that step's update relies more on replay/stale data (corresponding to a rise in partial/avg_staleness). It is also the core number for judging whether the sampler is healthy—if avg@n rises but the accepted count collapses at the same time, it means the model has improved on the problems that “would have been rejected anyway,” and the training value is limited. It naturally fluctuates inversely with problem difficulty: on high-difficulty steps, the sampler has to process more problems (a larger num_measurable) to accumulate enough accepted count.
read: First look at it together with num_measurable. A stable ratio between the two means the 「acceptance rate」 for this step has not changed much; a sudden decrease in the ratio means this step sampled many tasks but accepted few, usually because the tasks overall got harder or grading got stricter.

Look at its relationship with avg@n. In this run avg@n rose steadily, while the accepted count dropped from 2472 to 1090 (pro, shrinking to 44%), showing that 「accepting more」 and 「learning well」 are not the same thing in this run: the accepted count is more affected by task composition and difficulty distribution within the same step.
It has no trend with step number: pro slope -22.1/step (r=-0.292), flash -4.9/step (r=-0.097); it is purely up-and-down fluctuation, with a range of pro 2.92-fold and flash 2.14-fold.

Steps after a restart need to be viewed separately: pro step 16 is 848 (the lowest over the whole period, and num_measurable at the same step is also the lowest at 1636), flash step 21 is 1133, the lowest over the whole period——a single low point does not mean the trend is bad.
items.observed: pro: step 1 2472 → step 19 1090, minimum step 16 848, maximum step 1 2472, mean 1624.7, range 2.92×. flash: step 1 2357 → step 25 2075, minimum step 21 1133, maximum step 3 2421, mean 1560.1, range 2.14×. The means of both runs are 1500~1650 problems/step, on the same order of magnitude as num_target=1568 but slightly lower. The ratio to num_measurable is very stable: pro 1.63~2.04, flash 1.51~2.06. The sum of the 25 datasets is higher relative to it, but the ratio is stable (pro 1.10~1.18×, flash 1.10~1.13×).
traps: There is no official explanation; do not treat it as 「pass rate / compliance rate」 or 「sampling hit rate」——it has no denominator tag paired with it.
It differs from dynsam/num_measurable by nearly a factor of two, and the ratio fluctuates; the two cannot be converted into each other; also do not divide it by num_target to calculate 「completion」.
The sum of num_accepted at the dataset layer is inconsistent with it (10%~18% higher); this is a definitional difference, not a data error; do not use 「they should be equal when summed」 to validate.
Note the agentic in the tag name: it covers only the agentic category, not all training samples, and it also cannot be aligned with the sum of train/harness/*/training/rollouts.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts.
sources.topic: Dynamic sampling: discard all-correct/all-wrong (zero-advantage) groups
sources.note: We read it as “the subset of problems in dynamic sampling that are accepted and actually enter training”—the DAPO over-sample + filter definition means exactly this, and requires that the number of effective problems within a batch remains consistent.

items.name: Average agent turns per trajectory (agg_turn/mean)
items.what: On average, how many "turns" an agent trajectory needs to go through (one model output → one tool/environment call → concatenating the result back into the context counts as one turn). The official definition is just one sentence: agent turns per trajectory. It measures how many steps of interaction the task actually requires; it is affected both by task complexity and by the model's own decision quality: the better the model is at planning, the fewer detours it usually takes.
items.how: Official description: agent turns per trajectory. Average the turn counts of all trajectories in this step's training batch; agentic trajectories often have dozens of turns, while chat ones usually have only one or two, so this mean is dominated by agentic trajectories. The repository has a family of ctx_response_length/*, among which ctx_response_length/mean is the total token count generated per trajectory; the two have a correlation coefficient of 0.665 on pro (0.388 on flash), indicating that turn count and generation length largely move in the same direction——trajectories with more turns are also generating more tokens.
items.why: It is a composite reading of "task difficulty + model efficiency": if turn count drops noticeably while pass rate rises, it usually means the model has learned shorter solutions (less trial and error, fewer detours); if turn count rises but pass rate does not move, it is most likely that the model is repeatedly probing or the environment is retrying on timeout, a signal of burning compute; if turn count suddenly jumps, first suspect that the task composition or harness has changed. It is also a direct multiplier for cost and latency——turn count directly determines the number of sandbox calls.
read: In this run there is no downward trend; this is contrary to the intuition that 「the number of runs will decrease after long training」. Regressing on step number: pro slope +0.27 runs/step, r=0.261; flash slope +0.12 runs/step, r=0.188. Both r values are far from significant, so one can only say 「oscillating at a high level」.

But when viewed in segments, it does move downward in the second half: pro first-half slope +1.87 runs/step, second half -0.32 runs/step; flash first half +0.82, second half -0.43. The rise in the first half and the fall in the second half cancel each other out, which is why 「the whole segment looks flat」.

First-to-last comparison: pro step 1 47.47 → step 19 56.04 (+8.57 turns, +18.1%); flash step 1 47.31 → step 25 51.99 (+4.67 turns, +9.9%). First 5-step mean pro 48.57 / flash 53.77, last 5-step mean pro 50.85 / flash 55.10.

It is largely out of sync with pass rate: correlation with avg@n is pro 0.334, flash 0.090; with num_measurable it is weak negative correlation (pro -0.482, flash -0.223). In this run, the 'pass rate rise' and the 'change in number of turns' are two different things; you cannot use the number of turns to explain pass rate.
items.observed: pro: step 1 47.4689 → step 19 56.0396, lowest at step 2: 43.4, highest at step 13: 64.8149, mean 52.85, 1.49-fold range; there is no monotonic trend across the 19 steps (r=0.261), but the first half (steps 1~9) rises from 47.5 to 60.7, and the second half (steps 10~19) falls back to 56.04, and the final step is still +8.57 turns higher than the first step. flash: step 1 is already the lowest at 47.3148, highest at step 14: 64.5941, final step 51.9886, mean 57.25, 1.37-fold range, trend likewise not significant (r=0.188). That is: the task requires 43~65 turns on average, pro ends around 56 turns, slightly above its overall mean, and flash ends around 52 turns; over the same period avg@n rose by +6.88pp and +12.71pp respectively. Turn count did not drop noticeably with training, indicating that this run's capability improvement was not achieved by "solving the same tasks with fewer turns" (or the task composition was also changing, offsetting the efficiency gain).
traps: Do not write 'turn count decreases with training' based on intuition: the data in this repository does not support this claim; for pro/flash, the step-number regression r is only 0.261 and 0.188 respectively, and first-to-last it still rises.
Its denominator definition differs from that of num_measurable (docs/01 section 8, pitfall 7); dividing them (average turns per task) is meaningless.

The mean is dominated by long-tail trajectories: agentic trajectories with dozens of turns and chat trajectories with 1~2 turns are mixed in the same average; when the task composition changes, the mean moves, so do not treat it as a pure 'model efficiency' metric.
It is weakly correlated with avg@n (pro 0.334); do not treat it as a leading indicator or explanatory variable for pass rate.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: agent turns per trajectory
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

items.name: Average pass rate avg@n (main metric on the homepage)
items.what: For each task participating in training at this step, the model samples n times per task, counts how many of them succeed, and takes the proportion of n; then averages over all tasks. Intuitively, it is "the overall correctness rate of this batch of tasks" and is also the big number on the homepage. Note that it is not equal to "what proportion of tasks were solved correctly"——that is dynsam/passrate/one; avg@n is the mean of per-task proportions: a task with all 16 wrong and a task with all 16 correct contribute exactly 0 and 1 to it, while a task with 8 correct and 8 wrong contributes 0.5.
items.how: Official definition: for each prompt sampled this step, the fraction of its n attempts that succeed, averaged over prompts. n is 16 in this run: status.json's totals.prompts_per_step is 1568, docs/en/01-dashboard-data.md records the homepage display as 1,568 × 16 seqs, and the relation perf/total_num_tokens = 1568 × 16 × ctx_total_length/mean verified in the repo also indicates that each prompt corresponds to 16 sequences. What is averaged are those tasks in this step that "have a measurable pass rate"; the number of tasks differs per step (see dynsam/num_measurable), so it is "the average pass rate over this batch of tasks sampled in this step," not a score on a fixed task pool. In the data, it, critic/rewards/mean, and critic/score/mean, the three tags, are exactly identical value by value; when reading, just treat them as the same number.
items.why: It is the single overall objective for "how well the model is actually learning," and also the homepage headline. In engineering terms, watching it mainly means looking at the slope rather than the absolute value: a steady rise means the policy is improving; a long plateau means the task has already been mastered and the reward signal is thinning out; turning downward is usually collapse or a problem with the data/grading. Because it compresses "the task was answered correctly" and "what fraction of the task was answered correctly" into one number, looking at it alone cannot distinguish two completely different kinds of progress; it must be broken down together with dynsam/passrate/one and dynsam/passrate/zero (see below).
read: Look at the slope, look at r, not at single-step ups and downs. Run a univariate regression of avg@n on step number: pro slope 0.00420/step, r=0.947; flash slope 0.00531/step, r=0.963. Both are clean upward straight lines, not a 'rising to a plateau' shape.

Break the gain into two parts: 'questions that were all wrong start to be answered correctly' and 'questions that were partially correct become correct every time'. The upper bound of the former is the drop in passrate/zero; in this run both runs have only a little over 1 percentage point; the latter corresponds to the increase in passrate/one and is the main source.

Do not treat fluctuations within 1 percentage point between adjacent steps as signal: the number of questions included in the statistics is only one to two thousand to more than four thousand (varies by step), and the lower bound of sampling noise is on the order of 0.5~1 percentage point; see the dynsam/num_measurable entry for the specific estimate.

Judging that 'the model really got stronger' requires corroborating evidence: dynsam/agg_turn/mean has not decreased in sync (see that entry), indicating that the progress is not bought by 'less trial and error'; offline benchmarks also lag (pro only up to step 15, flash up to step 21), so they cannot immediately cross-validate.
items.observed: pro step 1 0.564662 → step 19 0.633419, up +6.88 percentage points; lowest step 2 0.555333, highest step 16 0.635523. flash step 1 0.513693 → step 25 0.640833, up +12.71 percentage points; lowest step 2 0.496314, highest is the final step 0.640833. Over the same period passrate/one: pro 17.79% → 26.20% (+8.41pp), flash 12.08% → 31.23% (+19.16pp); passrate/zero: pro 14.62% → 13.48% (-1.14pp), flash 16.05% → 14.74% (-1.30pp). That is, within the increase in avg@n, pro's all-wrong share dropped by only 1.14pp (equivalent to 17% of the 6.88pp increase), and flash's dropped by only 1.30pp (equivalent to 10%); the part that can be attributed to "tasks that were originally all wrong starting to be answered correctly" is just that much; the main body comes from tasks that were originally partially correct becoming all-correct every time. A stricter decomposition (identity avg@n = one + middle-bucket share × average pass rate of middle-bucket tasks): pro +8.41pp (one rises) + -4.32pp (middle bucket shrinks, a pure accounting term) + +2.78pp (tasks staying in the middle bucket are themselves also improving; their average pass rate 0.5723 → 0.6158) = +6.88pp, matching the measured value exactly; flash is +19.16 + -10.31 + +3.86 = +12.71pp. The correlations are also consistent: avg@n's correlation coefficient with passrate/one is pro 0.927, flash 0.973, and with passrate/zero only pro -0.477, flash -0.537.
traps: Do not read avg@n as 'task pass rate': it is the mean of per-task proportions; a task with 16 attempts and 8 correct contributes 0.5, and it will be pulled to the middle by a large number of 'half-correct' tasks, so its value is naturally much higher than passrate/one.

It is not the same as passrate in the homepage sampler snapshot (docs/01 section 3.3): that one is the statistics of sequences received so far in the current run; avg@n is the statistics of all prompts trained in this step, and the two generally differ by a few percentage points.

Steps that have been rerun are overwritten: for flash steps 16 and 17, avg@n has two entries each in events; series uses the post-rerun values (0.602504 → 0.594958, 0.585664 → 0.601257). Only trust series, or only trust the last entry for each step number in events; do not mix them.

Do not treat step-to-step differences within 1 percentage point either way as a trend: the denominator differs from step to step (pro 1636~4728), and the lower bound of single-step noise is half to 1 percentage point.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: mean pass rate: for each prompt sampled this step, the fraction of its n attempts that succeed, averaged over prompts
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
sources.quote: Instead, to evaluate pass@k, we generate n >= k samples per task (in this paper, we use n = 200 and k <= 100), count the number of correct samples c <= n which pass unit tests, and calculate the unbiased estimator
sources.topic: Unbiased pass@k estimator and sampling variance
sources.note: By avg@n we mean "sample n times per problem, count the fraction of successes out of n, then average over problems"; the construction logic of this unbiased estimator is exactly the same set: you cannot directly extrapolate the plug-in estimate of pass@1 to k, you must count by "c hits out of n".

sources.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
sources.quote: While RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small k (e.g., k = 1), the base models achieve a higher pass@k score when k is large.
sources.topic: RLVR improves pass@1 but shrinks pass@k coverage
sources.note: This directly corroborates our core reading: avg@n going up (pro +6.88pp / flash +12.71pp) only shows that small k got better; it does not imply the solvable range expanded; looking at avg@n alone reads "coverage shrinkage" as pure progress.

sources.title: When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion
sources.quote: The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups.
sources.topic: The mechanism of the pass@k reversal: boundary prompts and finite rollout groups
sources.note: The abstract states explicitly "after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large k", providing a second independent piece of literature support for "avg@n rises but coverage may narrow".

sources.title: Boosting LLM Exploration via Weak-Model Guidance in RLVR
sources.quote: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) significantly improves LLM reasoning but often causes a drop in policy entropy, leading to narrowed reasoning coverage and degraded pass@k for large k.
sources.topic: Entropy drop → coverage narrowing → pass@k degradation at large k
sources.note: Directly ties "avg@n going up" to "coverage shrinkage": that paper treats entropy drop as a common consequence of RLVR, showing that judging training quality from avg@n alone misses the coverage dimension.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: Empirically, the number of samples with accuracy equal to 1 continues to increase, as shown in Figure 3(b).
sources.topic: All-correct problem share rises monotonically with training
sources.note: That paper treats the growth of the all-correct group as a source of "the number of effective prompts continuously decreasing and batch gradient variance growing", supporting our use of passrate/one rather than avg@n to judge "how many problems have been fully digested".

sources.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
sources.quote: we show that GRPO exhibits a clipping bias from the clip term, which can amplify high-prior behaviors learned during pretraining even without informative rewards.
sources.topic: Bias introduced by the clipping term itself
sources.note: We take the rise in avg@n as evidence that "the model really got stronger"; that paper shows GRPO with random rewards can also raise MATH-500 by 21.4 percentage points (close to the 29.1 points of real rewards), indicating that such a rise may merely be clipping bias amplifying pretrained prior behavior.

sources.title: Pass@k Training for Adaptively Balancing Exploration and Exploitation of Large Reasoning Models
sources.quote: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), which typically adopts Pass@1 as the reward, has faced the issues in balancing exploration and exploitation, causing policies to prefer conservative actions, converging to a local optimum.
sources.topic: Using Pass@1 as the reward leads to coverage shrinkage
sources.note: We assume by default that "improving avg@n" is the only objective; that paper points out that using Pass@1-type metrics as the reward makes the policy favor conservative actions and converge to a local optimum, so the slope of avg@n cannot alone be taken as a conclusion about training quality.

sources.title: Site accounting: the three-term decomposition of avg@n
sources.quote: avg@n = p1 + M·m (p1 all-correct share, M middle pool share, m middle pool average pass rate). pro step 1→19 +6.88pp = all-correct rate +8.41 − middle pool shrinking 4.16 + middle problems getting better 2.62; flash step 1→26 +12.43pp = +17.08 − 8.52 + 3.88, and the three terms added algebraically match the measurement.
sources.topic: Which part is going up
sources.note: The single number avg@n mixes three things: how many problems became fully solved, how many problems went from "partially solved" to "fully solved/not solved at all" and thus left the middle pool, and how much the remaining middle problems improved. Looking only at the total misreads the negative contribution of "middle pool shrinking" as a capability decline.

items.name: Average pass rate after excluding infra failures, avg@n_no_infra
items.what: Nominally the "clean version" of avg@n: attempts that failed for infrastructure reasons (sandbox won't start, network down, grading service down, and the like) are removed from the denominator, and the pass rate is computed only from the attempts that actually ran. The question it answers is "if environment incidents are not counted, what is the model's true level at this step". This metric is in the official 22-item description, and also in the site's formats rules (matches ratio, three decimal places).
items.how: Official definition: avg@n with attempts that failed for infrastructure reasons excluded. Computationally, it replaces the per-question denominator n with 'the number of attempts for that question that returned successfully and were graded', then computes the ratio per question and averages across questions. But there is no data in this repo that can reproduce it: neither the series.json nor tags.json of pro and flash contain this tag (enumerating the dynsam/ prefix gives 83 in total, with only eight scalar tags: agentic/num_accepted/step, agg_turn/mean, avg@n, infra_error/seq_rate, num_measurable, num_target, passrate/one, passrate/zero, while the remaining 75 are num_accepted/* under each dataset). Its peer tags passrate/mid, passrate/zero_no_infra, passrate/one_no_infra, passrate/hist9_ratio all have format definitions in the formats rules, but likewise have no data at all.
items.why: Its purpose is to separate 'model capability' from 'cluster health': when there are many infra incidents, avg@n gets dragged down, while this number does not. The difference between the two is the performance eaten by environmental incidents. In this run, dynsam/infra_error/seq_rate is only 0.27%~3.04%; at this rate, very few attempts are excluded, so even if this curve existed, its difference from avg@n should be a few parts per thousand—if there really is a clear divergence, it means what should be checked is the reporting definition, not the model.
read: Neither run in this repo has this curve, so in the observed below there are no numbers to write—here we can only write "this set of data is not on the dashboard"; do not use the value of avg@n as a substitute for it.

If it is synced later: first look at its difference from avg@n; it is normal for the difference and dynsam/infra_error/seq_rate to amplify in the same direction; only when the difference and seq_rate do not line up does it indicate that the definition of "being judged as an infra failure" and this metric's exclusion criterion are inconsistent.

Do not use it instead of avg@n to judge training progress: excluding infra failures amounts to weighting by "attempts that actually ran"; the samples are no longer a fixed 16, and cross-step comparability is instead worse.

Other unreported metrics of the same kind are dynsam/passrate/mid, passrate/zero_no_infra, passrate/one_no_infra, passrate/hist9_ratio: the formats rule has format definitions, but neither pro nor flash has values (hist_prefix in meta.json points to dynsam/passrate/hist9_ratio/, which is only configuration, not data).
items.observed: There is no data in this repo: pro's tags.json lists 2019 metric names and flash's 2062, of which the dynsam/ prefix has 83 each and does not include avg@n_no_infra; this key also cannot be found in series.json. Among the official 22 notes, it is the 2nd and is not among the 18 pins on the homepage, so the most likely explanation is that the site retains this note and format rule, but neither run currently reports it. The dashboard does not explain why, and I also have not found any history of it appearing in the repo (tags.json's first_seen/last_seen have no record of it).
traps: This is the only one among the required metrics assigned this time for which no data can be found: do not use avg@n or any variant of avg@n to "fill" it.

Do not treat "it is in the description" as "it is on the dashboard": of the 4 metrics in the official descriptions that are not in pins (avg@n_no_infra, ctx_response_length/mean, passrate/hist9_ratio, train/harness/*/training/rollouts), the first two and hist9 have no data under dynsam.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: avg@n with attempts that failed for infrastructure reasons excluded
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

items.name: Share of sequences lost to infrastructure failures (infra_error/seq_rate)
items.what: What proportion of sampled sequences in this step were invalidated due to infrastructure reasons (sandbox failed to start/crashed, network disconnected, scheduling failed, etc.). It measures how dirty the cluster is, not how good or bad the model is: the higher the value, the more rollouts in this step are wasted, and the fewer samples are trained on. Note that it uses a 'sequence' definition (16 per question), not a 'question' definition.
items.how: Official definition: share of sequences lost to infrastructure failures. The denominator is the total number of sequences in this step (configuration says it should be 1568 × 16 = 25088), and the numerator is the number of sequences judged as infra failures. Because a question has 16 independent samples, losing a few parts per thousand of individual sequences will hardly make any question become 'unmeasurable', so it is essentially unrelated to fluctuations in num_measurable (measured correlation coefficient pro -0.299). It is not the same thing as 'restart': restart is an operations action, while this number is a judged failure; values during a restart can still be reported as usual.
items.why: It determines the actual output rate of the rollout, and is also the precondition for 'whether this step's pass rate can be trusted': large-scale infra failures simultaneously depress num_measurable and raise the noise in passrate. A persistently rising seq_rate usually first fills up the sandbox, then lengthens outer_gen, and finally triggers a restart. Its biggest limitation is that it can only count failures 'recognized by the pipeline' — the flash incident in the announcement was exactly 'a type of infra error was not correctly detected'; in that case this curve is low, and the dashboard instead appears clean, so a low value cannot prove health.
read: Look at the magnitude: the normal levels of both runs are in the 0.27%~1.39 range, i.e. 3~9 sequences are lost per 1000 sequences. The absolute value is not large, but this is the "detected" part.

Look at the correspondence between spikes and restarts. pro's highest over the whole run is 0.88% at step 8, and it does not coincide with restart events in the same period; flash's highest point is 3.04% at step 17, which is 5.2 times the full-period median of 0.58%, and it immediately follows the announced occurrence of "infra error was not detected" (see observed).
There is no long-term trend: pro slope 4.18e-5/step (r=0.152), flash 17.95e-5/step (r=0.247); both are flat white noise. Whether the cluster is dirty or not did not worsen over these 19/25 steps.
Use it as a "low value does not mean no problem" metric: the real signal is its co-occurrence with restarts/notices, not its own absolute level.
items.observed: pro: step 1 0.007257 (0.73%) → step 19 0.005518 (0.55%), lowest step 4 0.34%, highest step 8 0.88%, mean 0.59%, median 0.55%, range only 2.6×. flash: step 1 0.005716 (0.57%) → step 25 0.006765 (0.68%), lowest step 5 0.27%, highest step 17 3.04%, mean 0.73%, median 0.58%. flash's shape is worth noting: step 17 3.04%, step 18 1.39%, step 19 1.06% — three consecutive steps higher than all other steps, then falling back to 0.45%–0.85%. It matches the announcement in time: the announcement 'we restarted the flash run from step 15 ... a type of infra error on one of datasets was not correctly detected over the past ~3 hours' was published at 2026-09-17T01:07Z, the restart event was at 02:06Z, and in events, steps 16 and 17 each left a redo=true entry (avg@n 0.602504 → 0.594958, 0.585664 → 0.601257). In other words: during those two or three hours when the failure occurred, this curve was not prominent (the error was not detected); only after it was fixed and rerun did it surge to the period-wide maximum of 3.04% at step 17. The dashboard does not indicate which steps or which dataset were affected, so this can only be a temporal coincidence and cannot establish causality. In addition, flash had two more restarts at the end (2026-09-18T02:49Z, 05:09Z, both before step 25) with no corresponding announcement in notices.json.
traps: The sequence scope is not the task scope: the normal seq_rate is only three to nine per thousand (0.3%~0.9%); spread over 16 samples per task, there will almost never be an entire task completely lost, so do not use it to explain fluctuations in num_measurable.

A low value does not mean the cluster is healthy. The very characteristic of flash's failure was "not correctly detected", so this curve was low during that period. To judge operational status, look at notices.json and events.json together.

It is the proportion of sequences judged as failed, not "loss caused by restarts"; restart waiting is not counted in any step (timing_s/step also does not include it), and the two things must be looked at separately.

pro's 9 restarts have no obvious correspondence with its highs and lows (the highest point, 0.88% at step 8, falls on a normal step between two restarts), indicating that many restarts do not equal high infra_error.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts.
sources.topic: Dynamic sampling: discard all-correct/all-wrong (zero-advantage) groups
sources.note: Dynamic sampling must 'keep sampling until the batch is fully filled'; any invalidation/failure on the sampling side will fall into this set of counts; however, that article only states that the sampling cost is dynamic, and does not define our kind of metric definition for 'the proportion of detected infra failure sequences'.

items.name: Number of problems with a measurable pass rate (denominator of passrate)
items.what: How many problems in this step have a computed and passed 'measurable pass rate', i.e. the denominator of dynsam/passrate/zero, passrate/one (and the unreported mid/hist9). It is not 'how many problems this step has', but 'how many problems have grading results sufficient to be counted in'. It fluctuates substantially at every step, and is the figure in this group that most needs to be clarified first.
items.how: Official definition: prompts with a measurable pass rate this step; per data source under dynsam/<source>/num_measurable. That is, the official claim is that under each data source there is another layer dynsam/<source>/num_measurable that can be broken out, but neither run in this repository has this layer (enumerating the dynsam/ prefix gives 83 tags, with only 8 scalar metrics and 25 datasets × num_accepted/{step,held,carryover}). Another fixed quantity is dynsam/num_target, which for both runs is exactly 1568 at every step, exactly equal to totals.prompts_per_step in status.json (docs/01 records target=1568 in /live, meaning the target number of prompts per step).
items.why: It determines how credible those passrate curves are. A difference of the same 1 percentage point is not the same thing on 1600 problems as on 4700 problems; and when this number changes by a factor of 2~3, the composition of the problems entering the statistics has almost certainly changed too, so the rise and fall of passrate is mixed with a 'this batch of problems has been swapped for another' component. When doing cross-step comparisons, plotting trends, or computing correlation coefficients, it is the confounder most easily overlooked. It is itself also a readout of sampler workload: how many problems were processed in total this step to make up the training batch.
read: First look at its ratio to num_target, not the absolute value. num_target is constant at 1568, while num_measurable is greater than it throughout: pro ratio 1.04~3.02×, flash 1.23~2.79×. The two numbers are not a "target / achieved" relationship, and the dashboard doesn't give the formula either.

It is very well synchronized with dynsam/agentic/num_accepted/step (correlation coefficient pro 0.958, flash 0.925), and the ratio of the two is stable throughout at pro 1.63~2.04, flash 1.51~2.06. It looks closer to the total "how many problems were processed in this step to make up the batch", rather than "how many problems were graded".

Don't attribute its fluctuation to infra dropping sequences: infra_error/seq_rate is no more than 3.04% throughout, and the probability magnitude of all 16 attempts of one problem being dropped is 0.008^16 (about 10^-33); infra incidents simply cannot produce a 2.9× jump. Its changes mainly come from the sampling/accepted definition itself.

Before comparing passrate across steps, at least use its delta to estimate the noise: under the same true pass rate, as the denominator goes from 1636 to 4728, the standard error of the proportion estimate goes from 0.52pp to 0.88pp at p≈0.15.
items.observed: pro step 1 4040 → step 19 2081, lowest at step 16 1636 (smallest over the whole period), highest at step 15 4728 (largest over the whole period), range 2.89×, mean 2915, median 2756; regression slope against step number is only -3.4/step, r=-0.024, i.e. no trend, only up-and-down jumps. flash step 1 3642 → step 25 4281, lowest at step 5 1924, highest at step 16 4380, range 2.28×, mean 2731, median 2491, slope 24.0/step, r=0.261. Largest jump between adjacent steps: pro step 15 4728 → step 16 1636 (difference -3092, dropping to the lowest over the whole period), flash step 15 2443 → step 16 4380 (difference +1937, surging to the highest over the whole period). num_target for both runs is 1568 throughout. The data also shows no synchronization between dataset additions/removals and it: pro step 15 is exactly the step at which the announcement 'remove the cyber dataset from pro's next round' took effect (cyber's num_accepted is all null from step 15 onward, leaving only the first 14 steps), while its num_measurable is instead the highest over the whole period.
traps: It is the denominator of passrate/*, not passrate itself. When you see passrate jump, first check num_measurable for this step, then discuss the model.

num_measurable > num_target and the ratio fluctuates, which indicates the two have different definitions; don't use num_measurable − num_target as "extra problems", and don't divide by num_target as an achievement rate.

The official documentation mentions that under each data source there is dynsam/<source>/num_measurable, but this repository doesn't have this layer; therefore its fluctuation cannot be broken down to data source locally, and I can't give a conclusion on exactly what is changing.
It and dynsam/agg_turn/mean have different denominator definitions (docs/01 section 8, pitfall 7); dividing the two is meaningless.

sources.quote: prompts with a measurable pass rate this step; per data source under dynsam/<source>/num_measurable
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
sources.quote: Instead, to evaluate pass@k, we generate n >= k samples per task (in this paper, we use n = 200 and k <= 100), count the number of correct samples c <= n which pass unit tests, and calculate the unbiased estimator
sources.topic: Unbiased pass@k estimator and sampling variance
sources.note: The paper's original wording points out that directly computing pass@k 'can have high variance', and therefore requires sampling n>=k times per problem; this supports our treating num_measurable (1636~4728 problems per step) as a source of the lower bound on single-step pass rate noise.

sources.title: Calculation on this site: training token count per step = 1568 × 16 × context length
sources.quote: perf/total_num_tokens ≈ 1568×16×ctx_total_length/mean, pro's maximum relative error over 19 steps is 1.2%, flash's maximum is 2.7%. From this, each prompt is inferred to be sampled 16 times.
sources.topic: How the sampling count is derived
sources.note: Once n=16 is collected, the standard error of passrate can be calculated: at p≈0.15, the standard error of 16 samples is about 0.52~0.88pp. Do not read two-step differences below this magnitude as signal.

items.name: Per-step prompt target count num_target
items.what: The prompt target value for how many questions this step intends to sample. In this round, both runs have every step exactly equal to 1568, exactly consistent with totals.prompts_per_step in status.json, i.e. the 1568 in 「1,568 × 16 seqs」 written on the dashboard. It is a configuration constant, not a measurement result, so the curve is a straight line.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide a separate official explainer for dynsam/num_target (it is not among the 22), but it can be cross-checked from two places: status.json's totals.prompts_per_step = 1568, the /live snapshot recorded in docs/01 where target: 1568 is annotated 「= prompts_per_step」, and the verified relation perf/total_num_tokens = 1568 × 16 × ctx_total_length/mean. The unit is 「questions」, and multiplying by 16 gives the target sequence count for this step, 25088, which exactly equals totals.trained_step = 25088 in status.json (and trained_cum = 25088 × step count).
items.why: It is the yardstick for understanding other count-type metrics: num_measurable, agentic/num_accepted, and each dataset's num_accepted all need to be compared against it to know 「how much this step processed and how much was kept」. It is also the basis for judging 「whether the training batch has changed」—as long as it does not move, avg@n's same-step comparison is comparable; if it ever changes, all previous step-wise comparisons must be recalibrated.
read: It should be seen as a straight line. pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, all values are 1568, not changed once; any value other than 1568 means the site changed the configuration and is worth noting separately.
The ratio to num_measurable is not an achievement rate: num_measurable is greater than it throughout (pro 1.04~3.02×), and the two have different definitions.
It is the source of 16: 1568 × 16 = 25088; the number of sequences trained in this step is fixed; that is, the n=16 in avg@n is a configuration constant, not adaptively derived.

The "target" broken down by data source has appeared in the ds of /live (a group of [accepted, target, ?, remaining] per dataset), but there is no corresponding per-source target tag in the repository's series, so it cannot be checked by dataset.
items.observed: pro: all 19 steps are 1568 (no change). flash: all 25 steps are 1568 (no change). The accompanying status.json snapshot: in pro's totals, prompts_per_step=1568, trained_step=25088, trained_cum=476672 (= 25088 × 19); flash's trained_step=25088, trained_cum=627200 (= 25088 × 25). Meanwhile, the actually measurable number of questions per step, num_measurable, is 1636~4728 for pro and 1924~4380 for flash, always higher than the target value, indicating that 「target」 and 「measurable」 are not counts at the same level.
traps: This is a configuration constant, not a performance metric; don't plot it in trend analysis; its change only means the training configuration changed.
Don't use num_measurable / num_target as "completion degree": the ratio is 1.04~3.02 throughout (pro), always greater than 1.

trained_step = 1568 × 16 is the sequence count from the “training perspective”; train/harness/*/training/rollouts all together add up to about 22k. The two use different accounting conventions, so it is normal that they do not match (docs/01 Section 8, Pitfall 7).

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts.
sources.topic: Dynamic sampling: discard all-correct/all-wrong (zero-advantage) groups
sources.note: The paper's constraint 「keeping a consistent number of prompts」 explains why in this run num_target is identically 1568 (a configuration constant) while num_measurable fluctuates between 1636~4728: the former is the filled target slots, the latter is the number of questions actually processed during filtering.

items.name: Share of all-correct questions passrate/one
items.what: Of all the questions sampled in this step, what proportion succeeded in all 16 attempts. It measures the proportion of 「questions the model has completely mastered」, and together with dynsam/passrate/zero divides the questions into three blocks: 「all wrong / partially correct / all correct」. Note the difference between it and passrate/zero: zero is the lower bound of difficulty, one is the stock that has already been fully digested, and the middle block is the part the current training is actually chewing on.
items.how: Official definition: share of prompts where every attempt succeeded. The denominator is likewise dynsam/num_measurable; the numerator is the number of prompts where all 16 attempts succeeded, and the format matches the pct rule. It is also the term with the largest weight in the identity decomposition of avg@n: avg@n = one + mid bucket proportion × average pass rate of mid-bucket prompts, so the trend of one almost determines the trend of avg@n.
items.why: It is a direct reading of 'how much the model has mastered', more conservative and cleaner than avg@n: a prompt does not count if it fails even once. The most common bad shape in late RL training is one spiking then stalling—indicating that the remaining prompts are either all wrong or always just a little short; another is one rising while zero also rises (the prompt composition is changing), which is not pure progress. In dynamic sampling it also determines where compute goes: prompts with high one no longer need repeated sampling.
read: It is the largest single change in this run. pro rose from 17.79% to 26.20% (+8.41pp), flash from 12.08% to 31.23% (+19.16pp); slopes are pro 0.00638/step (r=0.961) and flash 0.00744/step (r=0.981), the best-fit regression line in this group.

Look at the growth trend in two segments: pro is flat at 17%~18% for steps 1~5, jumps to 20.8% at step 6 and then rises slowly, reaching 26%~28% at steps 15~19; flash is almost a straight-line climb all the way, with no plateau in between.

Read together with avg@n: one rises +8.41pp while avg@n rises only +6.88pp (pro); the difference in between consists of two terms—an accounting offset of -4.32pp caused by the shrinking middle bucket, plus +2.78pp from the problems remaining in the middle bucket improving on their own. Problems in the middle bucket becoming all-correct both add to one and subtract themselves from the middle bucket, so the net effect is not equal to the rise in one.

Read together with zero: one rises and zero does not fall, indicating that the improvement happens on the “half-known” problems, rather than turning problems it cannot do into ones it can. This is both good news (the learning signal is effective) and a hint that the next thing to care about is attribution for those 13%~17% all-wrong problems.
items.observed: pro: step 1 0.177866 (17.79%) → step 19 0.261996 (26.20%), up +8.41pp; lowest step 2 17.05%, highest step 18 28.28%. flash: step 1 0.120756 (12.08%) → step 25 0.312340 (31.23%), up +19.16pp; the lowest is the first step at 12.08%, the highest is the last step at 31.23%, and among the 25 steps there are only 8 small pullbacks, with an overall one-way upward trend. Comparing the two runs: flash's one increase is 2.28 times pro's, but flash starts lower (12.08% vs 17.79%) and overtakes by the last step (31.23% vs 26.20%)—the small model's number of 'fully mastered prompts' increases faster in this run. Over the same period passrate/zero barely moved (-1.14pp / -1.30pp), while avg@n rose +6.88pp / +12.71pp.
traps: Do not treat one as another way of writing avg@n: one is the proportion of all-correct problems, avg@n is the mean of per-problem proportions; in this run avg@n (0.633 / 0.641) is consistently higher than one (0.262 / 0.312), and the difference is the contribution of the middle bucket.

A large rise in one does not mean that many more problems were “learned”: a smaller middle bucket makes one rise, but those problems were half-known to begin with, and before being counted into one they were already contributing partial pass rate. Use the decomposition in the observed field of this item to see clearly what is moving.

The denominator likewise changes at every step (num_measurable 1636~4728); flash step 16 has the largest denominator over the whole period (4380), and it happens to be one of the steps that were rerun, so be extra careful when reading that segment.

The 9-bucket histogram (passrate/hist9_ratio) has no data in the repository, so it is impossible to see whether the “half-known” part is internally 1/16 or 7/16—this layer can only be inferred using the mean of 1 − zero − one.

sources.title: Boosting LLM Exploration via Weak-Model Guidance in RLVR
sources.quote: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) significantly improves LLM reasoning but often causes a drop in policy entropy, leading to narrowed reasoning coverage and degraded pass@k for large k.
sources.topic: Entropy drop → coverage narrowing → pass@k degradation at large k
sources.note: We write that a rise in passrate/one represents 'the model has fully mastered more prompts'; that paper suggests the same process (entropy decreasing, coverage narrowing) also raises one, so a one-way rise in one alone is not sufficient to prove capability expansion.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: Empirically, the number of samples with accuracy equal to 1 continues to increase, as shown in Figure 3(b).
sources.topic: All-correct problem share rises monotonically with training
sources.note: Directly corresponds to the one-way rise in one we observed (pro 17.79%→26.20%, flash 12.08%→31.23%): public work also treats 'more and more samples with accuracy=1' as a normal state of training and uses it to argue for the necessity of dynamic sampling.

sources.title: Site accounting: the three-term decomposition of avg@n
sources.quote: avg@n = p1 + M·m (p1 all-correct share, M middle pool share, m middle pool average pass rate). pro step 1→19 +6.88pp = all-correct rate +8.41 − middle pool shrinking 4.16 + middle problems getting better 2.62; flash step 1→26 +12.43pp = +17.08 − 8.52 + 3.88, and the three terms added algebraically match the measurement.
sources.topic: Which part is going up
sources.note: The all-correct proportion is the only one among these three items that consistently contributes the largest single share (pro +8.41 / flash +17.08 percentage points); it is the main engine of the rise in avg@n.

items.name: All-wrong prompt proportion passrate/zero
items.what: Of all prompts sampled at this step, what proportion had none of the 16 attempts succeed. It measures 'how many prompts the model completely cannot solve', and is the lower-bound scale for the difficulty of this batch of prompts. Its counterpart is dynsam/passrate/one (the proportion where every attempt succeeds), and the middle part is what the site documentation calls the mid bucket (the proportion whose pass rate is neither 0 nor 1, equal to 1 − zero − one).
items.how: Official definition: share of prompts where no attempt succeeded. The denominator is the number of tasks in this step that 'have a measurable pass rate', i.e. dynsam/num_measurable; the numerator is the number of those where all 16 attempts failed. Format follows the pct rule (multiply by 100 and append a percent sign). The same family also includes passrate/one and the unreported passrate/mid and passrate/hist9_ratio (splitting tasks into nine buckets by pass rate).
items.why: It is a measure of 'how many hard problems remain', and also the basis for whether the dynamic sampler should keep spending compute on a given task: all-wrong tasks contribute negative-sample information to the policy gradient, and tasks that stay all-wrong over the long term are either beyond its ability or have problems with grading/the environment. There are usually three explanations for why it won't come down—the task itself is too hard, the reward signal is too sparse (no positive feedback in any of the 16 attempts), or bad tasks got mixed into the data—and distinguishing them requires combining passrate/one and per-source counts. It is also the most stable number in this run: both runs stay pinned at 13%~17% throughout, barely moving.
read: Check whether it is really declining. Regress on step number: pro slope -0.0392pp/step, r=-0.285; flash slope -0.0489pp/step, r=-0.392. |r| is below 0.4 in both cases, meaning that over 19 steps / 25 steps it is essentially flat, with only a slight downward trend.

Look at its absolute level. Both sides are stable at 13%~17%, meaning that out of every 6~7 problems, 1 is one the model gets wrong in all 16 attempts. This “all-wrong floor” has not narrowed with training, and is key to understanding where the rise in avg@n comes from (see dynsam/avg@n).

For single-step jumps, first look at the denominator. The largest adjacent swing for pro over the whole period is step 18 16.26% → step 19 13.48% (-2.78pp); the denominators for these two steps are 3576 and 2081; at p≈0.15, the standard error of the difference between the two steps is about 0.98pp, and this swing is about 3 times the standard error—it is not yet a clear signal.
It is weakly negatively correlated with avg@n: pro r=-0.477, flash r=-0.537. That is, the vast majority of the variation in avg@n cannot be explained by the all-wrong rate.
items.observed: pro: step 1 0.146245 (14.62%) → step 19 0.134837 (13.48%), down only 1.14pp; over the whole run 12.91% (step 16) ~ 16.26% (step 18), mean 14.77%. flash: step 1 0.160460 (16.05%) → step 25 0.147422 (14.74%), down only 1.30pp; over the whole run 13.56% (step 19) ~ 16.94% (step 7), mean 15.50%. Over the same period avg@n rose +6.88pp (pro) / +12.71pp (flash), 6.0× / 9.8× the drop in zero. In other words: this run of training basically did not turn tasks where all 16 attempts failed into ones it can do; the all-wrong floor stayed at 13%~17% throughout.
traps: Don't treat the drop in zero as the main credit: it only dropped 1.14pp / 1.30pp, and the maximum explainable increase in avg@n is less than 20%.
The denominator changes at every step (pro 1636~4728), and the magnitude of the change (2.9 times) is far greater than zero's own variation; confirm the denominator before comparing across steps.

zero plus one does not equal 1: there is still a large block in between (pro step 1 67.59%, step 19 60.32%), and its order of magnitude is similar to zero. Focusing only on zero will severely misjudge the difficulty structure.

Grading-failed attempts cannot be distinguished from true failures in this data; if the grading service has problems for some period, zero will falsely rise. The dashboard does not explain how this layer is handled.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: share of prompts where no attempt succeeded
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
sources.quote: While RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small k (e.g., k = 1), the base models achieve a higher pass@k score when k is large.
sources.topic: RLVR improves pass@1 but shrinks pass@k coverage
sources.note: The paper says that when k is large the base model overtakes the RLVR model, indicating that the outer edge of the portion that 'gets all 16 wrong' will not disappear with training, which is consistent with our empirically measured reading of a 'capability wall' where zero drops only 1.14pp / 1.30pp.

sources.title: When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion
sources.quote: The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups.
sources.topic: The mechanism of the pass@k reversal: boundary prompts and finite rollout groups
sources.note: We read zero as 'how many tasks the model completely cannot do', and that paper points out that one category among them is a boundary prompt: the base model contains rare correct trajectories, but they are too sparse to be sampled in a finite rollout group, so zero is mixed with a component of sampling limitation and cannot be fully attributed to capability.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: A zero advantage results in zero policy gradients, shrinking the magnitude and increasing the noise sensitivity of the batch gradient, thereby degrading sample efficiency.
sources.topic: Why zero-advantage groups must be discarded
sources.note: That paper treats zeroing the advantage of the accuracy=1 group as a source of degradation; similarly, in all-wrong groups the within-group rewards are identical and the advantage is also 0, so steps with high zero are simultaneously steps where 'effective gradients are diluted', supporting our reading that zero should not be treated merely as a difficulty scale.

sources.title: Pass@k Training for Adaptively Balancing Exploration and Exploitation of Large Reasoning Models
sources.quote: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), which typically adopts Pass@1 as the reward, has faced the issues in balancing exploration and exploitation, causing policies to prefer conservative actions, converging to a local optimum.
sources.topic: Using Pass@1 as the reward leads to coverage shrinkage
sources.note: That paper uses Pass@k as a reward to improve exploration, which can serve as a public solution reference for the hypothesis that 'an all-wrong floor that does not move is actually insufficient exploration', but it does not directly validate the zero curve of our run.

sources.title: Site accounting: the three-term decomposition of avg@n
sources.quote: avg@n = p1 + M·m (p1 all-correct share, M middle pool share, m middle pool average pass rate). pro step 1→19 +6.88pp = all-correct rate +8.41 − middle pool shrinking 4.16 + middle problems getting better 2.62; flash step 1→26 +12.43pp = +17.08 − 8.52 + 3.88, and the three terms added algebraically match the measurement.
sources.topic: Which part is going up
sources.note: No matter how much the all-correct proportion rises, it may just be 'tasks it already could do being sampled repeatedly'. To judge whether the capability wall has moved, you have to look at the all-wrong proportion at the other end: pro dropped only 1.14pp, flash dropped only 1.49pp, and after 26 steps more than one-tenth of prompts still had not gotten a single correct attempt.

items.name: Batch composition table · rollout counts broken down by harness
items.what: The second preset table in batch composition: breaks down by train/harness/<harness>/training/rollouts how many rollouts each agent harness contributed; share and Δ share are as before. Switching the option in the "by" dropdown changes to a different composition breakdown, but the table structure is the same.
items.how: Directly take the series under that prefix, take the value at the last step and sort by size; when there are more than 8 sources, plot only the top 7 and merge the rest into a single row other. Implementation see the original site's app.js renderMetricComposition.
items.why: The harness data mix determines which agent forms are trained on at this step; a certain harness suddenly increasing or disappearing usually corresponds to changes in training configuration or environment availability.
read: The other row is a merge of multiple sources, not a single real source; don't read it as a separate category.
The unit is rollouts, not prompts: one problem can produce multiple rollouts, so the total of this table does not equal 1568.
share is comparable only within the current step; for cross-step comparison, look at Δ share or go to #metrics to see the series.
items.observed: pro step 27 has a total of 22 harnesses and 21593 rollouts: harness-C 3597 (16.7%), harness-A 3480 (16.1%), harness-B 3418 (15.8%), harness-D 3389 (15.7%) lead; harness-H 2454 (11.4%); the remaining 17 are all below 5% (smallest harness-P 96, 0.4%).
traps: The total is the number of rollouts, not the number of problems, and has no direct equality relationship with the batch size 1568.
The table lists only the first 7 sources; the rest are merged into other, so the individual values of long-tail harnesses cannot be seen.

sources.venue: Telemetry repository docs/01 and site/js/app.js (copy of the original site at data/upstream/js/app.js)

items.name: Batch composition table · training task count broken down by category
items.what: The first table of batch composition under dynamic sampler: one row per category, prompts is the number of tasks actually trained into this step, share is the proportion, Δ share is the difference from the previous step's proportion (unit pt).
items.how: The numbers in the table are not given directly by the API; they are inferred on the page using sampler counts: for each data source, compute held(previous step) + accepted(this step) − held(this step), then sum to the category; if this sum differs from the training batch size by more than 5%, then it is determined that this step immediately follows a restart and the pool counts were reported before consumption, fall back to the estimate of "carryover + apportion new accepted in proportion to accepted amount", and mark a ≈ in the table header. Implementation see renderTrainedComposition in the original site's app.js.
items.why: The category mix of the training batch determines which capability is being trained at this step; the mix is changed by the data recipe, not chosen by the model itself, so when it changes, look first at the recipe and the announcement.
read: The step where ≈ appears in the header is an estimated value, not an actual measurement; don't compare it strictly with other steps.
The sum of the prompts column should equal the training batch for this step (1568); if it doesn't match, it means this step hit the estimation branch.
Δ share looks at the change in proportion (pt), not the change in number of problems; the proportion can also move when the total number of problems hasn't changed.
The sources column is the number of data sources under that category, not the number of problems.
items.observed: pro step 27: code 1061 tasks (67.7%, 11 sources), visual 270 tasks (17.2%, 6 sources), general 190 tasks (12.1%, 4 sources), chat 47 tasks (3.0%, 3 sources), cyber 0 tasks (pro has removed this dataset), total 1568.
traps: The step after a restart is an estimate, not an actual measurement; only when the header does not have ≈ can it be used as an exact value.
This table renders only the latest step and has no history; to see historical proportions, go to #metrics and look at the series for dynsam/<source>/num_accepted.
cyber has 0 rows on pro but not on flash; when comparing category proportions across runs, first confirm that the row sets are consistent.

items.name: Sampler table · accepted / target columns (accepted count / quota)
items.what: accepted is the number of tasks accepted from that data source into this round's sampling at this snapshot moment; target is the quota allocated to it, and added up row by row it is identically equal to this step's training batch task count (1568).
items.how: The first two fields of the latest.ds quadruple from the /live endpoint, rendered on the page as "accepted / target"; the upper limit of the ratio bar in between is 100%. This site verified all archives one by one with sampler_report.ts (29 in total as of 2026-09-20): Σaccepted equals the accept on the panel (29/29), Σtarget equals the target on the panel and also equals 1568 (29/29). The site gives no text explanation for this layer; mechanism-wise the closest public material is the Data Scheduler in the MiMo-V2-Flash technical report: each data source has an independent sample quota, and the accepted count is determined by the pass rate and the configured ratio.
items.why: Accepted count above quota means extra sampling was done to make up "effective samples with gradient"; below quota means this source did not supply enough at this step. Dynamic sampling filters out full-score and zero-score tasks; as training progresses there are more and more full-score tasks, so the batch has to be filled by over-sampling — public material calls this extra sampled amount sample waste.
read: First look at the overall accept/target: if it is clearly greater than 1 over the long term, it means most sources in this step are oversupplying; only if it is less than 1 over the long term do you need to worry about the batch not being filled.

Look row by row at who is oversupplying: if one row oversupplies over the long term and another is short over the long term, it is usually not a coincidence, but a mismatch between quota and difficulty distribution.

accepted is an intra-step process quantity: it rises all the way as sampling proceeds; in the same archived record, values from 0.031 to 1.755 have appeared, so don't take a single point as a stable feature.
target is a quota, not an upper limit; oversupply is part of the design, not a data error.
items.observed: Latest pro archive accept 1840 / target 1568: of the 24 rows, 23 are over quota, 1 is exactly at quota, 0 are under; the largest overage is code/dataset-sin0 (192 / 154). Putting the 17 pro archives together, accept/target is at its lowest 0.031 (the step right after a restart) and at its highest 1.755. Both runs' Σtarget is 1568, so target cannot be used to compare the scale of the two runs.
traps: accepted is a process snapshot, not the final training volume for this step: it is usually greater than the dynsam/<source>/num_accepted/step for the same step in the series (e.g., pro step 23 snapshot 2160, end-of-step series 1865).
Treating accepted as the 'number of graded problems' is wrong: the third value is the grading column, and it is only reported for some data sources.
The sum of target on both runs is the same (1568), so 'a certain source's target on pro is larger than on flash' does not mean pro has a larger scale; it only means the quota allocation is different.

sources.title: This site's reconciliation: the summation identity of the sampler quadruple (all archives)
sources.quote: The recompute script sampler_report.ts verifies item by item the sampler archive of data/store/runs/<run>/live.jsonl (pro 18 / flash 11): Σaccepted == panel accept 29/29; Σtarget == panel target == 1568 29/29; judged_of == accept 29/29; Σ(in flight) == panel remain + remain_partial, max difference 2; the third number (labeled judged on the page) appears only on the 8 code data sources, and all 232 non-empty values satisfy c <= accepted; the hardest one is the exact decomposition of panel judged: Σc(reporting sources) + Σaccepted(non-reporting sources) == panel judged (29/29), equivalently accept − judged == Σ(accepted − c), and the gap comes only from those 8 reporting sources.
sources.topic: Which relations in the table are identities, and which hold only on some data sources
sources.note: The two identities Σaccepted and Σtarget hold on all archives, which is the data basis for reading this column.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report (§4.6.2 Data Scheduler: sampling quotas by data source)
sources.quote: The Data Scheduler supports data source-specific configurations (sample quota, scheduling priority, length limits, temperature) and fits pass rates to accept samples by configured ratios.
sources.topic: Each data source has an independent sampling quota; the accepted amount is determined by the pass rate and configured ratio.
sources.note: Public materials confirm that 'each data source has a sample quota and accepts by pass rate and ratio', consistent with one quota per row in this column.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts.
sources.topic: Dynamic sampling: discard all-correct/all-wrong (zero-advantage) groups
sources.note: DAPO describes the mechanism of oversampling then filtering; here only the result that the accepted amount exceeds the quota can be seen, not the filtering threshold.

sources.title: MiMo: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of Language Model -- From Pretraining to Posttraining (Table 2: Definition of Sample Waste Ratio)
sources.quote: Sample Waste Ratio represents the ratio of excess valid samples generated relative to the required batch size.
sources.topic: The proportion of extra valid samples collected relative to the batch requirement: accepted samples will exceed the target quota.
sources.note: The proportion of extra valid samples collected relative to the batch is the quantitative measure for 'accepted amount exceeds target' on this panel.

sources.title: mimo.xiaomi.com/rl official announcement: filter out problems that are too easy for the current model
sources.quote: we filtered out tasks that are relatively easy for the current pro model.
sources.topic: The official direct explanation that 'easy problems will be filtered out'
sources.note: The site announcement directly says 'filter out problems that are too easy for the current model'; this is the direct reason why the accepted amount exceeds the quota and further collection is needed.

sources.title: Third-party study notes: Xiaomi puts the RL training process on livestream (field-by-field version)
sources.quote: On the right is a real-time table broken down by data source: 25 data sources (all names hashed, such as code/dataset-obg8, visual/dataset-gtav, cyber/dataset-9aui, chat/dataset-8kb6), and for each source, what the current accepted / target / remaining / judged / in flight values are. You can see in real time which data pool is nearly exhausted and which source's samples are still running in the sandbox.
sources.topic: The only public material so far that explains this table field by field, but the author himself notes that it is an interpretation read from the page, not an official explanation
sources.note: Third-party study notes read this behavior as 'first accept in excess, then trim by group ratio'; this is an external interpretation, not an official explanation, and this site only treats it as corroborating evidence.

items.name: Sampler table · in flight column (in-flight amount)
items.what: The column name in flight also comes from the original site's rendering code and is reported by data source. The strongest relation this site can verify is: the per-source sum of this column is identically equal to remain + remain_partial at the top of the panel.
items.how: Checked all archived records one by one (as of 2026-09-20, 29 total): the maximum difference between Σ(in flight) and the panel's remain + remain_partial is 2 (synchronization rounding level). In the panel feed, pending work is written as 'remaining X +Y partial +Z rewarding'; this column corresponds to the sum of the first two buckets.
items.why: Dynamic sampling does not wait for all rollouts to finish before grading; it grades while replenishing. After a batch is gathered, it terminates in-flight tasks in FIFO order. So the in-flight count is a direct readout of 'how much longer this step has to wait'.
read: First look at the shape of the total within the step: normally it rises first and then falls as sampling proceeds, and dries up at the end of the step.
If the total does not drop for a long time, it means there are long-tail tasks that haven't returned, usually corresponding to this step taking longer.
It is not in a complementary relationship with accepted: adding the two is meaningless, don't subtract it from target.
This column does not include the part carried across steps by partial rollout; don't count the cross-step long tail as part of this step.
items.observed: In the 9 archived records for pro step 15, Σ(in flight) = 1066 → 1203 → 1474 → 1530 → 1545 → 1537 → 1326 → 861 → 720, rising first and then falling; the 4 archived records for flash step 20 are 2956 → 2073 → 1162 → 640, draining all the way. The latest pro archived record has Σ = 1594, and at the same moment remain + remain_partial = 1593.
traps: Don't equate it with the remain listed separately on the panel: it is the sum of the two buckets remain + remain_partial.
The same column varies greatly between different snapshots; the difference between two adjacent snapshots cannot be directly treated as a trend.
The counting unit (tasks or sequences) is not publicly specified; only the aggregate relationship and within-step shape are given here.
