sources.quote: The recompute script sampler_report.ts verifies item by item the sampler archive of data/store/runs/<run>/live.jsonl (pro 18 / flash 11): Σaccepted == panel accept 29/29; Σtarget == panel target == 1568 29/29; judged_of == accept 29/29; Σ(in flight) == panel remain + remain_partial, max difference 2; the third number (labeled judged on the page) appears only on the 8 code data sources, and all 232 non-empty values satisfy c <= accepted; the hardest one is the exact decomposition of panel judged: Σc(reporting sources) + Σaccepted(non-reporting sources) == panel judged (29/29), equivalently accept − judged == Σ(accepted − c), and the gap comes only from those 8 reporting sources.
sources.topic: Which relations in the table are identities, and which hold only on some data sources
sources.note: Across all archived records, the maximum difference for Σ(in flight) = remain + remain_partial is 2.

sources.title: MiMo: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of Language Model -- From Pretraining to Posttraining (§3.4.1 Early Termination: terminate in-flight tasks in FIFO order after a batch is gathered)
sources.quote: We terminate ongoing tasks only if the valid sample count meets the batch requirement and all tasks initiated prior to these selected samples have completed.
sources.topic: After valid samples meet the batch requirement, terminate in-flight tasks in FIFO order: the in-flight count drains at the end of the step
sources.note: Terminating in-flight tasks in FIFO order after a batch is gathered explains this column's draining behavior at the end of the step.

sources.title: MiMo: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of Language Model -- From Pretraining to Posttraining (§3.4.1 Seamless Rollout Engine: continuous rollout and asynchronous grading)
sources.quote: After computing rewards, we update the number of valid samples and the current step's pass-rate statistics, then launch new rollout tasks if active tasks are insufficient to meet training demands based on these statistics.
sources.topic: After grading completes, update the valid sample count and pass-rate statistics, then start additional rollout tasks as needed
sources.note: Grading and sampling overlap, so the in-flight count is an intermediate quantity in the process, not a queue length.

sources.title: This site's calculation: web search did not find the official definitions of these counters
sources.quote: Both the MiMo-7B technical report (arXiv:2505.07608) and the MiMo-V2-Flash technical report (arXiv:2601.02780) only describe the mechanisms of dynamic sampling, per-data-source sample quota, and early termination; they do not define the per-data-source counters accepted/target/judged/in flight; the 22 metric explanations on the mimo.xiaomi.com/rl site also do not include them.
sources.topic: Search gap: the mechanism has literature, the counter definitions do not
sources.note: Public materials do not give the definition of this column; this site only verified the aggregate relationship.

sources.title: QbitAI: Luo Fuli officially announces Xiaomi reinforcement learning, livestreams new model training process (asynchronous pipeline)
sources.quote: Some agents are still executing tasks in the environment, some have already finished and are waiting to be graded, some are computing reward, and new tasks are entering the system. Generation, execution, scoring, and training no longer queue strictly; instead, they form a continuously running asynchronous pipeline.
sources.topic: The asynchronous pipeline behind the sampler panel: tasks are simultaneously in three states: executing / waiting to be graded / computing reward
sources.note: Public reports describe an asynchronous pipeline in which 「executing / awaiting grading / computing reward / new tasks entering」 coexist, which is the mechanistic background for the existence of in-flight volume.

You can see in real time which data pool is nearly exhausted and which source's samples are still running in the sandbox.

sources.note: Third-party study notes read this column as 「samples are still running in the sandbox」; this is an external interpretation, not an official explanation.

items.name: Sampler table · judged column (the site labels it as per-data-source judged count)
items.what: The column name judged for this column comes from the original site's own rendering code. Its meaning can be pinned down by an identity: the judged at the top of the panel is exactly equal to 「the sum of the 8 data sources that report this column + the sum of accepted of the remaining data sources」, with not a single discrepancy across all 29 archived records. That is, for data sources that do not report this column, the panel directly records accepted as already graded.
items.how: Verify with sampler_report.ts: Σc(reporting sources) + Σaccepted(non-reporting sources) == panel judged (29/29); equivalently, accept − judged == Σ(accepted − c), and the gap comes only from those 8 reporting sources. In addition, all 144 + 88 = 232 non-null values satisfy c ≤ accepted, and within one step c increases monotonically with accepted. Other than this, the site has written no explanation for this counter.
items.why: This column shows how far the grading step has progressed. The Seamless Rollout Engine in public materials is 「after grading the reward → update the effective sample count and pass-rate statistics → then open additional rollouts as needed」; if grading cannot keep up, this step cannot start training.
read: Only 8 code data sources report this column (bvg7 / v7yx / dnpn / ta4j / sin0 / obg8 / zg6q / x7wh), and the two runs are exactly the same; the remaining 17 data sources have always been empty.
Empty is not 0, nor does it mean no grading: in the total, the panel records the entire accepted of empty-value sources as graded.
The sum of rows is not equal to the total row: total row = c of reporting sources + accepted of non-reporting sources. Summing rows to check against the total will definitely be short.
Look at c and accepted together: c rises slower than accepted, indicating that grading in this step is chasing sampling.
items.observed: In the 9 archived records for pro step 15, Σc/Σaccepted of the reporting sources rose from 0.879 to 0.965, while the overall panel judged/accept rose from 0.943 to 0.981 over the same period. The latest pro archive: accept 1840, judged 1766, of which the 8 reporting sources have Σc = 870 and the remaining sources have Σaccepted = 896; 870 + 896 = 1766, and the gap of 74 comes entirely from the not-yet-graded portion on the reporting sources.
traps: The easiest place to misread: the judged of the total row is not the row sum of this column; how much the two differ depends on how much the non-reporting sources account for.
Empty is not 0; don't use empty values in summation or averaging.
The column names are assigned by the site, and the identities are recomputed by this site; the unit of this counter (tasks or sequences) is not publicly specified, don't extrapolate.

items.name: Sampler table · remaining column (quota gap)
items.what: A column computed live on the page: remaining = max(0, target − accepted). It is not an API field; the API only provides accepted and target.
items.how: The source is Math.max(0, r.tgt - r.acc) in the original site's app.js, and the telemetry layer did not change this segment. Because it takes max(0, …), as long as the accepted amount reaches or exceeds the quota, this column is identically zero, and no matter how much it exceeds, it will not be negative.
items.why: Used to see at a glance which data sources are still not fully supplied at this step. It is a quota gap, not a workload.
read: 0 has two meanings: exactly fully supplied, or already over quota; only strictly greater than 0 is really not fully supplied.
If a row remains greater than 0 for a long time, it means this source's tasks are insufficient or too hard, and dynamic sampling keeps waiting for it.

Don't confuse it with remain / remain_partial at the top of the panel: the latter are the two buckets of in-flight work across all data sources (see the in flight column), and the definitions are completely different.
items.observed: In the latest pro archive, all 24 rows reach or exceed the quota, and the number of rows >0 is 0; while in the several archives right after restart, it is broadly greater than 0, with the lowest accept/target only 0.031. That is, whether this column "has a value" is basically equivalent to "what stage sampling has reached at this step".
traps: The name collides with remain at the top of the panel, but the two are not the same thing: one computes the quota gap, and the other is pending workload.
This column is computed by the page; if the site changes the rendering code, it will change; the interface fields are only accepted and target.

items.name: Sampler table · source column (data source)
items.what: In the table in the dynamic sampler panel, each row is a data source, and the key name has the form "category/dataset-shortcode". The category comes from the site's categories (code / general / visual / chat / cyber); the shortcode is an internal random id on the site, not the dataset name.
items.how: This column is exactly the key of latest.ds in the /live API. In every sampler snapshot archived on this site (29 total as of 2026-09-20), the set of rows is stable, with no mid-course renaming; the two runs have different row counts: the latest archive has pro 24 rows and flash 25 rows, and the only difference is that pro does not have the cyber row.
items.why: This column answers "who provides the training batch for this step". Only by matching row by row can you see recipe changes; looking only at the totals erases the entire matter of "who has more and who has less". Starting from step 15, pro no longer has a cyber row, corresponding to the official announcement's statement about removing the cyber dataset from pro's next run.
read: The short code is an internal site id; you cannot infer dataset content from the name; to compare, aggregate by category, or directly compare by the same id between the two runs.
The number of rows is not equal to the number of metrics: one data source occupies only one row in the table, and in /series it corresponds to three metric names: num_accepted/step, held, carryover.
The two runs have different row sets, don't align by row number; pro does not have cyber, flash has cyber/dataset-9aui.
items.observed: Latest archived copy: pro 24 rows (code 11 / general 4 / visual 6 / chat 3), flash 25 rows (one extra cyber/dataset-9aui). Same-named data sources appear on both runs, but the magnitudes differ greatly; for example, code/dataset-sin0 has a target of 154, while code/dataset-bvg7 has only 52.
traps: Don't use the dataset short code as a dataset name when searching: it is generated by the site, and the correspondence cannot be found in public materials.
The number of rows (24~25) and the number of tasks in the batch (1568) are not the same dimension; the former is the number of sources, and the latter is the number of tasks.

items.name: Max advantage at this step
items.what: The largest single advantage in this step's training batch, i.e. the trajectory or token that is encouraged most strongly relative to the baseline.
items.how: Takes the maximum over all advantages in the training batch. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name. Pointwise identical to critic/returns/max.
items.why: It determines the peak strength of the positive signal in the gradient. When it is abnormally large, a single sample will take on too much weight in this step's update, pulling the policy in one direction; when it shrinks to near 0, it indicates that no trajectory is significantly better than the baseline, and the positive learning signal disappears. It is also an observation point for 'whether the advantage has been clipped or capped by normalization'.
read: Look at whether the values are discrete. pro's max has only 10 distinct values across 19 steps, among which 1.12617 appears 6 times and 1.32344 appears 4 times, and these values repeat exactly across different steps. This looks very much like discrete tiers determined by within-group rank or pass count after relative normalization grouped by prompt (a group-relative baseline such as GRPO). This is an inference based on data shape; the dashboard does not state it.

Look at its symmetry with min. In this period, the positive side is capped at 1.33216 (pro) / 1.32344 (flash), and the negative side can reach −1.57626 (pro) / −1.66329 (flash); the negative side is 18%~26% deeper than the positive side.
Look at whether it grows without bound. The positive side repeatedly stops around 1.32~1.33, indicating that upstream has a soft cap on positive advantage or has applied normalization.
The two runs share the same set of discrete rubric tiers; this is more informative than a single value.
items.observed: pro range 1.08333~1.33216, minimum 1.08333 appears at steps 3 and 7, maximum 1.33216 at step 15; first value 1.32344, last value 1.26445. flash range is narrower, 1.08333~1.32344, minimum likewise at step 7, maximum 1.32344 repeats across as many as 7 steps (steps 3, 4, 5, 9, 12, 13, 25), first value 1.16071, last value 1.32344. The two runs share the same set of discrete levels: 1.08333, 1.12246, 1.12617, 1.1543, 1.18902, 1.32344 all appear on both sides. flash's 1.12246 appears 5 times, 1.12617 appears 3 times, differing from pro's distribution (1.12617 appears 6 times, 1.32344 appears 4 times).
traps: Do not interpret it as a reward cap. It is larger than the reward upper bound of 1 because it is a normalized advantage, not the raw reward.
The value repeating exactly across different steps (e.g., 1.32344) is not a coincidence, nor a unit error; do not treat it as an anomaly.
Do not use max alone to judge whether training is good or bad; it only describes the single best one within the batch.
It is exactly identical to critic/returns/max, not two independent metrics.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Mean advantage at this step
items.what: The arithmetic mean of the advantages participating in training at this step. Advantage is 'how much better this trajectory is than the baseline'; the sign directly determines whether that trajectory is encouraged or suppressed in this step's update.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation for this tag; translated literally from the tag name. It is measured to be pointwise identical to critic/returns/mean, and advantages/max and returns/max, advantages/min and returns/min are also respectively pointwise identical. If the conventional definition of advantage is 'return minus baseline', then it is anomalous for all three aggregates to be identically equal at the same time. There are two explanations for this shape: baseline is the constant 0 (in which case advantage equals return), or these two tags take the same tensor in the implementation. This is an inference based on the data shape; the dashboard gives no reason, and it should not be taken as a confirmed conclusion.
items.why: It is the main gauge of whether advantage is correctly centered. A healthy mean advantage should oscillate slightly around 0, with positive and negative advantages in the same batch canceling each other out; a persistent unidirectional drift indicates that the baseline estimate has systematic bias, and a constant direction unrelated to specific trajectories will be mixed into the gradient, equivalent to applying indiscriminate pressure to the entire batch of data. If it is biased positive or negative, it will also change the update direction, because positive and negative advantages are not symmetric in the clipped objective.
read: Look at whether it hugs 0. In this run, neither of the two runs hugs 0: pro is negative throughout, and flash turns negative from step 3 and gradually deepens to −0.047.

The magnitude of the mean should be read together with the advantage extremes. The mean is only 0.0x, while the extremes can reach ±1.6, indicating that positive and negative mass largely cancel out within the batch; the remaining imbalance is what this mean reflects.
It completely coincides with returns/mean; do not treat them as two independent pieces of evidence for cross-validation.
flash's drift magnitude is clearly larger than pro's, and this is the same thing as its rising share of negative advantage mass.
items.observed: pro's 19 steps are all negative, range −0.0142034~−0.00115565, first value −0.00336077, last value −0.0043556, deepest at step 14. flash's first two steps are positive (+0.00174863, +0.000117731), turns negative starting at step 3, then all 23 subsequent steps are negative, deepest −0.0466903 at step 19, last value −0.015268. flash's deepest value is approximately 3.29 times pro's deepest value. This is consistent with the same-period advantage quality ratio: pro's |negative advantage|/positive advantage remains in 1.0093~1.1257 throughout, while flash rises from 0.9867 at step 1 to 1.4346 at step 19, and falls back to 1.1524 at the last step.
traps: Its small absolute value does not mean the advantage is small. The extremes are on the order of ±1.6; a small mean is merely the result of positive-negative cancellation.

Do not read it as 「the model is regressing」. It is the net offset within the batch relative to the baseline, affected by baseline construction and data mix, and does not equal a decline in absolute capability.
It is identically equal to returns/mean; writing 「the two are highly correlated」 underestimates this relationship——they are pointwise exactly equal.

sources.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
sources.quote: GRPO foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores, significantly reducing training resources compared to Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
sources.topic: GRPO removes critic: within-group scores as baseline
sources.note: This is direct evidence for 「under the critic/ naming, what is actually installed is reward/advantage computation, with no independent value network」: GRPO uses within-group scores as baseline, and has no value model of the same scale as the policy, so advantages and returns being pointwise equal is not self-contradictory.

sources.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (Dr. GRPO)
sources.quote: Dr. GRPO introduces simple yet significant modifications to address the biases in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), by removing the length and std normalization terms.
sources.topic: Within-group standard deviation normalization is a bias term.
sources.note: Supports the reading 「within-group standard deviation normalization introduces systematic bias」: the paper lists std normalization and length normalization together as GRPO's bias terms and directly removes them, and states that after fixing them unbiased optimization is obtained.

sources.title: Why GRPO Needs Normalization: A Local-Curvature Perspective on Adaptive Gradients
sources.quote: In this work, we provide an explanation through the lens of local curvature of the sequence-level policy gradient: standard deviation normalization implements an adaptive gradient.
sources.topic: The two-sidedness of std normalization (adaptive gradient vs bias)
sources.note: We treat std normalization as 「a systematic bias against low-variance prompts」, whereas that paper proves that it is equivalent to adaptive gradient, that it strictly improves the convergence rate under mild conditions, and that its effect has three phases (the gain disappears when orthogonality is lost in the later phase) — so 「bias」 only holds in specific phases/conditions and cannot be generalized.

sources.title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation
sources.quote: which is simply the empirical returns minus the value function baseline
sources.topic: The limiting form of GAE and the definition of advantage
sources.note: Supports the conventional definition 「advantage = return − baseline」: the A^(k) given in the paper degenerates to empirical return minus baseline as k→∞, which is also the basis for our interpreting the equality of advantages and returns as baseline being identically zero.

items.name: Minimum advantage at this step
items.what: The smallest individual advantage in this step's training batch, that is, the trajectory or token that is suppressed the hardest.
items.how: Takes the minimum over all advantages in the training batch. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name. Pointwise identical to critic/returns/min.
items.why: It determines the peak intensity of the negative signal. When it becomes very deep, it indicates the existence of strongly suppressed samples; when it stays at some artificial lower bound for a long time, it indicates that negative advantages have been clipped or capped by normalization. It is also a confounder that must be ruled out first when judging 「whether the penalty has made the negative side more extreme」, because the scale of the advantage is determined by the baseline construction.
read: See whether it is pinned. pro's lower bound repeatedly appears around −0.93 (−0.929167, −0.929802, −0.931142, −0.93425, −0.935316, etc.), indicating that the negative side being roughly capped around −0.93 is the norm, and deeper values are only exceptions in a few steps.

Look at the frequency and persistence of deep values. flash becomes clearly deeper starting at step 18; all of the last 8 steps are at −1.39 or below, with 7 of them deeper than −1.5; among pro's 19 steps, only steps 14 and 19 are deeper than −1.4.
Compute the positive-negative asymmetry together with max; this is the most robust reading for cross-run comparison.
Do not use it to prove that the penalty is in effect; whether the penalty acts should be checked via penalty/action/* and train/adv_*_sum_*_penalty.
items.observed: pro range −1.57626~−0.929167, deepest −1.57626 at step 14, shallowest −0.929167 at step 15; first value −0.931142, last value −1.49076. flash range −1.66329~−0.92613, deepest −1.66329 at step 21, shallowest −0.92613 at step 7; first value −1.21154, last value −1.39426. flash's last 8 steps (steps 18~25) are −1.5831, −1.6599, −1.65426, −1.66329, −1.6341, −1.5823, −1.60341, −1.39426, staying below −1.4 throughout. The |min|/max asymmetry ratio is 1.1832 for pro and 1.2568 for flash.
traps: Do not treat it as 「the worst reward」. It is a normalized advantage; its magnitude is determined by the scale of the baseline, and it is not the same thing as the reward's −0.8 lower bound.
Do not treat it as evidence that the penalty is in effect. This tag can show deep values both with and without penalty.
Do not directly compare the absolute values of the two runs to judge which is better; flash being deeper may simply be because its baseline scale is larger.
It is exactly identical to critic/returns/min, not two independent metrics.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Mean return at this step
items.what: Arithmetic mean of the returns of this step's training batch. Intuitively, “return” is a global cumulative quantity, typically on the same order of magnitude as reward; but on the dashboard this entry has an absolute value only on the order of thousandths, two orders of magnitude smaller than the mean reward, so what it actually reports looks more like the “residual after removing the baseline” than the raw return.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official description for this tag; it is translated literally from the tag name. Empirically, it is pointwise identical to critic/advantages/mean (pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0), and returns/max and advantages/max, as well as returns/min and advantages/min, are also respectively pointwise identical. Being equal point by point across the three aggregation levels does not look like two quantities that happen to have the same mean, but more like the two tags reading the same data. This is an inference based on the data shape; the dashboard does not explain the implementation.
items.why: Watching mean-type return means looking at the direction of the net signal for the whole batch: a mean that is positive over the long term indicates that this batch as a whole is better than the baseline, while a long-term negative mean indicates it is worse overall than the baseline. It is also a health-check item for whether advantage is correctly centered—if the baseline is constructed reasonably, this mean should oscillate slightly around 0 rather than drift persistently in one direction. The farther it deviates from 0, the more it looks like a constant direction unrelated to the specific trajectory has been mixed into the gradient.
read: The magnitude is key. It is on the order of thousandths rather than hundredths, indicating that this is not the raw return; when reading it, do not interpret it at the level of reward.

Being persistently negative and increasing in magnitude indicates that within the batch, trajectories that are 「worse than baseline」 are becoming more numerous or worse; both runs in this period have this shape.
It completely coincides with advantages/mean and can only be viewed as one curve; citing both lines together would double-count.
Compare it with the ratio |negative advantage|/positive advantage; this can explain why it is biased negative.
items.observed: pro is negative for all 19 steps, from −0.00336077 at step 1 to −0.0043556 at step 19, with range −0.0142034~−0.00115565, deepest −0.0142034 at step 14 and shallowest −0.00115565 at step 2. flash has a different shape: step 1 is still positive at +0.00174863, step 2 at +0.000117731, then it turns negative starting at step 3 and runs all the way to −0.015268 at step 25, with deepest −0.0466903 at step 19. That is, this mean for flash slides from “slightly positive at the thousandths level” to −0.047, with a peak about 27 times the first value; pro, by contrast, always oscillates slightly within the negative range, and the absolute value of its deepest value is only about one third of flash's peak.
traps: Do not compare magnitudes or compute differences with critic/rewards/mean; the two have different definitions and magnitudes (one on the order of 0.5, the other on the order of 0.001~0.05).
Do not interpret flash being positive at steps 1 and 2 as 「better early on」. The absolute magnitude of those two steps is only 1e-3, smaller than the training noise.

The fact that it is identical to advantages/mean cannot prove that "advantage is return minus baseline"; it only shows that the two quantities reported by the dashboard are consistent; the dashboard does not explain why.

sources.title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation
sources.quote: which is simply the empirical returns minus the value function baseline
sources.topic: The limiting form of GAE and the definition of advantage
sources.note: The k→∞ (λ→1) form of GAE is likewise just “empirical return minus baseline,” and does not imply that γ=1 and λ=1 hold simultaneously; the three aggregations being pointwise equal more likely comes from baseline≡0 or the two tags reading the same tensor, so our original sentence “means the GAE's λ=1, γ=1” is too strong.

items.name: Highest reward for a single trajectory at this step
items.unit: Reward value (upper limit 1; measured, both runs are identically 1 across all steps)
items.what: Highest reward obtained by a single trajectory in this step's training batch. It answers “how good the best one in this batch of data is,” not an average, and does not reflect the typical level either.
items.how: Take the maximum over the rewards of each trajectory in the training batch. The dashboard does not provide an official explanation for this tag; it is translated literally from the tag name. It is pointwise identical to critic/score/max (all equal across pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps).
items.why: It is the most direct pointer to “task solvability”. If even the best trajectory cannot get a high score, it means the problem is out of scope, the grader is broken, or too few rollouts completed successfully; at this point, a drop in mean reward is a data problem rather than model degradation. It is also an observer of the reward upper bound: once the upper bound is not fixed, the scale of advantage will drift along with it, and the subsequent normalization will be unstable.
read: Being pinned at 1 for a long time indicates that at every step there is at least one fully successful trajectory; this is the prerequisite for usable data.
If it starts to drop or becomes jittery, check the grader and environment failure rate first, rather than first suspecting model capability.

It must be viewed together with min to know the within-batch spread. max identically 1 and min pressed against −0.8 indicate the spread is pinned to the extremes; then the movement of the mean reward is entirely determined by the distribution shape (the middle batch of trajectories).
A constant straight line is itself the conclusion; there is no need to look for its "trend".
items.observed: Both runs are 1 at all steps: pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps, 44 values in total with no exception; the minimum, maximum, first value, and last value are all 1. That is, from step 1 to each run's latest step, every step's training batch contained at least one trajectory that received a perfect score; the measured reward upper bound is 1, and a value greater than 1 has never appeared. By contrast, over the same period rewards/min in pro can go as low as −0.8 (step 14), and in flash it has long stayed close to −0.8 starting from step 15, so the within-batch range is real.
traps: It being identically 1 does not mean training has made no progress or the curve is bad. It is inherently an upper-bound observer; being constant is itself the conclusion.
Don't assume rewards are binary (0 or 1) just because max=1. min can be as low as −0.8, indicating that grading is finer than "pass/fail".
Comparing it across runs has no informational value; both sides are 1.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: Instead, we directly use the final accuracy of a verifiable task as the outcome reward, computed using the following rule:
sources.topic: Verifiable reward (rule-based verifiable reward)
sources.note: The rule immediately following in that text is to give 1 when is_equivalent and otherwise −1; the reward upper bound itself is 1, which is exactly the public basis for our observation that rewards/max is identically 1 across the 44 step values.

items.name: Mean reward of the training trajectories at this step
items.unit: Reward value (dimensionless; measured, both runs are in 0.51~0.60, and the value range of a single trajectory is −0.8~1)
items.what: The official explanation is mean reward over trajectories trained on this step. Intuitively, it is “the average score obtained by the batch of trajectories fed to the trainer at this step”. It is not the correctness of a single problem, but the arithmetic mean of the rewards of the whole batch of trajectories; the denominator is the batch of trajectories that actually entered the training batch, not all the prompts sampled at this step.
items.how: After each trajectory finishes the environment, the grading logic assigns a scalar reward, and then the arithmetic mean is taken over all trajectories in the training batch for this step. It is pointwise identical to critic/score/mean (pro's 19 steps, flash's 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0), so on the dashboard reward and score are the same quantity and the same data at this level. It is not equal to dynsam/avg@n; the two have different denominator definitions.
items.why: This is the most upstream gauge in the entire training process. If it drops, first distinguish whether the model has actually gotten worse on the current data, or whether the grading definition or environment success rate has gone wrong. It also determines the overall level of advantage: advantage is normalized around the baseline, and an overall shift in the reward level changes the mass ratio of positive and negative advantages, which in turn affects the relative strength of encouragement and suppression in the gradient. If it remains unchanged for a long time or continues to decline, it means the rollout at this step did not provide a new learning signal.
read: It is a slow variable; look at the trend, not single steps. pro over 19 steps only goes from 0.5522 to 0.5946, flash over 25 steps from 0.5167 to 0.5935; single-step jitter of 0.005~0.015 is within the normal range.

It must be viewed together with dynsam/avg@n. The two curves have similar shapes but are not the same curve; if the difference remains stable within an interval, the definition is normal; only if the difference suddenly widens or changes sign is it worth checking.

The level itself has meaning: close to 1 means almost everything in the batch passes, advantage variance will collapse and the learning signal will shrink; close to 0 or turning negative means almost everything in the batch fails. In this run, both runs are at 0.51~0.60, corresponding to "more than about half the trajectories succeeding".
Note that pro and flash have different step counts (19 vs 25); cross-run comparison can only be made on overlapping steps.
items.observed: pro rose slowly from 0.552211 at step 1 to 0.594634 at step 19; the full range is 0.552211~0.594634; the minimum is exactly step 1 and the maximum is exactly step 19, with no reversal. flash rose from 0.516717 at step 1 to 0.593547 at step 25; the range is 0.516717~0.595029; the peak 0.595029 occurs at step 24. The two runs' starting points differ by 0.035494 (pro higher). In the overlapping interval of steps 1~19, pro is higher than flash at every step; the minimum difference is 0.004271 (step 17), and the maximum difference is 0.042004 (step 7). In steps 20~25, where pro has no data, only flash's 0.595029 at step 24 is slightly higher than pro's final value 0.594634 (+0.000395); step 25's 0.593547 is lower again by 0.001087. So the 'flash late-stage overtake' holds only at step 24 and does not constitute a sustained crossover. Over the same period, dynsam/avg@n is clearly higher: pro 0.555333~0.635523, flash 0.496314~0.640833.
traps: Don't treat it and dynsam/avg@n as the same number. Maximum difference: pro 0.044750 (step 16), flash 0.059079 (step 23); avg@n is higher for 18/19 steps in pro and 18/25 steps in flash, while flash has another 7 steps where the reverse holds. The definitions differ (trajectory average over the training batch vs pass-rate average over sampled prompts); a difference of 0.01~0.06 is normal, do not write them as equal.

It is point-by-point identical to critic/score/mean; they cannot be treated as two independent pieces of evidence for cross-validation. When you see two completely overlapping lines, the first reaction should be that the same data has been plotted twice.

Comparing flash step 24 with pro step 19 would yield "flash exceeds pro," but that only stitches together values from two different training stages; no crossing ever occurs within the overlapping interval.

sources.quote: GRPO foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores, significantly reducing training resources compared to Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
sources.topic: GRPO removes critic: within-group scores as baseline
sources.note: The upstream of within-group relative advantage is the within-group reward distribution, which supports our reading of critic/rewards/* and critic/score/* as 'two aggregations on the same reward chain' rather than two independent subsystems.

sources.title: This site's calculation: reward mean is not equal to avg@n
sources.quote: critic/rewards/mean and critic/score/mean are exactly equal at every step; but their difference from dynsam/avg@n reaches up to pro 0.044750 and flash 0.059080, and the direction is not fixed.
sources.topic: The two 'averages' are not the same thing
sources.note: rewards/mean is the average reward over the training batch (possibly with weighting and filtering), avg@n is the average pass rate over all sampled prompts. The two have different denominators, so one cannot be used to validate the other.

items.name: Minimum reward of a single trajectory at this step
items.unit: Reward value (measured lower bound −0.8, upper bound 0)
items.what: The minimum reward obtained by a single trajectory in this step's training batch, measuring 'how bad the worst one is'.
items.how: Take the minimum over the rewards of each trajectory in the training batch. The dashboard provides no official explanation, so this is a literal translation of the tag name. It is exactly identical to critic/score/min point by point (all equal across pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps).
items.why: Together with max, it delineates the actual range of reward values [−0.8, 1]. If the lower bound is a fixed value, it means the grader assigns a fixed penalty score to failed trajectories; if the lower bound stays pinned to the floor, it means there are stable 'complete failure' trajectories in the batch. Such trajectories contribute a large amount of negative advantage and are the main source of negative advantage mass. It is also an indicator for judging reward steepness: the deeper the min, the greater the negative advantage of failed trajectories, and the stronger the negative pressure in the gradient.
read: Watch whether it stays pinned to the floor for a long time. Being pinned to the floor means there are always trajectories that fail completely, and the failure penalty has saturated, so further penalization cannot produce discrimination.
Watch whether it is exactly 0 or close to 0; that step indicates no trajectory was deducted to the floor, and within-batch quality is relatively uniform.
Its absolute value and max's are asymmetric (lower bound −0.8, upper bound 1); this is a design choice—do not interpret the mean reward according to a symmetric distribution.
When computing proportions, do not normalize to 0~1; the reward interval is [−0.8, 1].
items.observed: pro from step 1 −0.707069 to step 19 −0.763574, range −0.8~0, the minimum −0.8 appears only at step 14, and the only time it is 0 is step 3; 9 steps are not below −0.3 (steps 3, 4, 5, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 18), indicating that the worst trajectories within the pro batch are mostly still not too bad. flash is clearly worse: range −0.8~−0.178554, the maximum is only −0.178554 at step 3, and from step 15 onward it is basically pinned to the floor——steps 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 25 are exactly equal to −0.8, step 24 is −0.797654; across the whole run only steps 3 and 4 are not below −0.3. The reward lower bound for both runs is −0.8, never lower.
traps: Don't read flash's latter half being identically equal to −0.8 as missing data or broken reporting. It did report a value; the value just stays at the lower bound.
Don't use min to judge overall quality. min only describes the worst one: at pro step 14, when min=−0.8, the mean reward was instead at an upper-middle level for that period (0.587569).
Only together with rewards/max does it define the value range; citing it alone easily gives a wrong impression.

items.name: Average trajectory score at this step (same value as reward)
items.what: Average score of the training batch trajectories at this step. The dashboard does not provide an official description for this tag, so translate literally by tag name: score generally refers to the raw score given by the grader, and reward refers to the scalar the trainer actually uses to compute advantage. Nominally, the two have the relationship of 'raw score' and 'optimization target'.
items.how: Average the scores of each trajectory in the training batch. Empirically, it is exactly identical point by point to critic/rewards/mean: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0; critic/score/max and critic/rewards/max, critic/score/min and critic/rewards/min are also exactly identical respectively. At this level, the score and reward reported by the dashboard are the same quantity.
items.why: The point of watching it is to confirm whether 'the raw score given by the grader' and 'the reward the trainer actually optimizes' are the same thing. Once the two diverge, it indicates that normalization, clipping, or penalty post-processing was done in between; the optimization target has already been rewritten, and we must know by how much. In this round's data, the two do not diverge.
read: Its overlap with rewards/mean is the current fact; do not treat them as two independent metrics that corroborate each other.
Its level should be compared against dynsam/avg@n; a stable difference means the definition is stable.
If at some future step the two lines begin to diverge, that step is direct evidence that "the scoring was altered by post-processing" and is worth investigating separately.
Note that this "equality" has only been verified at the three aggregation levels mean/max/min; it does not mean other score-related tags are also the same.
items.observed: It is exactly the same set of numbers as critic/rewards/mean. pro: step 1 0.552211 to step 19 0.594634, range 0.552211~0.594634. flash: step 1 0.516717 to step 25 0.593547, range 0.516717~0.595029. In the step-by-step comparison over pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps, the maximum absolute difference is 0; no step has any difference. In the same period, dynsam/avg@n is clearly higher (pro maximum 0.635523, flash maximum 0.640833), so the statement 'score equals pass rate' does not hold.
traps: Do not treat it as a synonym for dynsam/avg@n. Their maximum differences are pro 0.044750 and flash 0.059079; they are different definitions.
Do not write "score and reward are highly correlated" — they are exactly equal pointwise.
The fact that it is identically equal to rewards/mean will change with the dashboard post-processing logic and cannot be cited as a long-term property.

items.name: Minimum advantage multiplier (identically 1)
items.what: The minimum multiplier that has appeared in action-type multiplicative adjustment. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name. It is the 'scaling strength': 1 means no scaling, 0.5 means the token's advantage is halved.
items.how: For all tokens multiplicatively adjusted at this step, take the minimum of the multipliers used. Measured across pro 19 steps and flash 25 steps, all are identically 1.
items.why: It explains better than token count whether the 'scaling strength threshold has been reached'. Identically 1 means the multiplicative branch has not actually overridden any sample; once it drops below 0.9, it indicates that strongly suppressed tokens have appeared, and one should check whether this is collateral damage. It is a threshold-type metric; look at the minimum, not the average.
read: Being identically 1 and adv_mul_tokens being identically 0 corroborate each other: no token entered the multiplicative adjustment, so the minimum multiplier naturally stays at its initial value.
When judging whether the penalty is in effect, it can only prove that the action-type multiplicative branch is not in effect; it cannot prove that the signed branch is not in effect.
Compare with penalty/signed/neg_scale to see the strength difference: the latter reaches as low as 0.970986 in flash, while this one is always 1.
1 is the baseline value for "no scaling"; do not read it as some complex normalization result.
items.observed: pro 19 steps are all 1, flash 25 steps are all 1, all 44 values without exception; the maximum, minimum, first value, and last value are all 1. By comparison, penalty/signed/pos_scale is between 1.00014~1.00306 (slightly greater than 1), and penalty/signed/neg_scale is between 0.970986~0.999773 (slightly less than 1); both clearly deviate from 1 but by a very small magnitude. In this run, the only penalty signals with numerical action are all in the signed branch.
traps: Do not conclude that the entire penalty module is ineffective just because it is identically 1; the signed branch does have data.
It is completely different from adv_mul_tokens: the former is a multiplier, the latter is a token count.
Do not treat it as the same thing as penalty/signed/pos_scale; the two belong to different branches.

sources.note: Same as above: public clipping-type changes do not produce a quantity like 'per-token advantage multiplier'; adv_mul_min being identically 1 only indicates that this private branch was not triggered, and one cannot use dual-clip's c or DAPO's ε to explain it by comparison.

items.name: Token count involved in advantage multiplicative adjustment (identically 0)
items.what: The token count covered by 'multiplicative adjustment' (multiplying advantage rather than subtracting) in the action-type branch. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when scaling advantage per token. Measured across pro 19 steps and flash 25 steps, all are 0.
items.why: Deduction and scaling are two different penalty actions, and their effects are also different: deduction only changes the total, while scaling changes the shape of the distribution, and if scaling is done too aggressively, it can directly wipe out the advantage of some samples. This number being 0 indicates that no token on the path was processed by multiplicative adjustment, and the action-type scaling path was not taken in this run.
read: It being identically 0 and adv_mul_min being identically 1 are a pair: no token was multiplicatively adjusted, so the minimum multiplier naturally stays at its initial value 1.

Keep it separate from pos_scale/neg_scale in the signed branch. Those two are scaling factors for "sign splitting + renormalization"; they are always near 1 but not 1, and are not the same mechanism as the action-type multiplicative adjustment here.
Viewed alone it carries zero information; it should be read within the entire penalty/action/ group.
It reports a token count, not a multiplier; for the multiplier, see adv_mul_min.
items.observed: All 44 step values for pro and flash are 0. In the same group, adv_reduction_total and adv_reduction_tokens are also 0. That is to say, among the 4 tags under the entire penalty/action/ prefix, 3 are identically 0 and 1 is identically 1, and no action-type penalty occurred at any step in either run. Meanwhile, pos_mass_removed, neg_mass_added, pos_hit_tokens, and neg_hit_tokens under the penalty/signed/ prefix are all non-zero for both runs.
traps: Do not assume it reports a multiplier just because it has mul in its name. It reports a token count.
Do not conflate it with penalty/signed/pos_scale or neg_scale; those two constantly deviate from 1.
Being identically 0 does not mean this tag is a placeholder; together with reduction_total it constitutes complete evidence that "the action type was not triggered."

sources.topic: The public counterpart of 'only one side moves the lower bound'
sources.note: The adjustments of dual-clip and DAPO are both at the surrogate/ratio level; in the public materials there is no action-type branch that 'multiplicatively scales advantage per token', so this tag on this site that is identically 0 cannot have its expected behavior explained using public methods.

items.name: Token count involved in advantage deduction (identically 0)
items.what: The token count covered by action-type deduction. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when deducting advantage per token. Measured across both runs, all steps are 0: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, 44 values in total are all 0.
items.why: It is the companion quantity to adv_reduction_total. A total of 0 could in theory be positive and negative mass exactly cancelling out, but a token count of 0 is unambiguous—indeed, no token was processed by this branch. Only by looking at the two together can the conclusion of “no deduction” be nailed down.
read: Confirm together with adv_reduction_total: if both are 0, it can be determined that the action-type branch was not triggered at all.

If in the future a combination appears where total is 0 but tokens is non-zero, that indicates it was triggered but the net effect was zero; this is another situation and is worth investigating separately.
Viewed alone it carries little information; it should be used paired with total and pre/post.
It counts the tokens processed by the deduction branch and is unrelated to batch size.
items.observed: pro and flash all 44 step values are 0; the minimum, maximum, first value, and last value are all 0. It is fully synchronized with adv_reduction_total (the step-by-step difference between the two is also 0). Under the entire penalty/action/ prefix, only adv_mul_min has a non-zero value, and it is identically 1.
traps: Do not interpret it as "no tokens participated in training"; it only counts tokens processed by the deduction branch.
Being identically 0 does not mean missing; both tags actually reported 19/25 values in both runs.
Do not compare magnitudes with penalty/signed/pos_hit_tokens or neg_hit_tokens; those are hit counts under a different definition, on the order of 1e5~1e6.

items.name: Advantage deduction total (action type, identically 0 across all steps in both runs)
items.unit: Advantage mass (total amount that should be deducted, measured identically 0)
items.what: The total amount of advantage deducted as recorded by the “action type” branch in the penalty module. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translate literally from the tag name: adv is advantage, reduction is deduction, total is total.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when deducting advantage. Measured exactly 0 at every step in both runs: pro 19 steps all 0, flash 25 steps all 0; the minimum, maximum, first value, and last value are all 0; no step has a non-zero value.
items.why: It is paired with the two pre/post total mass tags. If this value is 0 and pre and post are also exactly the same, the two pieces of evidence point in the same direction, and it can be concluded that “no advantage was deducted by this action-type branch”. Conversely, if it is non-zero while pre/post are the same, it means the deduction basis and the total ledger basis are not the same; this must be investigated first, otherwise the penalty effect will be misjudged.
read: First confirm whether it is identically 0. Being identically 0 is a clear conclusion: action-type deduction did not occur in this run.

Read train/adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty being the same as post and train/adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty being the same as post together; the three pieces of evidence point in the same direction, making it more credible.
Don't generalize its being identically zero into 「the penalty module as a whole isn't working」. penalty/signed/* has non-zero data; the two are not measuring the same thing.
Identically zero has two explanations—the feature was not enabled, or it was enabled but the condition was never hit. The dashboard doesn't say which one it is; don't draw a conclusion on its behalf.
items.observed: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, all 44 values are 0; there is not a single exception. The penalty/action/adv_reduction_tokens in the same group is also all 0. By contrast, train/adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty and train/adv_pos_sum_post_penalty are exactly identical step by step (maximum absolute difference 0), and train/adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty and post are likewise exactly identical. So deduction at the total level did not occur in either run. Under the same prefix, adv_mul_tokens is identically 0 and adv_mul_min is identically 1; none of the 4 tags in the entire penalty/action/ group shows any action at any step.
traps: Identically zero does not mean this tag is missing. Both runs actually reported 19/25 values; they are just all 0.
Don't read it mixed together with penalty/signed/*. The signed branch has non-zero data; mixing the two together will lead to contradictory conclusions.
Don't treat it as an anomaly. A curve that is identically zero is a normal 「not triggered」 representation on the training dashboard.

items.name: Negative-advantage side hit token count
items.what: In the sign-splitting branch, the token count on the negative-advantage side that is judged as hit and therefore processed. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translate literally from the tag name.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when making token-based judgments. Measured non-zero at all steps in both runs: pro 19 steps range 171,543~1,112,360; flash 25 steps range 209,223~7,837,940.
items.why: Paired with pos_hit_tokens, used to determine whether the penalty falls more on the positive side or the negative side. Together with neg_mass_added, it gives the two dimensions of “breadth” and “depth” for the negative side, and is the only metric in this group that has both complete step-by-step coverage and a large dynamic range.
read: The late-stage surge in flash is most noteworthy: step 19 1,866,600, step 20 2,882,750, step 21 5,834,740, step 22 7,837,940 (highest over the whole period), step 23 5,633,590, step 24 6,474,280, which is several times to thirty-odd times the first 18 steps (mostly 2e5~1.4e6); step 25 falls back to 846,491.

This wave is synchronized with the surge in neg_mass_added (steps 19~24, 2e6~6.8e6), and also synchronized with the dip in neg_scale (step 24, 0.970986); the three tags are talking about the same thing.

Use neg_mass_added / neg_hit_tokens to see the average change per token: flash step 22 6,234,810 / 7,837,940 ≈ 0.795, step 24 6,830,830 / 6,474,280 ≈ 1.055; pro step 14 1,430,260 / 1,112,360 ≈ 1.286. The negative-side per-token change is 4~10 times larger than the positive-side 0.1~0.2 order of magnitude.
The negative-side hit surface is far larger than the positive side in both runs; this is direct evidence that the penalty is biased toward the negative side.
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro are non-zero, range 171,543~1,112,360, highest at step 14, lowest at step 15, first value 1,020,450, last value 673,523. All 25 steps of flash are non-zero, range 209,223~7,837,940, lowest at step 8, highest at step 22, first value 1,343,760, last value 846,491. The highest value of flash is about 7.0× the highest value of pro. Comparison within the same step: pro step 14 neg 1,112,360 vs pos 21,957.2, the negative-side hit surface is about 50× the positive side; flash step 22 neg 7,837,940 vs pos 292,876, the negative side is about 27× the positive side.
traps: Don't treat it as 「the number of penalized trajectories」. A trajectory has many tokens; the dashboard doesn't specify the counting convention or whether a trajectory can be counted multiple times.

Don't read the surge in flash at steps 19~24 in isolation. In the same period, the total negative-advantage mass itself is deepening (step 19 −277,294,000 is the deepest over the whole period); the two should be attributed separately.
Its number of covered steps differs from that of pos_hit_tokens (this one has values for all 25 steps); don't assume the two tags are synchronized.

items.name: Added negative advantage mass
items.what: In the sign-split branch, the mass added to the negative advantage side, i.e. the portion of mass that pushes advantages that are not negative enough further negative. The dashboard gives no official explanation; this is a literal translation of the tag name.
items.how: The mass cumulatively added to the negative side by the penalty logic upon a hit. Measured: both runs have non-zero values at all steps: pro 19 steps range 29,940.3~1,430,260; flash 25 steps range 46,405.2~6,830,830.
items.why: It measures how much mass the penalty pushes to the negative side, and is a reading of 'the strength with which bad behavior is suppressed'. Together with pos_mass_removed it constitutes the entire action of the sign-split branch; the relative magnitude of the two indicates whether the penalty leans more toward the positive side or the negative side. In this run it is systematically larger than the positive side, indicating that the penalty mainly falls on negative-advantage samples.
read: The most noteworthy is the late-stage surge in flash: step 19 2,122,050, step 20 3,673,070, step 21 5,150,180, step 22 6,234,810, step 23 5,913,860, step 24 6,830,830, which is from ten-odd to over a hundred times the first 18 steps (mostly on the 1e5 order of magnitude); step 25 falls back again to 476,523. In the same period, penalty/signed/neg_scale synchronously dips to 0.970986 (step 24, lowest over the whole period).

Its ratio to |train/adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty| is exactly the part missing from neg_scale. pro step 14 1,430,260 / 181,450,000 ≈ 0.00788, corresponding to neg_scale 0.992055. This is inferred from the numerical relationship; the dashboard does not state it.
The pullback at flash step 25 is synchronized with neg_scale returning to 0.99765, indicating that the wave at steps 19~24 was one-off, not sustained deterioration.
Do not treat it as the total negative advantage. The total negative-advantage mass is on the order of 1e8; this one reaches at most 6.8e6, a difference of two orders of magnitude.
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro are non-zero, range 29,940.3~1,430,260, highest at step 14, lowest at step 17, first value 326,695, last value 146,793, overall downward trend. All 25 steps of flash are non-zero, range 46,405.2~6,830,830, lowest at step 8, highest at step 24; the first 18 steps are mostly in 46,405~738,695, steps 19~24 jump to 2,122,050~6,830,830, step 25 falls back to 476,523. The highest value of flash is about 4.8× the highest value of pro.
traps: Do not compare with train/adv_neg_sum_post_penalty. The latter is exactly identical to pre (difference 0); putting the two together leads to a self-contradictory conclusion—the reason is that after the sign-branch change, renormalization was performed, so the total is conserved.

Do not directly read the jump at flash steps 19~24 as "the penalty became stricter." The dashboard does not state the trigger condition, and the total negative-advantage mass itself was also increasing during the same period (step 19 is −277,294,000, the deepest of the whole period); the two should be attributed separately.
It is not the total negative advantage; it is only the small part that was modified.

sources.quote: When A_t<0, such a large ratio r_t(theta) will introduce a big and unbounded variance since r_t(theta)A_t << 0.
sources.topic: The public counterpart of 'only one side moves the lower bound'
sources.note: This lower bound acts on the surrogate objective (equivalent to truncating overly large negative updates), neither changing the distribution of advantage nor having the step of 'adding mass and then normalizing back to the original total by sign', so it does not constitute a counterpart to this site's neg_mass_added + neg_scale.

items.name: Negative advantage scaling factor
items.what: The scaling factor applied by the sign-split branch to the negative advantage side. The dashboard gives no official explanation; this is a literal translation of the tag name.
items.how: Measured, it agrees with added mass / total negative advantage mass: computing 1 − neg_mass_added / |train/adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty| for each step and comparing with the dashboard value, the maximum difference is 6.26e-5 for pro's 19 steps and 2.16e-4 for flash's 25 steps, with deviations concentrated in the steps with the largest added mass. This is inferred from the numerical relationship; the dashboard does not explain it.
items.why: Corresponding to pos_scale, it is the relative magnitude by which the negative side is modified, and the only penalty-strength reading that can be compared across runs. Its deviation is an order of magnitude larger than pos_scale, indicating that the penalty is mainly pressed onto the negative side. It is also a direct indicator for judging "whether that wave of negative-side actions got out of control".
read: It is always less than 1. Multiplying negative advantage by a factor less than 1 makes its absolute value smaller; together with the action of "adding mass to the negative side", this indicates that the added mass was proportionally absorbed by the subsequent renormalization, so the total negative-side quantity is conserved (train/adv_neg_sum_post_penalty is exactly identical to pre). This is an inference.

Look at its dip. pro ranges from 0.992055~0.999773 throughout, with the lowest at step 14. flash ranges from 0.970986~0.999684, with 8 steps deviating from 1 by more than 0.8% (steps 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24); it bottoms out at step 24 and returns to 0.99765 at step 25.
Its peaks and troughs are synchronized with neg_mass_added; the two curves can corroborate each other.
It was never clipped: penalty/signed/neg_scale_clamped has all 44 step values equal to 0.
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro have values, range 0.992055~0.999773, first value 0.996918, last value 0.999052, lowest at step 14, highest at step 17; the maximum deviation from 1 is 0.79%, and no step exceeds 0.8%. All 25 steps of flash have values, range 0.970986~0.999684, first value 0.995605, last value 0.99765, lowest at step 24, highest at step 8; steps 19~24 are consecutively 0.992288, 0.985195, 0.977847, 0.974525, 0.975996, 0.970986, and the maximum deviation reaches 2.9%. This is the only signal in this group with sustained, appreciable deviation; in the same period, neg_mass_added is also at a high level of 2e6~6.8e6.
traps: Do not read "less than 1" as negative advantage being weakened or the penalty becoming lighter. It and "adding mass to the negative side" are two steps of the same process; looking at the factor alone will read the direction backwards.
Its deviation is an order of magnitude larger than pos_scale; do not use the same threshold to measure across the two runs.
Do not use it to explain changes in train/adv_neg_sum_*; those two are exactly identical at the total level.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: We identify that the upper clip can restrict the exploration of the policy, where making an ‘exploitation’ token more probable is much easier yet the probability of an unlikely ‘exploration’ token is too tightly bounded to be uplifted.
sources.topic: The form of asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher) in public methods
sources.note: The paper explicitly keeps εlow unchanged (increasing it would push token probabilities toward 0 and cause the sampling space to collapse), indicating that the asymmetric adjustment in public methods is concentrated on the upper-bound side of the ratio; our neg_scale approach of "adding mass to negative advantages and then normalizing back to the original total by sign" has no counterpart in public materials.

sources.title: Calculation on this site: the "mass removal—mass addition—scaling back to the original value by sign" for positive and negative advantages
sources.quote: pos_scale ≈ 1 + pos_mass_removed / adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty (residual 5.2e-6 / 7.9e-6), neg_scale ≈ 1 − neg_mass_added / |adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty| (residual 6.3e-5 / 8.2e-4); at the same time, the pre/post values of adv_pos_sum and adv_neg_sum are exactly equal point by point (maximum difference 0).

sources.note: The processing magnitude on the negative side is far larger than on the positive side (in the final segment of flash, neg_mass_added once reached 6.83 million), but it is normalized back to the original total, so it cannot be seen at all from the single number "advantage sum"; this scaling factor must be examined separately.

items.name: Number of times negative-side scaling was clipped (identically 0)
items.what: The number of times the negative-advantage scaling factor hits the clipping boundary and is forcibly truncated. The dashboard provides no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when neg_scale goes out of bounds. Measured across pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps, all are 0; 44 values in total, with no exception.
items.why: It is the safety valve for negative-side scaling. neg_scale's deviation is an order of magnitude larger than pos_scale (flash reaches a minimum of 0.970986), so this metric is more worth watching: once it is non-zero, it means that part of the negative-advantage scaling has been truncated, and the reading of negative-side "penalty strength" will be distorted; neg_scale can no longer be taken directly as the strength.
read: Being identically 0 indicates that the scaling dip at flash steps 19~24 (minimum 0.970986) is still a real computation result, not a residual value after truncation.
Together with neg_scale, it determines the readable range of the "maximum compression strength" curve.
Compare with pos_scale_clamped: one covers all 25 steps, while the other is missing from step 20 onward; the reporting completeness of the two sign branches is different.
It only rules out distortion of the truncation kind; it does not rule out changes in the definition itself.
items.observed: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, all 44 values are 0. That is, even though flash pushed neg_scale down to 0.970986 at steps 19~24 (deviating from 1 by 2.9%, the only noticeable action in this group), it did not trigger clipping even once. In the same period, neg_mass_added surged to 6,830,830 and neg_hit_tokens surged to 7,837,940.
traps: Do not take its being identically 0 as "the negative-side penalty is very light." It only shows that it was not clipped; for strength, look at neg_scale and neg_mass_added.
Do not miss the difference that at flash steps 20~25 pos_scale_clamped is null while this one is 0; the two have different numbers of covered steps.
Being identically 0 is not missing data; both runs actually reported the complete 19/25 values.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Positive-advantage-side hit token count
items.what: In the sign-split branch, the number of tokens on the positive-advantage side that were judged as hits and thus processed. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when determining per token. Measured: both runs have non-zero values at all steps: pro 19 steps range 177,661~983,536; flash 25 steps range 115,445~1,706,710.
items.why: Its relationship with pos_mass_removed is the relationship between 'how many tokens' and 'how much mass was changed across these tokens'. Looking at the two together gives the average change per token, thereby distinguishing the two penalty forms 'wide hit coverage but very light per hit' and 'narrow hit coverage but very heavy per hit', which is crucial for judging whether the penalty is coarse or precise.
read: Use pos_mass_removed / pos_hit_tokens to compute the average per-token change: pro step 2 183,925 / 983,536 ≈ 0.187, step 1 122,871 / 825,655 ≈ 0.149, magnitude stable at 0.1~0.2.

Look at the trend. Both runs are declining: pro from 825,655 to 337,799, flash from 1,276,900 to 258,166 (the final value is only 20% of the first value). Over the same period the total positive-advantage mass is rising, so the hit share is declining.

Note that its covered steps differ from pos_mass_removed: for flash this one has values at all 25 steps, while pos_mass_removed is null from step 21 on. The completeness of the two tags in the same branch is inconsistent.
Hit token count does not equal training token count; do not use it to compute a share with perf/total_num_tokens as coverage.
items.observed: pro 19 steps all non-zero, range 177,661~983,536, highest at step 2, lowest at step 18. flash 25 steps all non-zero, range 115,445~1,706,710, highest at step 2 (1,706,710, highest over the entire period), lowest at step 24 (115,445), first value 1,276,900, last value 258,166. flash's hit coverage is overall larger than pro's (first value 1,276,900 vs 825,655), but its last value is instead smaller (258,166 vs 337,799).
traps: Hit token count does not equal training token count; the dashboard does not state the denominator of this number, so do not make up a coverage rate yourself.

This tag's covered steps are inconsistent with those of pos_mass_removed (for flash the latter is null from step 21 on); when computing an average across steps, compute it over the steps where each has values.
Don't treat it as the "number of penalized trajectories"; a trajectory contains many tokens, and the dashboard does not state how many times a trajectory is counted.
