items.name: Removed positive-advantage mass
items.what: In the 'sign-split' branch of the penalty module, the mass removed from the positive-advantage side. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name: signed means processed separately according to the sign of advantage, and mass is the amount of advantage accumulated per token.
items.how: After the penalty logic determines hits per token, it accumulates the removed positive-advantage mass. Measured: both runs have non-zero data: pro covers all 19 steps, range 20,198.7~183,925; flash covers steps 1~20, steps 21~25 are null, range 29,106.5~353,572.
items.why: That it is non-zero while penalty/action/adv_reduction_total is identically zero is the easiest thing in this group to read as a contradiction. The difference lies in what is measured: the action branch reports 'how much of the total was deducted', while this one reports 'how much mass was modified'; after modification, renormalization is also performed, so the total can remain unchanged while this is non-zero. It reflects how many positive-advantage samples the penalty actually touched, and is a direct basis for judging penalty frequency and intensity.
read: Looking at the trend is more useful than looking at a single step. pro drops from 122,871 at step 1 to 58,648.1 at step 19, with a minimum of 20,198.7 at step 18; flash drops from 328,569 at step 1 to 51,874.2 at step 20 (the last step with a value), with a minimum of 29,106.5 at step 16. Both runs are converging, and the removed positive mass is decreasing.

Look at its ratio to the total positive advantage. pro step 2 183,925 / 98,946,700 ≈ 0.00186, flash step 1 328,569 / 107,630,000 ≈ 0.00305, exactly equal to the part by which penalty/signed/pos_scale exceeds 1 (1.00186 and 1.00306). These two numbers are the two ends of one formula; this is a judgment inferred from the numerical relationship, and the dashboard does not state it.
Note that the step coverage of the two sign branches is asymmetric: for flash this one is null from step 21 on, while neg_mass_added is reported all the way to step 25.
To compute the average per-token change, divide by pos_hit_tokens, not by the batch's token count.
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro are non-zero, minimum 20,198.7 (step 18), maximum 183,925 (step 2), first value 122,871, last value 58,648.1, the last value drops to 47.7% of the first value. flash has values only for steps 1~20, and steps 21~25 are null; for the 20 steps with values, the range is 29,106.5~353,572, highest at step 2, lowest at step 16, first value 328,569, step 20 is 51,874.2, dropping to 15.8% of the first value. Over the same period, total positive-advantage mass is rising (pro from 1.04e8 to 1.49e8, flash from 1.08e8 to 1.76e8), so the decline in the removed proportion is more pronounced than the decline in absolute value.
traps: Do not conclude that this one should also be 0 just because penalty/action/adv_reduction_total is identically zero. The two do not measure the same level; this one being non-zero and that one being identically zero are not contradictory.
Do not directly compare its absolute value with the negative-side mass. flash's neg_mass_added reaches 6,830,830 at step 24, which is hundreds of times the magnitude of this one over the same period.
flash is null from step 21 on; this means "there is no such value at this step", not 0. When computing the mean, do not treat null as 0.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: We identify that the upper clip can restrict the exploration of the policy, where making an ‘exploitation’ token more probable is much easier yet the probability of an unlikely ‘exploration’ token is too tightly bounded to be uplifted.
sources.topic: The form of asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher) in public methods
sources.note: What Clip-Higher relaxes is 'the probability upper bound of low-probability exploration tokens', which does not correspond to 'taking away part of the mass from the positive advantages'; public materials have no operation that moves positive-advantage mass away and then scales it back, so pos_mass_removed can only be read as a private post-processing of this implementation.

items.name: Positive advantage scaling factor
items.what: Scaling factor applied by the sign-split branch to the positive-advantage side. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name.
items.how: Empirically it closely matches pos_mass_removed / adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty: computing 1 + removed mass / total positive-advantage mass for each step and comparing it digit by digit with the dashboard values, the maximum difference over pro's 19 steps is 5.16e-6, and over flash's 20 steps is 7.88e-6, both on the order of the precision reported on the dashboard. That is, pos_scale ≈ 1 + pos_mass_removed / adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty. This is an implementation detail inferred from the numerical relationship; the dashboard does not explain it.
items.why: It tells you the relative magnitude by which the positive side is changed, and it is a normalized reading—unaffected by batch size, comparable across steps and across runs, and more useful than mass-type tags. Once it approaches the clipping boundary, it means the penalty strength is already large enough to change the shape of the entire batch's positive advantages.
read: It is slightly greater than 1. The removed positive mass did not make the total positive-side amount smaller; rather, it was compensated back by a factor slightly greater than 1——this exactly explains why train/adv_pos_sum_post_penalty is identical to pre. This is an inference.

Look at how far it deviates from 1. pro is 1.00014~1.00186 throughout (deviation 0.014%~0.186%), flash 1.0002~1.00306 (deviation 0.02%~0.306%). Both runs are moving downward (pro from first value 1.00119 to last value 1.00039, flash from first value 1.00306 to step 20 at 1.00026), consistent with the decline in pos_mass_removed.
It was never clipped: penalty/signed/pos_scale_clamped is 0 on all steps where the two runs have values.
For flash, this is null from step 21 onward; that means it was not reported for this step, do not treat it as the factor being equal to 1.
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro have values, range 1.00014~1.00186, first value 1.00119, last value 1.00039, highest at step 2, lowest at steps 14 and 18. flash has values only for steps 1~20 (steps 21~25 are null), range 1.0002~1.00306, first value 1.00306, step 20 is 1.00026, highest at step 1, lowest at step 16. flash's overall deviation magnitude is larger than pro's (maximum 0.306% vs. 0.186%), consistent with its larger pos_mass_removed peak (353,572 vs. 183,925).
traps: Don't treat it as “no change” just because it is 1.0x. Its magnitude is determined by the ratio of removed mass to total mass; this ratio is small to begin with, so what you need to look at is its deviation from 1.
Don't compare it with penalty/action/adv_mul_min; the latter is the minimum of the action-type multiplier and is identically 1, belonging to a different branch.
For flash, being null from step 21 onward means it was not reported for this step, not that the factor equals 1.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.quote: We identify that the upper clip can restrict the exploration of the policy, where making an ‘exploitation’ token more probable is much easier yet the probability of an unlikely ‘exploration’ token is too tightly bounded to be uplifted.
sources.topic: The form of asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher) in public methods
sources.note: The public asymmetric treatment looks like this: split the upper and lower clipping bounds into εlow/εhigh, and only relax the upper bound to increase entropy—what is changed is the bound of the importance sampling ratio, not the mass allocation of advantage; this is not the same mechanism as this site's pos_scale, which 'takes away positive-advantage mass and then scales it back'.

items.name: Number of times positive-side scaling is clipped (identically zero)
items.what: The number of times the positive-advantage scaling factor hits the clipping boundary and is forcibly truncated. The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name: clamped means restricted truncation.
items.how: Accumulated by the penalty logic when pos_scale is out of bounds. Measured: pro covers all 19 steps, all are 0; flash covers steps 1~19, all are 0, and steps 20~25 are null.
items.why: Together with neg_scale_clamped, it is a safety-valve observation for "has the scaling logic gone out of control". If it is non-zero, it means that for some samples the scaling did not follow the formula but was forcibly clipped; in that case the pos_scale curve cannot fully reflect the true strength, and the measure must be changed.
read: Identically 0 means that for this period the scaling factor stays within the allowed range throughout; the pos_scale reading is as-is and has not been contaminated by clipping.
It echoes the magnitude upper bound of pos_scale: flash's maximum deviation is only 0.306%, far from the typical clipping threshold.
Be careful about step coverage: for flash it is null from step 20 onward, consistent with this tag's reporting interval but one step off from pos_scale (pos_scale still has a value up to step 20).
It only indicates that there was no clipping, not that there was no scaling.
items.observed: pro's 19 steps (steps 1~19) are all 0. flash steps 1~19 are all 0, steps 20~25 are null, and all 19 steps that have values are 0. Neither run ever had a single clip. As a control, the measured range of pos_scale is 1.00014~1.00306, never approaching the magnitude that would require clipping.
traps: Identically 0 means “no clipping occurred,” not “no scaling.” Scaling is indeed happening (pos_scale deviates from 1); it is just that the magnitude is small enough that clipping is not needed.
flash's null does not equal 0. Saying “flash has 0 occurrences throughout” must be qualified to steps 1~19.
Don't conflate it with penalty/action/adv_mul_min being identically 1; one is a count and the other is a multiplier, belonging to different branches.

items.name: Total mass of negative advantage after penalty (negative value)
items.what: The same quantity as train/adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty, with the measurement point after the penalty. The value is still negative.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official description; translated literally from the tag name. Measured point-by-point completely identical to pre: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0.
items.why: Corresponding to the positive side, it is used to measure whether the penalty adds mass on the negative side. If the purpose of the penalty is to make bad behaviour more suppressed, post's absolute value should be greater than pre; if it never changes, it means the negative-side total was not touched, and judging the penalty state must rely on the penalty/signed/* group.
read: For this run, pre − post = 0; the negative-side total was not changed.

penalty/signed/neg_mass_added is non-zero (pro 29,940.3~1,430,260, flash 46,405.2~6,830,830), and penalty/signed/neg_scale is always less than 1. So “the negative-side total did not change” and “mass was added to the negative side” can both hold—the added mass is normalized back by a scaling factor less than 1, and the overall total is conserved. The dashboard does not explain this; it is inferred from the numerical relationship.

flash's neg_mass_added scales up to the millions at steps 19~24 (maximum 6,830,830 at step 24), but over the same period this post negative-side total does not have a corresponding jump, further supporting the reading that “the total is conserved and only the distribution is changed.”
It is a negative number; when discussing the direction of change, you must first state whether it is by numeric value or by absolute value.
items.observed: pro is completely identical to pre: step 1 −106,332,000, last step, step 19, −154,911,000, range −181,450,000~−99,864,500. flash is likewise completely identical to pre: step 1 −106,200,000, last step, step 25, −203,268,000, range −277,294,000~−106,200,000. On all 44 step values the difference between pre and post is 0.
traps: Don't use these two tags to judge penalty strength; at the total level they are always the same number.
It is a negative number; statements like “post is larger than pre” must first state whether they mean by numeric value or by absolute value.
Don't take pre and post being the same as reporting deduplication or missing data; both tags are actually reported, their values just happen to be the same.

sources.quote: When A_t<0, such a large ratio r_t(theta) will introduce a big and unbounded variance since r_t(theta)A_t << 0.
sources.topic: The public counterpart of 'only one side moves the lower bound'
sources.note: dual-clip only clips the update magnitude and does not conserve the total within a sign, so the fact that "pre and post are point-by-point completely equal" likewise has no corresponding implementation in the public materials.

items.name: Total mass of negative advantage before penalty (negative value)
items.what: The total amount of negative advantage at this step, with the measurement point before the penalty. The value is negative; to talk about magnitude one must first state whether it is the numeric value or the absolute value.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official description; translated literally from the tag name. Measured point-by-point completely identical to train/adv_neg_sum_post_penalty (pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0).
items.why: It is the ledger of negative pressure. How much larger it is than the positive side directly determines how negative critic/advantages/mean is. A continuously growing absolute value means that within the batch there are more trajectories that are "worse than baseline", or that they are getting worse, and the push in the suppressing direction in the gradient is strengthening.
read: Pair it with the positive side to compute a ratio; this is its most useful reading. For pro, |negative|/positive > 1 throughout (1.0093~1.1257); for flash, step 1 is still 0.9867 (positive side slightly larger), exceeds 1 starting at step 3, rises all the way to 1.4346 at step 19, and falls back to 1.1524 at the final step.

It is also strongly correlated with token count (pro −0.9656, flash −0.9614; negative correlation because it is itself negative), so a substantial part of the increase in absolute value is just the batch getting larger.
It is the same as post, indicating that this step did not remove or add mass from the negative side (at the aggregate level).
When discussing the trend, you must specify whether it is 'the value increasing' or 'the absolute value increasing'; otherwise the conclusion will be reversed.
items.observed: pro goes from −106,332,000 at step 1 to −154,911,000 at step 19, range −181,450,000~−99,864,500, deepest at step 14, shallowest at step 2. flash goes from −106,200,000 at step 1 to −203,268,000 at step 25, range −277,294,000~−106,200,000, deepest at step 19. flash's final value has an absolute value 31.2% larger than pro's, and its deepest value 52.8% larger. The negative-to-positive ratio is 1.0093 at minimum and 1.1257 at maximum for pro; 0.9867 at minimum and 1.4346 at maximum for flash (step 19). This and flash's advantages/mean being more negative than pro's (−0.0466903 vs −0.0142034) are two sides of the same thing.
traps: It is negative, so when saying 'increases' you must clarify the direction; otherwise the conclusion will be reversed.
Comparing absolute values across runs is unfair; it is likewise affected by the batch's token count.
It is exactly equal to post and cannot be used to argue that the penalty is taking effect.

items.name: Total mass of positive advantage after penalty
items.what: Same quantity as train/adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty, only the statistical time point is after penalty processing. The design intent is to subtract it from pre to see how much the penalty took from the positive side.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name. Measured, it is exactly the same as pre at every step in both runs: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute per-step difference 0, including every digit position identical.
items.why: pre/post exist as a pair precisely to do subtraction for “how much the penalty moved.” Watch it because once post is clearly smaller than pre, it means positive advantage was deducted and the positive-side learning signal is weakened, so the deduction ratio must be checked for reasonableness; if the two are always identical, another tag must be used to judge the penalty state.
read: For this run, its answer is 'no change': pre − post = 0, and it is 0 at every step.

This 0 only indicates that the total amount of positive advantage has not changed; it does not mean the penalty module is not working. penalty/signed/pos_mass_removed is non-zero on the same batch steps (pro 20,198.7~183,925, flash 29,106.5~353,572), indicating that the removed mass was normalized back into the total; the total is conserved while the distribution changes. This is an explanation inferred from the data shape; the dashboard does not state it, nor does it explain why penalty/action/* is identically zero.
It is exactly the same as pre; on the dashboard they are two identical lines. When citing, state that this is the same set of numbers.
It is likewise strongly correlated with perf/total_num_tokens; when reading the trend, you must first subtract the effect of batch size.
items.observed: pro is exactly identical to pre: step 1 103,591,000, final step 19 148,776,000, range 98,946,700~161,182,000. flash is likewise exactly identical to pre: step 1 107,630,000, final step 25 176,394,000, range 107,630,000~199,197,000. Across all 44 step values in both runs, the difference between pre and post is 0; no step had any deduction.
traps: Do not write 'the penalty has taken effect, how much the positive advantage decreased'—the data shows the decrease is 0.
Also do not write 'the penalty is completely not working'—penalty/signed/pos_mass_removed is non-zero; the two are not talking about the same thing.
It cannot be used together with pre as two independent observations to cross-validate each other; they are the same set of numbers.

sources.title: Calculation on this site: the "mass removal—mass addition—scaling back to the original value by sign" for positive and negative advantages
sources.quote: pos_scale ≈ 1 + pos_mass_removed / adv_pos_sum_pre_penalty (residual 5.2e-6 / 7.9e-6), neg_scale ≈ 1 − neg_mass_added / |adv_neg_sum_pre_penalty| (residual 6.3e-5 / 8.2e-4); at the same time, the pre/post values of adv_pos_sum and adv_neg_sum are exactly equal point by point (maximum difference 0).
sources.topic: Conservation structure of the penalty term
sources.note: Pre and post being exactly equal is easily read as “this step did nothing.” In fact, mass was moved away and then scaled back to the original total by sign, so conservation of the total does not mean there was no intervention — look at the pairing of pos_scale/neg_scale and mass_removed/mass_added.

items.name: Total positive advantage mass before penalty
items.what: The total positive advantage for this step; the statistical time point is before penalty processing. The so-called “mass” is the sum of each token's advantage accumulated, so it is affected by both the number of tokens in the batch and the size of individual advantages; it is a scale quantity rather than an intensity quantity.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name. Measured, it is exactly identical point by point to train/adv_pos_sum_post_penalty: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, maximum absolute difference 0, every digit identical.
items.why: It is the ledger for the positive side of advantage. Watching it is to know how much total positive driving force this step has, and whether penalty processing took anything from the positive side. Together with the negative-side total, it determines the positive/negative ratio within the batch, and thereby explains why critic/advantages/mean is skewed positive or negative.
read: First look at its relationship with token count. Its correlation coefficient with perf/total_num_tokens is pro 0.9874 and flash 0.9943, and the ratio is stable (pro 0.0563~0.0608, flash 0.0596~0.0635). Therefore its growth mainly comes from the batch getting larger, not from the positive signal getting stronger—this is the point most easily misread.
Pair it with the negative side to compute a ratio; this is the most informative usage: for pro, |negative|/positive is 1.0093~1.1257 throughout, and for flash it rises from 0.9867 to 1.4346.

pre is the same as post, indicating that this step did not subtract from the total positive advantage. But do not read 'the total has not changed' as 'the penalty was not triggered'; the penalty is handled in sign-specific branches—see penalty/signed/*.
Comparing across runs requires first normalizing with pos_sum / total_num_tokens; directly comparing absolute values is meaningless.
items.observed: pro goes from step 1 103,591,000 to step 19 148,776,000, range 98,946,700~161,182,000, with the lowest at step 2 and the highest at step 14. flash goes from step 1 107,630,000 to step 25 176,394,000, range 107,630,000~199,197,000, with the lowest at step 1 and the highest at step 24. Both runs are rising; flash's final value is about 18.6% higher than pro's final value, and its highest value is about 23.6% higher. The correlation coefficient with token count over the same period is 0.9874 (pro)/0.9943 (flash), and the ratio is also basically stable, so this growth mainly follows the batch size, not the positive advantage intensity getting stronger.
traps: Do not compare absolute values across runs. It is not normalized by token; a run with a larger batch is naturally larger, so to look at it you must use pos_sum / total_num_tokens.
It is exactly equal to post; do not write 'the total positive advantage decreased by X% after the penalty'.
Do not think training is getting better just because it is rising; it is almost synchronized with token count.

items.name: agentic category policy entropy
items.what: This is the policy entropy computed separately for the agentic data stream (multi-turn tool-calling trajectories); its definition is exactly the same as the global actor/entropy_loss, except that the sample scope is limited to the agentic category. It is used to answer 'whether the degree of exploration of long trajectories such as tool calling follows the same trend as the overall.'
items.how: Same algorithm as the global metric (mean per-token entropy of the policy), except that the tokens included in the statistics are limited to trajectories under the agentic category that actually participate in training in this run. The dashboard reports it separately as a category aggregate; at the dataset level there is also a finer-grained actor/agentic/... breakdown.
items.why: agentic trajectories often run to tens of thousands of tokens and involve multi-turn interactions, and are the main source of context length and generation cost. If their entropy diverges from the global, it indicates that the training dynamics of this data category differ from the other categories, requiring separately adjusting the data mix or separately suppressing entropy. items.name: PPO ratio clipping upper bound (clip high)
items.unit: Dimensionless ratio increment; for this run, it is identically 0.27
items.what: This is the upper bound of the PPO clipping interval relative to 1, i.e., how much the log-prob ratio of the new and old policies is allowed to exceed 1 at most. It is not a measured quantity but a configuration constant—reading it is equivalent to reading the hyperparameter used for this training run. Paired with it is actor/clip_low.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official description; a literal translation of the tag name is clip upper bound. Across both runs and all steps, the value is 0.27 and never changes, matching the characteristics of a "hyperparameter" rather than a "statistic". The paired actor/clip_low is identically 0.2. Together they form the ratio clipping interval, i.e., if the ratio falls outside [1-0.2, 1+0.27] = [0.8, 1.27], it is clipped.
items.why: It determines the maximum amount PPO can change per step, and is the direct prerequisite for pg_loss and pg_clipfrac. When the interval is widened, the allowed policy update is more aggressive: training progresses faster but is more prone to instability; when the interval is narrowed, the update is more conservative, more stable but slower. When investigating "why pg_loss stays very small" or "why policy drift is fast", the first thing to look at is these two boundary values. Here 0.8~1.27 is a relatively wide asymmetric interval (the upper bound is 0.07 looser than the lower bound), indicating that the configuration allows the policy to move more toward "increasing probability".
read: This is a constant; do not expect it to have a trend. There are only two possible reasons it would change: hyperparameters were changed, or annealing was done during training—neither happened in this run.
It is a precondition for interpreting pg_loss and pg_clipfrac; viewed alone it carries no information.

The upper bound 0.27 is larger than the absolute value of the lower bound 0.2; the interval is asymmetric, so when reading “how much was clipped,” one must look separately at the positive and negative sides (this run has side-specific submetrics such as actor/pg_tis_clipfrac_pos_high / _neg_low, but they measure TIS, not the ratio clip here).
Do not confuse it with actor/pg_clipfrac: this one is the “allowed bound,” while that one is the “proportion that actually hits the bound.”
items.observed: All 19 steps of pro are 0.27, all 25 steps of flash are 0.27, with no step as an exception and no null. The paired metric actor/clip_low is 0.2 for both runs and all steps. Therefore, throughout the entire training period, the ratio clipping interval remains stable at [0.8, 1.27]. The dashboard does not explain how these two values were chosen, nor does it give their linkage with pg_clipfrac.
traps: It is a configuration constant; do not treat it as a monitoring metric to analyze trends.
Conflating it with actor/pg_clipfrac will lead to completely wrong conclusions: one is a bound, the other is a trigger proportion.
The interval is asymmetric (0.27 / 0.2), meaning the tolerance is different in the positive and negative directions; directly saying “the clipping range is ±0.23” is wrong.
The dashboard does not explain the reason for the value; do not explain it on its behalf as some kind of adaptive mechanism—in the data it is just a straight line.

items.name: PPO ratio clipping lower bound (clip low)
items.unit: Dimensionless ratio increment, identically 0.2 in this run
items.what: This is the lower bound of the PPO clipping interval relative to 1, i.e. the maximum amount by which the new and old policy log-prob ratio is allowed to be lower than 1. Like actor/clip_high, it is a configuration constant rather than a measured value; reading it is equivalent to reading the hyperparameter used for this run.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation; translated literally from the tag name, it is the clip lower bound. Both runs, all steps are 0.2, never changing. Together with actor/clip_high (identically 0.27), it forms the ratio interval [1-0.2, 1+0.27] = [0.8, 1.27].
items.why: The lower bound governs the step-size upper limit in the direction of “pressing down the probabilities of certain tokens,” while the upper bound governs the opposite direction. Setting the two sides separately is generally because the gradient behavior in the two directions is asymmetric: pressing probabilities down often corresponds to negative advantage; if unconstrained, the model can easily kill an answer outright in one step, causing rapid entropy collapse and stereotyped responses. Therefore the lower bound is tighter than the upper bound, usually an intentionally conservative setting. When investigating entropy dropping too quickly, or answers becoming stereotyped, the lower bound is the first config item to check.
read: A constant; do not read it as a trend. That it does not change means the clipping range was not adjusted during this training run.
It is only meaningful when used as a pair with actor/clip_high; citing 0.2 on its own says nothing.

In this run the lower bound (0.2) is tighter than the upper bound (0.27), i.e. more conservative on the “push the probability down” side. This is a configuration fact; do not extrapolate it into policy performance.
Do not confuse it with actor/pg_clipfrac: this one is the bound, that one is the trigger fraction, and that one is identically zero in this run.
items.observed: pro has all 19 steps at 0.2, flash has all 25 steps at 0.2, no exceptions, no null. Paired with actor/clip_high identically at 0.27, the ratio clipping interval remains stable at [0.8, 1.27] throughout training. It is worth noting that during the same period actor/entropy_loss rises in both runs, which is not the direction that the lower bound crushes. The dashboard does not explain the basis for the values of these two bounds.
traps: A configuration constant; do not treat it as a monitoring metric and analyse its trend.

“The lower bound is tighter” does not equal “clipping mainly happens at the lower bound” — the actual trigger fraction cannot be read from the dashboard for this run, actor/pg_clipfrac is identically zero.
Do not mix this up with actor/pg_tis_clipfrac_neg_low: the latter also has neg_low in its name, but it measures clipping on the TIS side and has non-zero data.
The dashboard gives no official explanation; do not make up an adaptive or annealing story for it.

sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Policy entropy (mean per-token entropy of the policy)
items.what: This number answers “how hesitant the model is when generating each token”. The larger the value, the flatter the probability distribution for the next token, and the more the model is willing to try different phrasings; the smaller the value, the sharper the distribution, and the more the model tends to output the same token every time. It is not loss, but the entropy of the policy distribution; it merely continues to use loss as the reported name.
items.how: The original official description is mean per-token entropy of the policy. For the tokens in this round's training batch that actually participate in training, compute the entropy of the current policy's output distribution one by one, then average over all tokens. Prompt tokens in the context do not produce a generation distribution and are not counted.
items.why: Entropy is the policy's exploration headroom. Dropping to very low indicates that the model has collapsed into a few fixed responses, RL basically receives no effective gradient, and further training will hardly change it—this is one of the most common failure modes in training (entropy collapse). Rising too high is the opposite: it means the model starts answering randomly, and the discriminative power of the reward signal is diluted into noise. So it is a leading indicator of “whether it can keep learning”, not an outcome indicator of “whether it is learning well”.
read: Look at the trend direction first, then the absolute value. A steady slow decline is the norm for most RL runs; a sudden drop to the bottom is collapse; this run is a steady slow rise, which is the third kind and also the easiest to misread.

Absolute values should be interpreted in the context of the task. 0.38~0.46 is a moderately flat distribution, far from 0 (fully deterministic) and log(vocab) (fully uniform), and does not by itself constitute danger.
Look at it together with dynsam/avg@n: if entropy rises and the success rate also rises, exploration is producing results; if entropy rises and the success rate does not move, it is wasted money.

Weighted by token, so long responses (agentic trajectories often run to tens of thousands of tokens) have much greater weight than short responses, and overall entropy is dominated by long trajectories.
items.observed: The entropy of both runs rises with training, not falls. pro step 1 0.395265 → step 19 0.406269, up 0.011004 (relative +2.8%); the process is not monotonic, 8 of 18 intervals are decreases, the lowest point is step 2 0.379237 and the highest point is step 17 0.408738; overall, it raises the 0.38~0.40 plateau of steps 1~9 to the 0.40~0.409 plateau of steps 13~19. flash step 1 0.413307 → step 25 0.456110, up 0.042803 (relative +10.4%), nearly 4 times that of pro; 9 of 24 intervals decrease, the lowest point is step 5 0.408574, and the highest point is exactly step 25. Over the same period dynsam/avg@n rises for pro from 0.5647 to 0.6334, and for flash from 0.5137 to 0.6408 (critic/rewards/mean is a different measure, it measures the reward average of trained trajectories, its values are lower than avg@n, pro rises from 0.5522 to 0.5946 and flash from 0.5167 to 0.5935, the two are not equal); dynsam/passrate/one rises from 0.1779 to 0.2620 (pro), and from 0.1208 to 0.3123 (flash). The correlation coefficient between entropy and avg@n is pro 0.827, flash 0.861; with rewards it is pro 0.716, flash 0.821; both are clearly positive correlations.
traps: The loss in the name is misleading: it does not participate in backpropagation, a rising value does not mean training is getting worse, and expecting it to decrease like a loss will make you read it backwards.
It rises in both runs, indicating this is not an accident of a particular restart or dataset; do not treat it as single-point noise.

Entropy and “within-batch diversity” are not the same quantity: entropy is the degree to which the token distribution within a single sequence is flattened, while batch diversity also depends on whether different rollouts give different answers. Rising entropy only means the former is widening.

Apparent correlation does not equal causation: entropy and avg@n both rise over time, and each may simply follow training progress; there are only 19/25 points here, so no causal judgment can be made.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: mean per-token entropy of the policy
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: DAPO: an Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale (official project page, Algorithm Insights)
sources.quote: We observe an entropy-collapsing phenomenon in our initial experiments. We propose increasing the upper clip range of the importance sampling ratio in policy gradient loss to mitigate this problem.
sources.topic: Clip-Higher and entropy collapse
sources.note: This page directly links entropy to “diversity/exploration”, supporting our statement that reads the rise in actor/entropy_loss as an increase in exploration intensity.

sources.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
sources.quote: we identify an optimization bias in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which artificially increases response length (especially for incorrect outputs) during training.
sources.topic: Length bias of the group-relative objective
sources.note: The same bias makes answers longer and changes the token weight structure, so the rise in entropy_loss may partly come from length inflation rather than the distribution flattening—this run's ctx_response_length/mean happens to be clearly longer on flash.

sources.title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
sources.quote: In practice, we establish a transformation equation R=-a*e^H+b between entropy H and downstream performance R.
sources.topic: The trade-off between entropy and performance (entropy collapse narrative)
sources.note: The direction given by the paper, R=-a·e^H+b, is “the higher the entropy, the lower the performance”, and it treats entropy collapse as the norm; in this run entropy rises while avg@n also rises at the same time, which is opposite to that empirical law, so the reading that “rising entropy is benign” falls into a boundary case outside that paper's framework.

sources.title: SimpleTIR: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning
sources.quote: This issue compounds over successive turns, causing catastrophic gradient norm explosions that derail the training process.
sources.topic: Gradient norm explosion in multi-turn agentic scenarios
sources.note: The same mechanism (external feedback introduces low-probability tokens) is also a candidate explanation for entropy fluctuation in the agentic branch; this item serves only as background, and we do not use it to determine the nature of the entropy rise in this run.

sources.title: DISPO: Enhancing Training Efficiency and Stability in Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Model Mathematical Reasoning
sources.quote: For correct responses, weights >1 increase the average token entropy (i.e., exploration) while weights <1 decrease it (i.e., distillation) -- both beneficial but causing gradual performance degradation when excessive.
sources.topic: How the clipping direction raises/lowers entropy
sources.note: The paper's ablation shows that which side's clipping pushes entropy up makes a difference, and that “excess” brings slow performance degradation; therefore, the entropy rise in this run cannot be uniformly read as benign, and one must also see whether the magnitude is excessive—this is exactly the boundary condition of our reading.

sources.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization（Overall Loss and Entropy Bonus）
sources.authors: Shengyi Huang, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Antonin Raffin, Anssi Kanervisto, Weixun Wang
sources.quote: The overall loss is calculated as `loss = policy_loss - entropy * entropy_coefficient + value_loss * value_coefficient`, which maximizes an entropy bonus term.
sources.topic: Entropy is a quantity explicitly maximized by the objective function
sources.note: PPO's objective already includes a -entropy*coef bonus term; so entropy is not a pure “spontaneous exploration” reading, it is simultaneously explicitly maximized by the objective function, and before attributing the entire entropy rise to the model's active exploration, this term must first be accounted for.

items.name: general category policy gradient objective (broken down by dataset)
items.unit: Dimensionless, measured in this run as -0.011~0.066 (excluding the single-step 0.1642 of dataset-1doa)
items.what: The policy gradient objective under general (general question-answering category) likewise has only dataset-level tag (actor/general/dataset-xxxx/pg_loss), with no category aggregation. It is the category that best reveals 「the mean masks the fluctuation」: the magnitudes differ among datasets by more than an order of magnitude.
items.how: Statistics are computed separately for each dataset under the clipped policy-gradient objective; the clip interval uses the global 0.27 / 0.2.
items.why: A magnitude jump on an individual dataset is a common signal of a change in data quality or task difficulty. The role of this kind of fine-grained metric is not to look at trends, but, when the global pg_loss becomes anomalous, to quickly identify which data source pulled it up. The dataset-1doa of this run flash is a typical example.
read: Focus on whether any single dataset jumps by an order of magnitude, rather than on the overall trend.

The steady-state levels of the four general datasets differ greatly: the means of dataset-epqd and dataset-5610 are 0.009~0.011, while the means of dataset-1doa and dataset-trla are between 0.002~0.033 and fluctuate more.

This run has a clear outlier: the maximum of flash's actor/general/dataset-1doa/pg_loss is 0.1642, while its mean is 0.03344 and minimum is -0.01054; the magnitude is clearly off the group and this step is worth investigating separately.
Negative values also exist (some steps are negative for three datasets); do not assume pg_loss is necessarily positive.
items.observed: Four datasets, pro 19 steps / flash 25 steps. pro: dataset-1doa first 0.008889, last -0.003855, mean 0.002451, range -0.007474~0.01338; dataset-5610 first 0.008850, last 0.009104, mean 0.01122, range 0.0007542~0.02312; dataset-epqd first 0.01238, last 0.002755, mean 0.008681, range -0.0009120~0.01619; dataset-trla first 0.004553, last 0.03114, mean 0.009504, range -0.002430~0.03114. flash: dataset-1doa first -0.004153, last 0.02908, mean 0.03344, range -0.01054~0.1642; dataset-5610 first 0.005909, last 0.008499, mean 0.01013, range -0.006234~0.03302; dataset-epqd first 0.01195, last 0.007850, mean 0.01055, range -0.001976~0.05985; dataset-trla first 0.001938, last 0.009389, mean 0.01203, range -0.002815~0.06535. Negative-value steps: pro's 1doa 7/19, epqd 2/19, trla 1/19, 5610 0/19; flash's 1doa 7/25, 5610 5/25, epqd 3/25, trla 3/25. Outliers are concentrated in the later part of flash (dataset-1doa single step 0.1642, dataset-trla 0.06535, dataset-epqd 0.05985), consistent with the period when pg_loss rose overall in the latter half of flash.
traps: There is no category-aggregated tag actor/general/pg_loss; do not combine the numbers from the four datasets into a single “general category value”.

Negative values are not errors. pg_loss is an objective function value with clip, and a single step being negative is common at the dataset level, especially when there are few samples and advantages have both signs.
The single-step 0.1642 for flash's dataset-1doa is an outlier; when citing the mean 0.03344, state that it is inflated by this one point.
Comparing absolute values across datasets is meaningless; their prompt compositions and difficulties may differ, and the dashboard provides no normalization explanation.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Global gradient norm (global gradient norm before clipping)
items.unit: Dimensionless (L2 norm), measured 0.0048~0.0335 in this run
items.what: Treat all parameter gradients computed at this step as one large vector and measure how long it is. The official description explicitly states it is the pre-clipping value (global gradient norm before clipping), so it reflects how large a step the model originally wanted to take before the optimizer acts; the step size actually applied to the parameters has already been reduced once by the optimizer's clipping rule, and the dashboard does not give the post-clipping norm.
items.how: Collect gradients for all parameters participating in the update, concatenate them into one global vector, take the L2 norm, and report the pre-clipping value. In this run, actor/lr is identically 0.000003 (unchanged across both runs and all steps), so relative changes in the gradient are directly reflected in the actual update magnitude at this step.
items.why: It is the thermometer for optimizer stability. A slow rise over the long term usually means the loss surface is getting steeper or the learning rate is relatively too large; the most common cause of a violent single-step spike is encountering an anomalous sample or anomalous batch (dirty data, overly long sequences, mis-scored reward, an abnormal log-prob value for some rollout), such samples produce huge gradients, and if not clipped, a single update can wreck the model, and the following several steps are spent recovering. So in engineering practice it is often used paired with the optimizer's clipping threshold, and is the first switch for "whether manual intervention is needed".
read: First check whether it is a one-off. Sort all steps; if the second place is far from the first, treat it as a single-point event and do not judge the trend based on it.

A spike must be checked against other metrics at the same step: whether pg_loss, entropy_loss, rewards/mean, train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl, avg@n, and timing_s/* are also anomalous at the same time. If only grad_norm jumps alone, it usually means this step's update was absorbed by clipping and did not affect the result.

Look at this together with actor/num_zeros_in_grad: a sudden change in the share of zero-gradient parameters indicates that this batch of data did not cover certain parameters, and it may share the same root cause as the grad_norm spike.

This metric is the pre-clipping value, so a large value does not mean the parameters were actually pushed a big step. Conversely, it being flat also does not prove that the clipping threshold was not triggered—the dashboard does not give the post-clipping norm, nor the proportion of clipping triggers.
items.observed: pro step 19 0.0335148 is the only occurrence, and also the last step. The steps before and after: step 15 0.00537442, step 16 0.00532933, step 17 0.00699047, step 18 0.00480826, step 19 0.0335148. The median of the 18 steps excluding step 19 is 0.005626 (mean 0.005833, range 0.004808~0.008726); the spike is 5.96× the median of the remaining steps, and by the 0.0054 criterion given in the brief it is 6.2×; the second-highest peak is step 9 at 0.00872634, only 26% of the spike. flash is smooth throughout: 25 steps range 0.004928~0.009054, median 0.005700, mean 0.005836, with the maximum at step 16, only 1.59× the median, and no comparable one-off spike. As for whether it is accompanied by other metric anomalies: comparing the same step (pro step 19) with step 18, actor/pg_loss 0.00392328→0.00529222, actor/entropy_loss 0.406803→0.406269, critic/rewards/mean 0.590478→0.594634, dynsam/avg@n 0.617368→0.633419, dynsam/passrate/zero 0.162622→0.134837, actor/pg_tis_clipfrac 0.00025761→0.00019634, actor/lr is identically 0.000003, actor/skipped_iter and actor/update_skipped are identically 0, all within the normal fluctuation range and none became anomalous along with it. Relative to the mean of steps 15/16/17, timing_s/trainer_ops at step 19 is on the high side at 7332.5 seconds (the first three non-stationary steps are 3822.2, 6353.6, 6443.8); ctx_response_length/mean rising from 59k to 97k in token magnitude falls within the normal rise range for this run; train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl rising from 0.00679548 to 0.00768816 is likewise a continuous gradual rise, not a jump. Conclusion: this spike is isolated in the data and is not accompanied by any other metric anomaly; the dashboard does not explain its cause. One more point to add: looking only at the time series cannot rule out the coincidence that "this is the first time in this run, and step 19 is the last step"; subsequent steps are what determine whether it is a new normal.
traps: It is the pre-clipping value, and it is not the same thing as the update magnitude actually applied to the parameters; you cannot directly say 'the model was pushed a big step'.
Judging training divergence from a single-point spike alone is overinterpretation; this time all other metrics at the same step are normal.
pro's spike happens to occur at the last recorded step, and flash has never had a similar spike; the sample size does not support any trend conclusion.
The median and mean differ a lot here (0.005626 vs. 0.007290, pulled up by spikes); citing this metric requires stating which definition is used.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: global gradient norm before clipping
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Why gradient clipping accelerates training: A theoretical justification for adaptivity
sources.quote: Further, this smoothness positively correlates with the gradient norm, and contrary to standard assumptions in the literature, it can grow with the norm of the gradient.
sources.topic: The theoretical connection between gradient norm and instability
sources.note: The paper proves that gradient smoothness is positively correlated with gradient norm and can grow with the norm, i.e. a large-norm step means the effective curvature becomes larger and a single-step update may go out of control; this supports treating the 6× spike at pro step 19 as a "single-step anomaly" to be investigated separately, rather than merging it into the trend.

sources.title: GradientStabilizer: Fix the Norm, Not the Gradient
sources.quote: Training instability in modern deep learning systems is frequently triggered by rare but extreme gradient-norm spikes, which can induce oversized parameter updates, corrupt optimizer state, and lead to slow recovery or divergence.
sources.topic: Gradient norm spikes and training instability
sources.note: The paper directly lists “rare but extreme gradient norm spikes” as a trigger source of training instability, and points out that they cause oversized updates and pollute optimizer state; this is our first basis for troubleshooting “grad_norm spikes should be checked as anomalous single points.”

sources.title: SimpleTIR: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Tool-Integrated Reasoning
sources.quote: This issue compounds over successive turns, causing catastrophic gradient norm explosions that derail the training process.
sources.topic: Gradient norm explosion in multi-turn agentic scenarios
sources.note: The paper gives the mechanism: multi-turn tool feedback causes distribution drift, low-probability tokens accumulate round by round, ultimately manifesting as gradient norm explosion and crashing training; this run is exactly 43~65 rounds of agentic training, and this links grad_norm spikes to the crash.

sources.title: Beyond Precision: Training-Inference Mismatch is an Optimization Problem and Simple LR Scheduling Fixes It
sources.quote: we find that the mismatch can be effectively suppressed by shrinking the update size.
sources.topic: Use learning rate scheduling to suppress training-inference mismatch
sources.note: The paper states that gradient noise and training-inference mismatch escalate in sync with training; but the grad_norm of this run pro has only single-point spikes and no monotonic rise, which is inconsistent with that narrative, indicating that this rule does not necessarily apply to this run.

sources.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization（Global Gradient Clipping）
sources.authors: Shengyi Huang, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Antonin Raffin, Anssi Kanervisto, Weixun Wang
sources.quote: For each update iteration in an epoch, PPO rescales the gradients of the policy and value network so that the “global l2 norm” (i.e., the norm of the concatenated gradients of all parameters) does not exceed `0.5`.
sources.topic: The definition of global gradient norm
sources.note: This explains that gradient clipping targets the “global L2 norm after concatenating all parameters,” and is paired with a fixed threshold; it supports reading actor/grad_norm as the global norm before clipping, and it must be viewed together with the clipping threshold.

sources.title: Computed here: the gradient spike at pro step 19 is isolated within the recorded range
sources.quote: At pro step 19, grad_norm is 0.0335148, which is 5.96 times the median 0.005626 of the other 18 steps; in the same step, pg_loss, entropy_loss, rewards/mean, train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl, avg@n, and passrate/zero are all within the normal fluctuation range; flash has no similar spikes throughout (25-step range 0.004928~0.009054).
sources.topic: Whether the spike is anomalous
sources.note: The basis for judging it as a “single-step anomaly” is: the same batch of performance metrics did not move along with it. But note that step 19 is the last step within the recorded range, and there are no subsequent steps to verify whether it is a new normal or an isolated event — this is insufficient evidence, not proof of innocence.

items.name: actor learning rate (learning rate)
items.unit: Dimensionless, this run is constant at 0.000003 (3e-6), and the dashboard formats it in scientific notation
items.what: This is the learning rate currently used by the actor optimizer, i.e. the scaling coefficient when converting gradients into parameter updates at each step. It is a configuration quantity (or the output of a scheduler), not a measured value. In this run, both models are 3e-6 throughout.
items.how: The dashboard does not give an official explanation for this tag, but in meta.json's formats, a sci (scientific notation) formatting rule is specifically configured for ^actor/lr$, so the dashboard homepage and detail page display it in scientific notation. The value stored in the repository is 0.000003, identical for both runs and at every step. The dashboard does not provide any information about the learning rate scheduler (warmup, decay, cosine, etc.).
items.why: The learning rate determines “how far you can go when the gradient direction is correct.” When it is too large, grad_norm, pg_loss, and entropy_loss will jitter along with it, and in severe cases training diverges; when it is too small, all metrics are stable but barely move, looking healthy but actually stagnating. Because it is also a multiplier for grad_norm, when troubleshooting “whether grad_norm spikes have caused actual harm,” you must first confirm whether the learning rate changed in sync — in this run it did not, so the spike of 0.0335148 at step 19 was not amplified by the learning rate.
read: This is a straight line, indicating that this training run did not use a learning rate schedule, or that the scheduler's output was saturated at 3e-6. The dashboard does not state which one it is.
Do not infer 'training is stable' from 'the learning rate is constant': stability also depends on the fluctuations of grad_norm and pg_loss.

Numerical precision has only 1 significant digit (0.000003); any schedule change smaller than 5e-7 is invisible in this repository; do not assert based on this that 'the scheduler is not working at all'.
To see the actual effect of the learning rate, read it together with grad_norm; their product is the per-step parameter update magnitude.
items.observed: pro step 19, flash step 25, all 0.000003, with no step as an exception, no null. That is, from the start of training on 2026-09-15 to pro step 19 / flash step 25, the actor-side learning rate did not undergo any visible change, including before and after pro's 9 restarts and flash's 4 restarts. By contrast, actor/grad_norm at the same step fluctuates (pro 0.004808~0.033515), indicating that this straight line is not the result of “all optimizer states being frozen”; it is just that the learning rate itself did not move. The dashboard does not state whether this is a constant configuration or the scheduler output was truncated.
traps: The learning rates of the two runs are exactly the same; do not use it to explain the performance difference between pro and flash.
Storage precision is only 1 significant digit; saying 'the learning rate is exactly equal to 3e-6' is overinterpretation; the accurate statement is 'displayed as 0.000003'.
Do not skip it because it is constant: it is the conversion factor from grad_norm to the actual update magnitude, and it must be cited when explaining the impact of spikes.
The dashboard does not provide scheduler information; do not speculate that warmup or decay exists—no scheduling trace is visible in the data.

sources.title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization
sources.quote: We provide empirical evidence that our proposed modification (i) decouples the optimal choice of weight decay factor from the setting of the learning rate for both standard SGD and Adam
sources.topic: Coupling of the learning rate and regularization in adaptive optimizers
sources.note: The paper explains that in adaptive optimizers weight decay and the learning rate are not equivalent and need to be decoupled; therefore, “actor/lr is identically 3e-6” can only show that the learning rate configuration was not changed, and cannot incidentally assert that the effective step size or regularization strength also did not change.

sources.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
sources.quote: We identify two crucial techniques for scaling up Muon: (1) adding weight decay and (2) carefully adjusting the per-parameter update scale.
sources.topic: Different optimizers make the same lr value incomparable
sources.note: The paper emphasizes that changing optimizers requires retuning the per-parameter update scale; the same lr value has a different effective step size under AdamW and Muon, so our actor/lr=3e-6 has no explanatory power without “which optimizer is used”.

sources.title: Disentangling Adaptive Gradient Methods from Learning Rates
sources.quote: We introduce a "grafting" experiment which decouples an update's magnitude from its direction, finding that many existing beliefs in the literature may have arisen from insufficient isolation of the implicit schedule of step sizes.
sources.topic: Common confusion about the learning rate metric
sources.note: The paper points out that many conclusions about adaptive optimizers come from “the implicit step-size schedule not being isolated”; although actor/lr is constant throughout this run, which rules out schedule confounding, it also amounts to our not having done any lr sensitivity experiments; “lr not changing is not a problem” is only a configuration fact, not a conclusion.

sources.title: GradientStabilizer: Fix the Norm, Not the Gradient
sources.quote: Training instability in modern deep learning systems is frequently triggered by rare but extreme gradient-norm spikes, which can induce oversized parameter updates, corrupt optimizer state, and lead to slow recovery or divergence.
sources.topic: Gradient norm spikes and training instability
sources.note: The paper also points out that gradient clipping “requires tuning the threshold and indiscriminately clips large updates”, indicating that grad_norm is coupled with the clipping threshold (and the effective step size); when reading actor/lr, one cannot assume that the step size is constant.

sources.title: Beyond Precision: Training-Inference Mismatch is an Optimization Problem and Simple LR Scheduling Fixes It
sources.quote: we find that the mismatch can be effectively suppressed by shrinking the update size.
sources.topic: Use learning rate scheduling to suppress training-inference mismatch
sources.note: The paper advocates triggering dynamic lr decay based on response length to suppress mismatch; actor/lr is constant throughout this run, which is another route of “not doing dynamic decay”, so “lr not changing is itself not a problem” holds only when mismatch has not worsened.

sources.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization（Global Gradient Clipping）
sources.authors: Shengyi Huang, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Antonin Raffin, Anssi Kanervisto, Weixun Wang
sources.quote: For each update iteration in an epoch, PPO rescales the gradients of the policy and value network so that the “global l2 norm” (i.e., the norm of the concatenated gradients of all parameters) does not exceed `0.5`.
sources.topic: The definition of global gradient norm
sources.note: The same mechanism means that once the norm crosses the threshold, the actual update step size is clipped by the threshold and is no longer the same thing as actor/lr; when reading lr, one cannot assume “lr constant ⇒ step size constant”.

items.name: PPO clipping ratio (clip fraction)
items.what: It is supposed to answer “what proportion of tokens at this step were blocked by PPO's ratio clipping because the difference between the old and new policies was too large”, and is one of the most commonly watched health metrics in PPO. But in this repository's data it is identically 0. The dashboard does not provide an official description for this metric, nor does it explain why it is 0.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. Literally translated from the name, it is the proportion of tokens whose PPO ratio was clipped, usually counted over the effective tokens of this run's training batch. Here one can only report that the value read is itself 0; one cannot infer back how it is actually aggregated.
items.why: In normal PPO training, this number represents how much gradient signal is discarded by the clipping rule. Persistently above 0.1~0.2 often indicates that the policy moves too far each step and the learning rate needs to be reduced or data staleness shortened; staying near 0 for a long time indicates that the clipping rule is basically not taking effect and the policy update is very conservative. So it forms a pair with actor/pg_loss: the former says “how much was changed but blocked”, and the latter says “whether the direction of change is right”.
read: This run cannot use it to judge whether clipping occurred. Being identically zero only means this column carries no information; it does not mean 'never clipping', nor does it mean 'always clipping'.

To judge clipping, you can only look at actor/clip_high (identically 0.27) and actor/clip_low (identically 0.2), the two clip interval boundaries: they prove that the clipping interval was indeed configured, but they likewise do not contain the trigger proportion.
Alternative readings are elsewhere: the actor/pg_tis_clipfrac series has data, and train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl also changes genuinely; to look at policy drift, you should read these two.
First confirm that it is not your own misreading. This column is 0 across both runs, all steps, and all same-named tags by category and dataset; it is not an issue of a missing step or a subset.
items.observed: Confirm identically zero. Across the two runs combined: pro has 25 tags containing pg_clipfrac (1 global, 3 category aggregates, 1 agentic, 20 dataset-level), totaling 475 values, with 0 non-zero; flash likewise has 25 tags, totaling 625 values, with 0 non-zero. All values are the number 0, not null, meaning that this column is reported, but everything reported is 0. By contrast, the same-named clip range bounds actor/clip_high are identically 0.27 and actor/clip_low identically 0.2, unchanged across all steps in both runs; while the TIS-related actor/pg_tis_clipfrac series has non-zero data throughout. Therefore it can be concluded: the dashboard is configured with the clip range and also with TIS clipping statistics, but does not provide the clip fraction of the PPO ratio. The dashboard does not explain the cause of this 0, so we can only report this observation.
traps: The most common misreading is interpreting 0 as 'training is very healthy, with no clipping at all'. This is a reported value, not a measurement conclusion.
Nor should you go the other way and speculate that 'the clipping function is broken'—the dashboard gives no explanation, and both interpretations exceed what the data can support.
Do not conflate it with actor/pg_tis_clipfrac; the latter has non-zero data and a clear trend, and the two are not measuring the same thing.

Its 0 is different from actor/lr being identically 3e-6: a constant learning rate is itself a valid factual description, whereas clip fraction being identically 0 more likely means this column is not connected to actual statistics.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
sources.quote: Whereas standard policy gradient methods perform one gradient update per data sample, we propose a novel objective function that enables multiple epochs of minibatch updates.
sources.topic: PPO clipped surrogate objective and single-epoch/multi-epoch updates
sources.note: The paper defines PPO's selling point as 'multiple epochs of minibatch updates on the same batch'; the ratio only deviates from 1 under multi-epoch updates; in this run pg_clipfrac is identically zero throughout, which precisely shows that this premise is not fulfilled, rather than that clipping is ineffective.

sources.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
sources.quote: we show that GRPO exhibits a clipping bias from the clip term, which can amplify high-prior behaviors learned during pretraining even without informative rewards.
sources.topic: Bias introduced by the clipping term itself
sources.note: The paper attributes GRPO's behavior bias to the clip term; but in this run pg_clipfrac is identically zero (clipping was never triggered), indicating that this mechanism is inactive in this run; do not directly transfer the failure mode described in this paper to this run.

sources.title: Batch size-invariance for policy optimization
sources.authors: Jacob Hilton, Karl Cobbe, John Schulman
sources.quote: Our key insight is to decouple the proximal policy (used for controlling policy updates) from the behavior policy (used for off-policy corrections).
sources.topic: Decoupling of proximal policy and behavior policy
sources.note: The paper's core insight is to separate the 'proximal policy that controls updates' from the 'behavior policy that performs off-policy correction'; in this run pg_clipfrac(≡0) and pg_tis_clipfrac(>0) are precisely the readings for these two things, so pg_clipfrac being identically zero only negates the former.

sources.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization（Debug variables）
sources.authors: Shengyi Huang, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Antonin Raffin, Anssi Kanervisto, Weixun Wang
sources.quote: `clipfrac`: the fraction of the training data that triggered the clipped objective.
sources.topic: Standard definition of clipfrac
sources.note: This gives the standard definition of clipfrac = the proportion of data that triggers clipping; in this run all values are identically zero, which by definition means 'no token ever triggered clipping', supporting our statement that 'clipping never took effect'.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) — verl documentation（Configuration）
sources.quote: `actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio`: The PPO clip range. Default to 0.2
sources.topic: verl's clipping interval is a single-parameter symmetric setting
sources.note: Combining this default value with the definition of clipfrac, we can confirm that the clipping range for this run is [1−0.2, 1+0.27] = [0.8, 1.27], rather than [0.8, 1.2] in the documentation.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) — verl documentation（ppo_epochs）
sources.quote: `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_epochs`: Number of epochs for PPO updates on one set of sampled trajectories for actor
sources.topic: Configuration implications of single-epoch updates
sources.note: In a single-epoch update, the ratio is identically equal to 1 before the update, so clipfrac is destined to be 0 at the first step; this turns 'pg_clipfrac is identically zero' from an observation into an explainable configuration consequence.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation（Important Note on Common Implementation Mistakes）
sources.quote: Many LLM-RL implementations incorrectly apply PPO by **ignoring the actual rollout policy** π_rollout and assuming the training reference policy π_old is the behavior policy.
sources.topic: π_rollout and π_old are two different policies
sources.note: The documentation points out that π_rollout and π_old are two different things, and many implementations mistakenly treat π_old as the behavior policy; therefore pg_clipfrac being identically zero (π_θ and π_old are consistent) cannot lead to the conclusion that 'there is no off-policy bias'; this conclusion must be tied to that TIS item.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation (Overview: Common off-policy scenarios / two-stage drift)
sources.quote: This is the distribution shift between the data collection policy and the training reference policy.
sources.topic: Two-stage drift: rollout→old and old→current
sources.note: This page splits “rollout→old (off-policy discrepancy, corrected with importance sampling)” and “old→current (parameter update drift, controlled with PPO clipping)” into two drifts; in this run, the readings of the two drifts are pg_tis_clipfrac>0 and pg_clipfrac≡0, respectively, corresponding exactly one-to-one.

sources.title: This site's calculation: clip fraction and PPO KL are identically zero throughout (it is 0, not empty)
sources.quote: actor/pg_clipfrac and actor/ppo_kl are equal to the value 0 on all steps in both runs: pro 50 tags / 940 values, flash 50 tags / 1250 values, all non-empty and 0.
sources.topic: How to read identically zero
sources.note: First rule out “not reported”: these points are numeric 0, not null values. By the definition of clipfrac, when the new-to-old policy ratio is identically 1, it is 0 by definition; this also shows that this step performed only one round of updates and that the clipping interval was never triggered.

items.name: policy-gradient objective (clipped policy-gradient objective)
items.what: the objective function value that PPO is actually minimizing (in the official wording, the clipped policy-gradient objective); intuitively, it's 「how much the policy at this step has changed relative to the version of the policy used at sampling time, and whether the direction of the change is right」. It is not on the same order of magnitude as language model pretraining loss; a small absolute value is normal. What you look at is the trend and relative magnitude, not 「how low it needs to drop to count as converged」.
items.how: The official description is the clipped policy-gradient objective. Multiply the log-prob ratio between this run's rollout (old policy) and the current policy by the advantage estimate; if the ratio falls outside the clip interval, clip it; average over the tokens participating in training. This run's clip interval can be read from two constant columns: actor/clip_high is identically 0.27 and actor/clip_low is identically 0.2, unchanged across the two runs and all steps.
items.why: It is the primary readout of 「whether the policy is still being effectively driven」. Close to 0 and flat for a long time usually means the advantage estimate has no longer any discriminative power (for example, a batch of prompts is all correct or all wrong, and the advantage is all 0); the training at this point is basically wasted. A sudden increase by an order of magnitude indicates that the old and new policies differ greatly on this batch of data, and is a signal of distribution drift or data quality change.
read: Do not look at the absolute value; look at magnitude and trend: a slow rise while stable on a small plateau is healthy; a single-step jump of 5~10 times requires going back to check that step's data composition and effective sample size.

Look at it together with dynsam/avg@n. If the success rate rises and pg_loss also rises, this step is indeed changing the policy; if the success rate rises while pg_loss stays pinned at 0, the improvement mainly comes from sampling luck rather than policy updates.
Compare with actor/pg_tis_clipfrac: when the TIS clipping ratio rises, more importance sampling weights are clipped off, and the pg_loss reading is pushed down; the two must be interpreted together.

Cross-run comparisons are meaningless unless the two runs have identical batch composition, sequence length, and hyperparameters. The pg_loss magnitudes of pro and flash differ by nearly a factor of 2; the first thing to suspect is that these differ, not that “flash is learning more aggressively.”
items.observed: pro, 19 steps: first 0.00411032, last 0.00529222, mean 0.004061; min 0.00199298 (step 17), max 0.00738070 (step 13). First-half mean 0.003535, second-half 0.004534 — a slow rise rather than divergence. flash, 25 steps: first 0.000840813, last 0.00952360, mean 0.007565; the min is step 1 at 0.000840813, max 0.01947720 (step 19). First-half mean 0.003431, second-half 0.011380; the rise is far larger than pro's. So the statement "flash is about 3× larger than pro" has to be said in two steps: by mean, flash is 1.86× pro (0.007565 / 0.004061); step 19 against step 19 it is 1.80× (0.00529222 / 0.00952360, take the reciprocal, i.e. 1.80); only by taking pro's low end (about 0.002) against flash's high end (about 0.006~0.020) do you get more than 3×. Across all 19 steps pro never went negative (min 0.00199298), and flash is likewise all positive.
traps: “A 3× difference” is a magnitude impression, not a strict ratio: on the mean basis it is 1.86×, and same-step to same-step it is 1.80×. Comparing this number across runs has no absolute standard.
This small value cannot be compared with the absolute value of pretraining loss; the dimensions and the normalization method are both different.

Global pg_loss is all positive, but when broken down by dataset a large amount is negative (see actor/visual/dataset-pt5v/pg_loss), so the global sign cannot be used to infer the sign of an individual dataset.

Part of flash’s increase comes from long contexts getting longer (ctx_response_length/mean rose from about 55k to the 120k token range); token weighting changes affect the mean reading, and this should be known when looking at the trend.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: clipped policy-gradient objective
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
sources.quote: Whereas standard policy gradient methods perform one gradient update per data sample, we propose a novel objective function that enables multiple epochs of minibatch updates.
sources.topic: PPO clipped surrogate objective and single-epoch/multi-epoch updates
sources.note: This passage shows that pg_loss is a surrogate objective rather than a supervised loss, so its absolute value has no dimensional meaning; only the relative trend is readable.

sources.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
sources.quote: we identify an optimization bias in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which artificially increases response length (especially for incorrect outputs) during training.
sources.topic: Length bias of the group-relative objective
sources.note: The paper points out that GRPO-style objectives carry an optimization bias toward "artificially lengthening responses (especially incorrect ones)", so a slow rise in pg_loss cannot be read directly as "the policy is getting better"; our reading of that trend must carry this confounder.

sources.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
sources.quote: we show that GRPO exhibits a clipping bias from the clip term, which can amplify high-prior behaviors learned during pretraining even without informative rewards.
sources.topic: Bias introduced by the clipping term itself
sources.note: That paper shows that the clip term affects the optimization direction even without "useful reward", and is necessary background for understanding what pg_loss measures.

items.name: TIS clip fraction (truncated importance sampling clip fraction)
items.what: This is the clip fraction on the TIS (truncated importance sampling) side, i.e. when correcting the difference between "the policy at sampling time" and "the policy at training time", how much of the weight gets truncated for exceeding the allowed range. It is a completely different thing from actor/pg_clipfrac: that one counts clipping of the PPO ratio, this one counts truncation of the importance sampling weights. In this run pg_clipfrac is identically zero, while this group has real data with a trend.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. Literal reading of the tag name: pg means policy gradient, tis means truncated importance sampling, clipfrac is the share of weights that get clipped. The reported values are on the order of 1e-5~1e-3, far smaller than 1, indicating that the vast majority of importance sampling weights fall within the allowed range. The same family also has four side-specific sub-metrics that break clipping down by direction and boundary: pg_tis_clipfrac_pos_high, pg_tis_clipfrac_pos_low, pg_tis_clipfrac_neg_high, pg_tis_clipfrac_neg_low.
items.why: The TIS clipping ratio measures how much of "how far the policy version used for training differs from the policy version at data sampling time" gets cut off. When it rises, it indicates that data staleness or the magnitude of in-flight updates is increasing; at this point, a portion of old data is truncated, the samples actually participating in training become fewer, equivalent to a shrinking effective batch. This is a type of efficiency loss in long training that gets overlooked but is very real, and it is also a direct readout for judging whether partial/avg_staleness is starting to harm training.
read: Look at the trend, not the absolute value: this run is on the order of 1e-4, itself far from dangerous; what is worth mentioning is that it rises with training.
Reading it together with partial/avg_staleness is most informative. In this repository it correlates highly with staleness (pro 0.825, flash 0.920); they are two sides of the same thing.

The four per-side submetrics should be examined separately for direction: pos_low and neg_low are clearly larger than pos_high and neg_high, indicating that the clipped weights are concentrated on the “low boundary” side.
Don’t confuse it with actor/pg_clipfrac, which is identically zero. When the dashboard has no pg_clipfrac, this group is currently the only reading that reflects “how much signal is clipped.”
items.observed: pro: first 0.0000212671 (step 1, also the global minimum) → last 0.000196341 (step 19), mean 0.0001742, max 0.000332057 (step 14). The rise mainly occurs at steps 1~6 (0.0000213 → 0.0002465, more than tenfold); afterward it fluctuates on a high plateau of about 0.00024~0.00033 at steps 9~14, drops to 0.0000266~0.0000665 at steps 15~17, returns to the 0.0002 order in the last two steps, and overall is "first climb, then fluctuate at a high level". flash: first 0.0000451336 → last 0.000100572, mean 0.0001863, max 0.000312428 (step 24), min 0.0000403914 (step 16); at steps 1~11 it steadily rises from 0.000045 to 0.000271, then oscillates back and forth between 0.00004~0.00031, with no unidirectional trend in the final segment. Looking by side, pro's pos_low last value 0.0000962139, neg_low last value 0.0000796201, whereas pos_high last value 0.0000111908, neg_high last value 0.00000931605; the low-boundary side is about one order of magnitude higher than the high-boundary side, and this ratio relationship is stable throughout.
