The correlation coefficients with partial/avg_staleness are pro 0.825, flash 0.920, the most strongly correlated pair in this set of data; the relationship with entropy_loss is not this strong (pro's pg_loss correlation of the order of 0.23; staleness itself is almost uncorrelated with entropy, pro -0.112, flash 0.121).
traps: The most common misreading is treating it as an alias for actor/pg_clipfrac. The two have different statistical objects, and the latter is identically zero, so they cannot substitute for each other.
A value on the order of 1e-4 does not mean it is unimportant: it measures the proportion of discarded weights, which is not the same thing as “how many tokens participate in training.”

In the names of the four per-side submetrics, pos/neg refers to weight direction and high/low refers to the boundary; do not read them as “positive/negative clipping amounts.” The dashboard provides no official explanation; all definitions here are translated literally from the tag names.
Its high correlation with staleness does not equal causation; in this run both rise over time, and there are only 19/25 points.

sources.title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization
sources.quote: Unlike previous algorithms that adopt token-level importance ratios, GSPO defines the importance ratio based on sequence likelihood and performs sequence-level clipping, rewarding, and optimization.
sources.topic: token-level vs sequence-level importance ratio
sources.note: GSPO explicitly states that token-level importance ratio variance is high and switches to sequence-level ratios; therefore, the fact that this token-level truncation ratio is very small in this run does not imply that "off-policy bias is safe overall"—it only means that under the token metric, few are truncated.

sources.title: Learning to Explore with Parameter-Space Noise: A Deep Dive into Parameter-Space Noise for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
sources.quote: To mitigate the resulting sampling-update mismatch, we incorporate truncated importance sampling (TIS).
sources.topic: TIS is used to handle sampling-update mismatch
sources.note: The paper explicitly uses TIS to mitigate "the mismatch between sampling and updating", consistent with our reading of pg_tis_clipfrac as the truncation ratio of the probability deviation between rollout and training recomputation.

sources.title: GIPO: Gaussian Importance Sampling Policy Optimization
sources.quote: GIPO (Gaussian Importance sampling Policy Optimization) is proposed as a policy optimization objective based on truncated importance sampling, replacing hard clipping with a log-ratio-based Gaussian trust weight to softly damp extreme importance ratios while maintaining non-zero gradients.
sources.topic: The cost of TIS hard truncation
sources.note: The paper points out that existing TIS with hard truncation directly zeros out the gradients of extreme ratios and instead uses Gaussian trust weights as a replacement; therefore, although that truncation ratio of the order of 1e-4 in this run is small, the portion of samples that are truncated does not contribute gradients, and it cannot be read simply as "the ratio is small, so it's fine".

sources.title: F-TIS: Harnessing Diverse Models in Collaborative GRPO
sources.quote: prior work has identified that off-policy samples can hurt GRPO convergence.
sources.topic: The harm of off-policy samples to GRPO convergence
sources.note: The paper reiterates that off-policy samples harm GRPO convergence; the truncation ratio in this run is only of the order of 1e-4, which can only indicate that the off-policy problem is not prominent, and cannot be used to infer in reverse that "off-policy bias does not exist"—this is exactly the boundary when we read this curve.

sources.title: Efficient Multi-turn RL for GUI Agents via Decoupled Training and Adaptive Data Curation
sources.quote: stabilizing learning via truncated importance sampling for policy mismatch between policy rollout and updating.
sources.topic: Definitional description of TIS
sources.note: The paper describes TIS as a stabilization method for "handling policy mismatch between policy rollout and updating", corresponding word-for-word to our literal reading of this tag (measuring the ratio of probability deviation between rollout and training recomputation that is truncated).

sources.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
sources.quote: we show that its root cause lies in the floating point precision itself. The widely adopted BF16, despite its large dynamic range, introduces large rounding errors that breaks the consistency between training and inference.
sources.topic: Precision source of train-inference mismatch
sources.note: The paper traces a concrete source of π_rollout≠π_old to BF16 rounding error; this gives the most direct physical explanation for why the TIS truncation proportion is nonzero, and at the same time reminds us that a “low proportion” only indicates that numerical consistency is acceptable, not that the two engines are equivalent.

sources.title: Diagnosing Training Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
sources.quote: TIM is difficult to inspect because it is entangled with off-policy drift and common stabilization mechanisms.
sources.topic: Entanglement of mismatch and off-policy drift
sources.note: The paper points out that train-inference mismatch is entangled with off-policy drift and various stabilization mechanisms, making it difficult to observe in isolation; therefore, one cannot conclude “train-inference consistency” just because pg_tis_clipfrac is small. This curve is a small-sample detector, not a proof of equivalence.

sources.title: Batch size-invariance for policy optimization
sources.authors: Jacob Hilton, Karl Cobbe, John Schulman
sources.quote: Our key insight is to decouple the proximal policy (used for controlling policy updates) from the behavior policy (used for off-policy corrections).
sources.topic: Decoupling of proximal policy and behavior policy
sources.note: Same as above: the TIS one corresponds to the difference between the behavior policy and the proximal policy, and is a different matter from the proximal/current ratio (the one governed by pg_clipfrac); the two curves cannot substitute for each other.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation（Key Design Principle: Separation of IS Weights and Rejection Sampling）
sources.quote: **Truncated**: Upper clamped via `.clamp(max=rollout_is_threshold)` (TIS: Truncated Importance Sampling)
sources.topic: The standard definition of TIS
sources.note: Official documentation defines TIS as upper-bound truncation of importance weights (clamp(max=threshold)); in this run, pg_tis_clipfrac is precisely the proportion of weights truncated by this upper bound, consistent with our statement that “what is measured is the truncated proportion”.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation（Important Note on Common Implementation Mistakes）
sources.quote: Many LLM-RL implementations incorrectly apply PPO by **ignoring the actual rollout policy** π_rollout and assuming the training reference policy π_old is the behavior policy.
sources.topic: π_rollout and π_old are two different policies
sources.note: The documentation lists the ratio correction of π_old/π_rollout as a separate path, exactly corresponding to the independent reading pg_tis_clipfrac, supporting our reading of it as “a separate path, measuring the difference between rollout and training recomputation”.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation (Overview: Common off-policy scenarios / two-stage drift)
sources.quote: This is the distribution shift between the data collection policy and the training reference policy.
sources.topic: Two-stage drift: rollout→old and old→current
sources.note: Same as above: this reading belongs to Drift 1 (the difference between the data collection policy and the training reference policy); it and Drift 2, to which pg_clipfrac belongs, are two independent diagnostic quantities that cannot substitute for each other.

sources.title: Your Efficient RL Framework Secretly Brings You Off-Policy RL Training
sources.authors: Feng Yao, Liyuan Liu, Dinghuai Zhang, Chengyu Dong, Jingbo Shang, Jianfeng Gao
sources.venue: Notion engineering blog (verl/THUDM ecosystem, listed by the verl documentation as a TIS source)
sources.quote: In modern RL training frameworks (e.g., VeRL), different implementations are used for rollout generation (e.g., vLLM) and model training (e.g., FSDP). Here, we show the implementation gap implicitly turns the on-policy RL to be off-policy
sources.topic: Original definition of train-inference inconsistency and truncated importance sampling (TIS)
sources.note: We wrote 「what it measures is the truncated proportion of the deviation between rollout and training recomputation probabilities」. The TIS proposed in the blog is exactly the truncated ratio min(π_learner/π_sampler, C) itself; the metric name pg_tis_clipfrac corresponds directly to this method family, not to the clip of the PPO ratio.

sources.title: Your Efficient RL Framework Secretly Brings You Off-Policy RL Training
sources.authors: Feng Yao, Liyuan Liu, Dinghuai Zhang, Chengyu Dong, Jingbo Shang, Jianfeng Gao
sources.quote: Therefore, we use a clamp operation in our truncated importance sampling (TIS) for training stabilization.
sources.topic: TIS's clamp definition
sources.note: We wrote 「the value is on the order of 1e-5~1e-3, far less than 1, indicating that the vast majority of importance sampling weights fall within the allowable range」. The official definition of TIS is to apply clamp(max=C) to a ratio, so 「the proportion that is clamped」 being on the order of 1e-4 is indeed equivalent to 「almost no truncation」; the same page also gives an alternative definition (AReaL directly discards entire over-threshold samples), showing that this reading has been publicly implemented.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: A common heuristic, often inspired by algorithms like PPO and used in (Yao et al., 2025), applies a per-token importance ratio. While this typically has lower variance than the sequence-level ratio, it is a biased estimator that is theoretically unsound for autoregressive models.
sources.topic: Token-level IS is biased; only sequence-level is unbiased
sources.note: Our pg_tis_clipfrac is a token-level definition (and is further split into four sides by pos/neg×high/low). The paper explicitly says that token-level importance ratios for autoregressive models 「are theoretically unsound/biased」, and only sequence-level IS is unbiased; therefore, this reading can only be used to answer 「how many weights are truncated」, and cannot serve as evidence that 「off-policy has been correctly corrected」.

sources.title: FP8-RL: A Practical and Stable Low-Precision Stack for LLM Reinforcement Learning
sources.authors: Zhaopeng Qiu, Shuang Yu, Jingqi Zhang, Shuai Zhang, Xue Huang, Jingyi Yang, Junjie Lai
sources.quote: low-precision rollouts can deviate from the higher-precision policy assumed by the trainer, causing train-inference mismatch and potential instability
sources.topic: TIM caused by low-precision rollout and KV cache
sources.note: We wrote 「its increase indicates that data staleness or the magnitude of in-flight updates is growing, and at this point some old data is truncated」. The mitigation used in the paper is exactly importance-sampling-based rollout correction (token-level TIS/MIS variants), showing that this TIS clipping reading is the current mainstream public engineering definition.

sources.title: Prosperity before Collapse: How Far Can Off-Policy RL Reach with Stale Data on LLMs?
sources.authors: Haizhong Zheng, Jiawei Zhao, Beidi Chen
sources.quote: M2PO sharply reduces the fraction of clipped tokens under high staleness (from 1.22% to 0.06% over training), precisely masking high-variance tokens while maintaining stable optimization.
sources.topic: Order of magnitude of the clipped token fraction under high staleness
sources.note: We wrote 'a value on the order of 1e-4 does not mean it is unimportant... the vast majority of importance sampling weights fall within the allowable range.' Under an explicitly high-staleness setting, that paper reports a clipping fraction of 0.06%~1.22%, which is 2~3 orders of magnitude higher than this run's first value of 2.1e-5, supporting the relative judgment that 'the weights actually truncated in this run are very few.'

sources.title: Missing Old Logits in Asynchronous Agentic RL: Semantic Mismatch and Repair Methods for Off-Policy Correction
sources.authors: Zhong Guan, Yongjian Guo, Haoran Sun, Wen Huang, Shuai Di, Likang Wu, Xiong Jun Wu, Hongke Zhao
sources.quote: This missing-old-logit problem entangles discrepancy repair with staleness correction, breaks the intended semantics of decoupled correction, and makes clipping and masking thresholds interact undesirably.
sources.topic: The total ratio should be split into two terms: the 'engine difference term' and the 'staleness term'
sources.note: Our pg_tis_clipfrac interprets the clipping direction along the four sides pos/neg×high/low. That paper points out that in an asynchronous pipeline lacking old logits, the thresholds of clipping and masking contaminate each other (interact undesirably), so our four-sided interpretation holds only under the premise that 'old logits are fully available'.

sources.title: Trust Region Masking for Long-Horizon LLM Reinforcement Learning
sources.authors: Yingru Li, Jiacai Liu, Jiawei Xu, Yuxuan Tong, Ziniu Li, Qian Liu, Baoxiang Wang
sources.quote: a sequence-level quantity that cannot be controlled by token-independent methods like PPO clipping
sources.topic: What determines the error bound is the maximum token-level divergence (a sequence-level quantity)
sources.note: We wrote 'it measures how much weight is truncated because it exceeds the allowable range,' implicitly treating it as evidence of whether the trust region is effective. That paper proves that all error bounds depend on the maximum token-level divergence, a sequence-level quantity, and that it 'cannot be controlled by token-independent methods such as PPO clipping'; the token-level TIS clipping fraction therefore cannot be used to argue that the trust region is effective.

sources.title: Group-Relative REINFORCE Is Secretly an Off-Policy Algorithm: Demystifying Some Myths About GRPO and Its Friends
sources.authors: Chaorui Yao, Yanxi Chen, Yuchang Sun, Yushuo Chen, Wenhao Zhang, Xuchen Pan, Yaliang Li, Bolin Ding
sources.quote: without assuming a specific training data distribution, showing that it admits a native off-policy interpretation. This perspective yields two general principles for adapting REINFORCE to truly off-policy settings: regularizing policy updates, and actively shaping the data distribution.
sources.topic: GRPO-type algorithms themselves have an off-policy interpretation
sources.note: The abstract of that paper explicitly states that it 'reinterprets the role of importance sampling and clipping in GRPO,' and uniformly explains recent algorithms such as Asymmetric REINFORCE as a regularization form of the REINFORCE loss. This is the closest source in the public literature to the 'asymmetric' branch, but it is not a four-sided IS clipping definition split by positive/negative advantage or high/low boundaries.

sources.title: Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning
sources.quote: we show that the instability of RL under TIM is primarily caused by drift: a persistent bias between training and inference engines that accumulates with every training step.
sources.topic: There is a persistent bias between the two engines that accumulates over steps
sources.note: We wrote 'its rise indicates that data staleness or the magnitude of in-flight updates is increasing ... it is a direct readout for judging whether partial/avg_staleness is beginning to hurt training.' That paper reports that under quantization, score centering alone can match or exceed importance-sampling-based methods, indicating that IS/TIS-type corrections are not the only fix and may not even be optimal; pg_tis_clipfrac can only be read as the clipped fraction, not as the effectiveness of the correction.

sources.title: Beyond Precision: Training-Inference Mismatch is an Optimization Problem and Simple LR Scheduling Fixes It
sources.authors: Yaxiang Zhang, Yingru Li, Jiacai Liu, Jiawei Xu, Ziniu Li, Qian Liu, Haoyuan Li
sources.quote: standard remedies, such as Importance Sampling, might fail during extended training runs
sources.topic: IS-type corrections may fail in long training
sources.note: We wrote 'this run is on the order of 1e-4, itself far from dangerous; what is worth mentioning is that it rises with training,' implicitly treating the sustained upward trend of the TIS clipping fraction as a correction signal worth tracking. That paper explicitly states that standard corrections such as importance sampling may fail in long training, and this run has only 19/25 steps; extrapolating it to long training requires adding this premise.

items.name: PPO policy KL (new/old policy KL)
items.unit: KL divergence (nats), identically zero for this run
items.what: It is supposed to answer 'how far apart the old policy used for this step of training is from the current policy'; it is the standard quantity in PPO for judging 'how large a step was taken.' Like actor/pg_clipfrac, it is identically zero in this repository's data, and the dashboard gives no official explanation and does not explain why it is 0.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. Literally translated by name, it is the KL divergence between the current policy and the old policy used at sampling time, usually computed over the tokens of the training batch. Here one cannot infer its aggregation method from 0.
items.why: Policy KL is the core reading for controlling update step size. Too small KL means each step barely moves and training efficiency is low; a sudden amplification of KL means the policy drifts too fast, and it is easy for reward to rise while true capability drops (reward hacking / degeneration to mode responses). In engineering, it is often used to trigger early stopping or roll back this step's update. An identically zero KL column means this layer of protection is blind on the dashboard.
read: Don’t use this column to judge policy drift. To judge drift, read train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl—that is the log-prob difference between the inference engine and the trainer on the same batch of tokens, and it changes for real (pro final segment 0.004~0.008, flash final segment 0.006~0.010).

Also don’t use it to judge whether training has stalled. actor/pg_loss and actor/entropy_loss are both moving, indicating the policy is indeed changing, which contradicts the 0 in this column and further shows that this column is not a valid reading.
Being identically zero is a global phenomenon (both runs, all steps, all sub-tags with the same name), not a transient at a particular step.
There are two KLs on the dashboard: here it is actor/ppo_kl, and the other is train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl. When reading charts and citing, you must be clear about which one it is.
items.observed: Confirmed identically zero. Exactly the same pattern as pg_clipfrac: pro has 25 tags containing ppo_kl, 475 values, and 0 non-zero; flash has 25 tags, 625 values, and 0 non-zero; all are the numeral 0 rather than null. At the same time, train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl genuinely varies within the same data: pro's last four steps are 0.00415293, 0.00441681, 0.00679548, 0.00768816, and flash's last four steps are 0.00968806, 0.00883846, 0.0101065, 0.00597094, and the briefing has verified that it is highly correlated with partial/avg_staleness (pro 0.930, flash 0.925). So policy drift does have a reading in the data, just not in the actor/ppo_kl column. The dashboard does not explain the cause of this 0.
traps: Reading ppo_kl = 0 as 'the policy has not changed at all' is wrong: pg_loss, entropy_loss, and the overall success rate are all changing.
Treating actor/ppo_kl and train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl as the same metric is a common confusion; the latter is the valid drift reading in this repository.
Do not think training has a problem just because it is 0—the dashboard gives no explanation; all you can say is that this column has no information.

The 0s of the two runs are exactly identical; this looks more like a reporting-convention issue than a model-behavior issue, but this is only an observed pattern, and the data itself does not support further conclusions.

sources.title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
sources.quote: We describe an iterative procedure for optimizing policies, with guaranteed monotonic improvement.
sources.topic: The starting point of trust region methods
sources.note: The trust region idea of “trading distance constraints for monotonic improvement” is the reason the ppo_kl curve exists; in this run ppo_kl being identically zero means the constraint was never activated, so “trust region not taking effect” does not equal “policy not updating”; the latter should be checked via pg_loss/entropy_loss.

sources.title: Batch size-invariance for policy optimization
sources.authors: Jacob Hilton, Karl Cobbe, John Schulman
sources.quote: Our key insight is to decouple the proximal policy (used for controlling policy updates) from the behavior policy (used for off-policy corrections).
sources.topic: Decoupling of proximal policy and behavior policy
sources.note: The paper explains that the proximal policy is frozen during the training period over a batch of data, so the “distance between old and new policies” can inherently be 0 within the same step, while the off-policy part of the difference still exists—this explains why ppo_kl identically zero and TIS truncation non-zero can hold at the same time.

sources.title: The 37 Implementation Details of Proximal Policy Optimization (definition of approxkl)
sources.authors: Shengyi Huang, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Antonin Raffin, Anssi Kanervisto, Weixun Wang
sources.quote: `approxkl`: the approximate Kullback–Leibler divergence, measured by `(-logratio).mean()`, which corresponds to the `k1` estimator in John Schulman’s blog post on approximating KL divergence.
sources.topic: Definition of the KL curve in PPO
sources.note: This one defines PPO's KL diagnostic as (-logratio).mean() (the k1 estimator); when ratio is identically 1, this expression is identically 0, so ppo_kl being 0 throughout this run is completely consistent with “the old-new policy ratio being identically 1” and is not a reporting failure.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation（Important Note on Common Implementation Mistakes）
sources.quote: Many LLM-RL implementations incorrectly apply PPO by **ignoring the actual rollout policy** π_rollout and assuming the training reference policy π_old is the behavior policy.
sources.topic: π_rollout and π_old are two different policies
sources.note: Same as above: ppo_kl being 0 only indicates that the old and new policies are consistent; the deviation in the rollout segment is not on this curve, and using ppo_kl=0 to infer “training is very on-policy” is wrong.

sources.title: Approximating KL Divergence
sources.quote: This post will explain why this expression is a good (though biased) estimator of KL, and how to make it unbiased while preserving its low variance.
sources.topic: Definition and bias of the KL estimator
sources.note: The paper points out that the commonly used low-variance KL estimator is biased and gives three variants k1/k2/k3 (the verl documentation also categorizes them this way); therefore ppo_kl=0 can only be read as “the implemented estimator is 0 when ratio≡1”; comparing this curve across implementations is meaningless.

sources.title: This site's calculation: clip fraction and PPO KL are identically zero throughout (it is 0, not empty)
sources.quote: actor/pg_clipfrac and actor/ppo_kl are equal to the value 0 on all steps in both runs: pro 50 tags / 940 values, flash 50 tags / 1250 values, all non-empty and 0.
sources.topic: How to read identically zero
sources.note: For the same reason: ppo_kl measures the difference between the policy before and after the update, and under a single-round update it is identically 0. So “the trust region has not taken effect” is not an anomaly, but a necessary result of this training pipeline — it cannot be used to judge whether the policy change is large or small.

items.name: Average per-token entropy for each freshness bucket
items.what: The average per-token entropy within each freshness bucket; the definition shares the same origin as actor/entropy_loss (the official wording for the actor version is mean per-token entropy of the policy), except that it is bucketed by data staleness. The question it answers is: is the entropy of stale data and fresh data different. The dashboard does not provide an official explanation.
items.how: Average the entropy over the tokens in each bucket. Use n_tokens weighting to combine the bucket entropies, and it basically matches the global actor/entropy_loss: for pro, most steps differ by -0.003~+0.016 nats, for flash by -0.012~+0.027 nats, and for pro at step 17 the two are exactly identical (both 0.40874). So the two are most likely two ways of slicing the same definition, but the dashboard does not explain the source of this discrepancy. The dashboard does not provide an official explanation.
items.why: Entropy is a measure of policy exploration. If the entropy of older buckets is systematically higher, it means samples collected by an earlier policy have a flatter distribution and are more off-policy, and during training the gradient direction of these tokens is more uncertain; if the entropy of older buckets is lower, it means those buckets lean toward samples that have already converged and are high-confidence. The value of looking at entropy by bucket is that it can decompose “global entropy change” into two things: “the policy itself changed” and “data of different freshness was put into the batch”.
read: In this round's data, entropy is indeed higher for older buckets, but it is only a weak trend and not monotonic. After token-weighting and pooling all pro 19 steps / flash 25 steps, the correlation coefficient between bucket index and entropy is pro +0.2551, flash +0.1780; the unweighted pooled correlation is pro +0.2490, flash +0.1346.

The evidence for non-monotonicity is clear: flash bucket 2's pooled mean 0.40417 is instead lower than bucket 1's 0.44010; pro bucket 4's 0.37550 is also lower than bucket 3's 0.41834. Do not treat 'the older the bucket, the higher the entropy' as a law.

Comparing bucket by bucket against bucket 0 is instead more stable: pro has 16 steps where 'oldest bucket entropy is higher than bucket 0 entropy', and only 1 step opposite (step 11 -0.0363); flash is 23 steps to 0 steps, all in the same direction, with a maximum difference of +0.2287.
Correlation coefficient between bucket index and entropy within a single step: pro mean +0.5928 (10 of 11 computable steps are positive), flash mean +0.4088 (18 of 20 steps are positive).
Before comparing across buckets, you must first look at n_tokens: buckets with fewer than a million tokens will give absurdly low entropy on the order of 0.01.
items.observed: Bucket mean entropy after pooling (weighted by token): for pro, bucket 0 is 0.39524, bucket 1 0.40488, bucket 2 0.40618, bucket 3 0.41834, bucket 4 0.37550, bucket 5 0.41192, bucket 6 0.45464, bucket 7 0.43428; for flash, bucket 0 is 0.42296, bucket 1 0.44010, bucket 2 0.40417, bucket 3 0.44039, bucket 4 0.42664, bucket 5 0.42502, bucket 6 0.46165, bucket 7 0.47791, bucket 8 0.50889, bucket 9 0.50745. The cleanest single-step comparison is flash step 14: bucket 0 entropy 0.4101, bucket 9 entropy 0.6388, difference +0.2287; at step 15 bucket 0 is 0.4100, bucket 8 is 0.5378, bucket 9 is 0.5281. pro step 10 is the same: bucket 0 is 0.3749, bucket 7 is 0.4683. A counterexample is flash step 24 bucket 4 at only 0.1832 and step 25 bucket 6 at only 0.0126, while these two buckets have only 3,170,140 and 321,727 tokens respectively, which is a small-sample anomaly; in the same step, bucket 9 at step 25 instead reports 0.4968, indicating that this is not “older data has lower entropy”. Global actor/entropy_loss over the same period rises slowly: pro 0.39526→0.40627, flash 0.41331→0.45611.
traps: 'The older the bucket, the higher the entropy' is a weak trend, not true in every step, and the correlation coefficient is only 0.18~0.26, so its explanatory power is limited. When writing it as a conclusion, include this strength.

Bucket-level entropy and actor/entropy_loss are not strictly equal: after weighted merging, they differ by 0.005~0.015 nats in most steps, and are exactly identical in isolated steps. The dashboard does not explain the definitional difference; do not assume the two can be used interchangeably.

The entropy of extremely small buckets (fewer than 1e6 tokens) will drop to the 0.01 order of magnitude; this is a sample/numerical issue, not the policy suddenly becoming deterministic. flash step 25 bucket 6 is a typical example.

High entropy does not mean training has a problem. High entropy from old data is itself a natural result of 'the old policy distribution being flatter'; it only needs to be handled when it simultaneously raises global entropy and masks the policy's own entropy trend.

sources.title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
sources.quote: In practice, we establish a transformation equation R=-a*e^H+b between entropy H and downstream performance R.
sources.topic: The trade-off between entropy and performance (entropy collapse narrative)
sources.note: The empirical law in that paper only concerns a single global entropy H and completely lacks the layer of “entropy bucketed by data staleness”; so our reading that “the older the bucket, the higher the entropy” has no counterpart in the public material, can only count as a local observation, and cannot cite that paper as backing.

sources.title: Deconstructing Off-Policy Ratios: Entropy-Scaled Trust Regions for Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
sources.authors: Guanqun Zhao, Zijun Xie, Binbin Zheng, Enlei Gong, Jiafeng Lu, Yehan Yang, Aoqi Hu, Zeyu Chen
sources.quote: we reveal that the natural scale of the importance ratio varies systematically with token entropy. Under asynchronous dynamics, this entropy-ratio scaling dictates two distinct phenomena: at low entropy, the inherent train-inference discrepancy is drastically amplified into substantial sampling noise
sources.topic: The scale of off-policy bias is systematically correlated with token entropy.
sources.note: We observed that 'older buckets do have somewhat higher entropy, but it is only a weak trend (correlation 0.18~0.26)', and suggest decomposing the global entropy change into 'the policy itself changed' and 'data of different freshness being put into the buckets'. The article says the natural scale of off-policy bias is systematically related to token entropy: at low entropy, the train-infer difference is amplified into sampling noise. Therefore, when comparing entropy across buckets, one must first control for the interaction between entropy and staleness; 'older buckets have higher entropy' cannot be directly read as off-policy being more severe.

items.name: Token weight frac_k of the freshness bucket
items.unit: Proportion 0~1 (normalized within the same scope, Σ_k frac_k = 1)
items.what: Bucket the tokens used for training at this step by 'how many policy versions elapsed between sampling and being trained'; bucket 0 is the freshest. frac_k is the share of bucket k's tokens within this step. It is central to understanding why global KL, global entropy, and global nll difference fluctuate: these global quantities are all averages weighted by frac. The maximum value of k differs between the two runs; pro is partial/0..7 (8 buckets), flash is partial/0..9 (10 buckets). The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.how: frac_k equals n_tokens_k divided by the sum of n_tokens over all buckets. I verified three things: first, the sums of frac for pro's 8 buckets per step and flash's 10 buckets per step are both 1.000000 (deviation no more than 1e-6); second, frac_k and the n_tokens share match bucket by bucket to 7.5e-7; third, Σ_k (k × frac_k) exactly reproduces partial/avg_staleness (deviation 4.0e-6 / 6.7e-6). Also note that Σ_k n_tokens_k is only 44%~56% of perf/total_num_tokens for the same step, so this 1.0 is normalized within partial's own accounting, not relative to the whole step's token count. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It determines how much stale data inflates global KL, global nll difference, and global F(tau). When frac_0 falls and the frac of large k rises, it indicates training is consuming inventory; it is a signal that rollout generation cannot keep up with the trainer: it may be slow generation, waiting for restart, or a backlog in the remote rollout queue. Conversely, if frac_0 stays high while global KL is still rising, that is a problem with the engine itself.
read: frac_0 during the stable period is usually 0.12~0.20; after restart, the first step is 1.0000, and then it gradually falls back.

The center of weight falls on bucket 1 most of the time (pro whole-period mean 0.4414, flash 0.4798), not bucket 0. This is a normal phase of the asynchronous pipeline: data that is about one version behind accounts for the bulk.
What to look at is 'whether the stalest few buckets have grown'. flash step 23 bucket 7 got 0.0926, step 24 bucket 8 got 0.0953, corresponding to staleness surging to a historical peak of 2.1832.

The shape of the bucket distribution is more informative than the value of a single bucket. At step 24, flash's frac spreads all the way from 0.1607 in bucket 0 to 0.0953 in bucket 8, a very wide long tail; after the restart at step 25, 0.8445 is concentrated in bucket 0, with only 0.0002/0.0003/0.0005 left in buckets 6/7/8.
A restart clears the bucket structure and starts over, so early steps report only 1~3 buckets, and at this point frac_0 is close to 1.
items.observed: pro's frac_0 is between 0.1488~1.0000: step 1 and step 15 are 1.0000, and during the stable period it is mostly 0.16~0.27 (step 9 0.1965, step 14 0.2740). flash's frac_0 is between 0.1136~1.0000: step 1 and step 16 are 1.0000, during the stable period 0.12~0.18, and after the restart at step 25 it returns to 0.8445. The weight of bucket 1 can reach as high as pro 0.8234 (step 16), flash 0.8519 (step 2), and 0.8437 (step 4). pro bucket 7 appears only twice, with a share of 0.0017~0.0036; flash bucket 9 appears five times, with a minimum of 0.0009.
traps: Bucket numbering is not globally monotonic. pro reports only 2 buckets at step 12, 4 at step 14, and only steps 10 and 11 have the full 8. Bucket k only means “lagging k policy versions behind the sampling time of the current step”; counting restarts after a restart.
frac_k is not the proportion of that dataset's or category's tokens in the whole step: the denominator is only about half of the whole step's perf/total_num_tokens.
pro has 8 buckets and flash has 10 buckets; do not apply the same upper limit to both, and do not directly compare the absolute values of same-named frac.
The sum of frac being 1 is an identity by construction, not a health signal; do not treat “sum equals 1” as passing data validation.

sources.title: PipelineRL: Faster On-policy Reinforcement Learning for Long Sequence Generation
sources.authors: Alexandre Piche, Ehsan Kamalloo, Rafael Pardinas, Xiaoyin Chen, Dzmitry Bahdanau
sources.quote: PipelineRL employs concurrent asynchronous data generation and model training, distinguished by the novel in-flight weight updates.
sources.topic: In an asynchronous pipeline, sequences are generated across policy versions.
sources.note: We wrote that 'the center of mass of the weights falls most of the time on bucket 1 (pro full-period mean 0.4414), not bucket 0; this is the normal phase of an asynchronous pipeline: data lagging by about one version accounts for the majority'. The article describes exactly this operating mode of 'generation and training running concurrently, with data lagging by a margin on average'.

sources.title: Computed here: global KL is the weighted average of the KL of the freshness buckets
sources.quote: Point-by-point verification: global KL = Σ(bucket token share × bucket KL): pro 19 steps, flash 26 steps, the bucket shares each sum to 1.0000, maximum relative error 0.15%.
sources.topic: CL blended scope
sources.note: The bucket share is not incidental information; it is the weight of global KL. When the share changes, global KL moves with it, while each bucket's own KL may not change at all.

sources.title: Computed here: split global KL into a "data mix change" part and an "in-bucket change" part
sources.quote: The reconstructed curve that fixes the data mix and plugs in only the true per-step bucket KL correlates with the true global KL at only pro 0.53 / flash 0.55; plugging in only the true data mix and averaging the bucket KL instead gives a reconstruction R² of pro 0.79 / flash 0.90.
sources.topic: Is it the data mix or the buckets that got worse
sources.note: The reverse check is even more telling: the data mix alone can almost reconstruct the trend of global KL, whereas the in-bucket KL cannot. The rise in global KL is driven mainly by the change in the share of stale tokens in the training batch, not by every freshness bucket getting worse.

items.name: Token count per freshness bucket n_tokens_k
items.what: The absolute token count in each freshness bucket. Because the global metrics on the dashboard are all token-weighted, the absolute token count in a bucket determines how large its influence on the global curve is; it also determines whether the bucket-level metrics (KL, entropy, F(tau)) can be trusted. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.how: Same source as frac: frac_k equals n_tokens_k divided by the sum of n_tokens over all buckets (verified to agree to 7.5e-7). Bucket-level tags take the form partial/0/n_tokens to partial/7/n_tokens (pro), partial/0/n_tokens to partial/9/n_tokens (flash). The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It is the precondition for judging whether bucket-level readings are usable. When a bucket has fewer than a million tokens, KL, entropy and F(tau) all start to jump wildly, because there are too few samples. It also lets you convert "how many tokens in this step are behind": summing n_tokens_k times k gives the total "count of versions behind".
read: Bucket 0's token count is on the order of 1.3e8~1.3e9, while the stalest buckets usually have only 1e6~4e6, a difference of three orders of magnitude.

Bucket-level metrics for small buckets are not trustworthy. At step 25, flash's bucket 6 has only 321,727 tokens; the KL it reports is 0.000606 and the entropy is 0.0126, while other buckets at the same step have KL in 0.0149~0.0302 and entropy in 0.42~0.51. This bucket's readings are almost certainly caused by small samples/boundary cases, and cannot be used to support any conclusion.
The first step after a restart has all tokens in bucket 0, so n_tokens_0 for that step is the total for that step under the entire partial accounting.
To see trends, you should look at the relative changes in n_tokens_0 and Σ_k n_tokens_k, rather than the absolute values of individual small buckets.
items.observed: For pro, n_tokens in bucket 0 ranges from 158,133,000 (step 6) to 1,131,070,000 (step 15), mean 4.47e8; the stalest bucket, 7, appeared only twice, mean 2,922,060, minimum 1,811,550. For flash, bucket 0 ranges from 130,855,000 (step 5) to 1,300,260,000 (step 25), mean 3.40e8; bucket 9 appeared five times, mean 2,780,618, minimum 1,315,060. The total token count over the whole partial scope (Σ_k n_tokens_k) is 7.93e8~1.41e9 for pro, only 45%~55% of perf/total_num_tokens in the same step; for flash it is 8.17e8~1.78e9, 44%~56%.
traps: Do not treat Σ_k n_tokens as “how many tokens were trained in this step”. It is systematically only about half of perf/total_num_tokens; the dashboard does not explain this discrepancy, and the two tags simply have different accounting.
At step 25, flash's buckets 6/7/8 have only 321,727 / 385,133 / 835,957 tokens respectively; all bucket-level metrics for these buckets are not comparable.
Bucket-level tags are not present at every step: pro's bucket 3 is reported for only 7 steps, and bucket 7 for only 2 steps (steps 10 and 11); null means not reported, not 0.
Under flash's partial/cyber/dataset-9aui/, there are no bucket-level n_tokens or frac at all, only a single tag avg_staleness.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: Rollout batches were collected within the following three vllm-kl ranges, with five batches (around 5M tokens) in each group
sources.topic: Minimum sample size when grouping statistics by degree of inconsistency
sources.note: We wrote "When a bucket's token count is below the million scale, KL, entropy, and F(tau) all start fluctuating wildly, because there are too few samples," and used flash step 25 bucket 6 (320k tokens) as an unreliable example. When the article did the same kind of "statistics grouped by degree of inconsistency," each group used about 5M tokens before it dared to draw a conclusion, providing a verbatim-quotable order-of-magnitude reference for "bucket-level readings require million-plus tokens."

items.name: mean data staleness of agentic slices
items.what: The staleness sliced out only by the agentic layer is defined the same as partial/avg_staleness: the average number of policy versions between sampling and training. The dashboard gives no official explanation. Note that the categories declared in meta.json are code, general, cyber, visual, chat, and do not include agentic, so it is a slice independent of those five data sources; the dashboard does not state which part of the traffic this slice covers.
items.how: Same algorithm as global staleness, only restricted to agentic-related tokens. Its bucket-level tags also exist (pro has partial/agentic/0..7/n_tokens and frac, flash has partial/agentic/0..9/...). There is a definitional issue that must be noted: adding up the partial/agentic/<k>/n_tokens buckets can reach 92%~95% of the total partial/<k>/n_tokens; adding up the partial/<category>/<dataset>/<k>/n_tokens buckets gives 76%~95% of the total; the two together sum to more than 1.6 times. This shows that the agentic slice and the dataset slice are not two halves of the same partition; the dashboard does not explain what their respective denominators are. The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.why: Its purpose is to determine whether the increase in global staleness is 「dragged by a certain type of task」 or a global phenomenon. If agentic is noticeably staler than global, you should check the rollout latency of agent tasks, environment startup queueing, and grading time; if it is synchronized with global, then it is not an agentic-specific problem.
read: It is almost a carbon copy of global staleness: its correlation with partial/avg_staleness is 0.9999 in both runs, and its level is only slightly higher than the global one (pro mean 0.9096 vs. global 0.8777, flash 1.4077 vs. 1.3595).
Therefore it currently provides no additional information. If you really want to look at category differences, you should look at partial/<category>/<dataset>/avg_staleness.
Every one of its resets to zero is synchronized with the global one (pro steps 1 and 15; flash steps 1 and 16), indicating that restart treats all data equally.
The peaks are also synchronized with the global one, with peak heights differing by only 0.03~0.09.
items.observed: pro first/last 0.0000→1.0502, peak 1.8974 at step 9 (globally, the same step is 1.8208), minimum is 0.0000 at steps 1 and 15, full-run mean 0.9096. flash first/last 0.0000→0.3392, peak 2.2717 at step 24 (globally, the same step is 2.1832), minimum is 0.0000 at steps 1 and 16, full-run mean 1.4077. The correlation coefficients for both runs are 0.9999.
traps: Do not assume it reveals a problem specific to the agentic category. It nearly overlaps the global curve (0.9999), the level difference is only 0.03~0.09, and the information content is essentially zero.
agentic is not in the categories declared by meta.json, and putting it on par with code/general/cyber/visual/chat for a category comparison is not tenable in terms of scope.

The denominator relationship between partial/agentic/<k>/n_tokens and partial/<category>/<dataset>/<k>/n_tokens is unclear (their sum exceeds the total), so do not try to treat them as two complementary halves to reconstruct the step's token composition.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: The mismatch primarily occurs in non-first-round model outputs, manifested by a larger mean absolute difference in both log-ppl and token probability between FSDP policy and vLLM policy compared to the first-round output
sources.topic: The inconsistency in multi-turn/agentic outputs is more severe.
sources.note: We write, "Its purpose is to determine whether the rise in global staleness is dragged by a certain category of tasks or is a global phenomenon; if agentic is noticeably staler, one should go check the rollout latency of agent tasks." The article provides corresponding evidence on the mechanism side: agentic multi-turn outputs (non-first turn) bear OOD tool returns, the train/infer gap is largest, and the higher the tool call limit, the earlier it crashes——so the agentic slice is worth looking at separately, even though on this site it correlates with the global at 0.9999.

items.name: Average data staleness
items.unit: Number of policy versions (0 means brand new, range 0~2.2)
items.what: The official description is policy versions between sampling and training, on average. That is, for the tokens used for training at this step, from being sampled by the inference engine to being consumed by the trainer, how many policy updates intervene, weighted by token. 0 means the data was sampled at the current step; 1.8 means an average lag of nearly two policy versions.
items.how: I verified by calculation: this number is exactly equal to Σ_k (k × frac_k), where k is the freshness bucket index and frac_k is the bucket's token share. The maximum deviations at pro step 19 and flash step 25 are 4.0e-6 and 6.7e-6 respectively, purely caused by dashboard rounding. This also conversely proves that bucket index k is exactly staleness itself (k equals how many policy versions behind), not an arbitrary bin ordinal. Number of buckets and reported steps: pro has partial/0..7, 8 buckets in total, and many steps report only the first few (step 12 has only 2; steps 10 and 11 have the full 8); flash has partial/0..9, 10 buckets in total, and steps 12~15 and step 25 have the full 10.
items.why: It is the most easily misread metric on the entire dashboard, and also the key to explaining global KL. A rise in staleness itself is not necessarily bad; an asynchronous pipeline inherently has one to two versions of latency; but it will simultaneously raise global KL, global nll difference, global F(tau), and global diff_abs_*, making all "training-inference consistency" metrics look like they are deteriorating. When you see such metrics deteriorating, look at staleness first, then decide whether to touch the engine or adjust the parallel strategy.
read: The normal level during the stable period is 1.2~1.9 (pro steps 5~10: 1.1668~1.8208; flash steps 5~15: 1.2779~1.8895). Below 1.0 means the pipeline is very tight, which is a good state.
0.0000 is good news: pro step 1 and step 15, flash step 1 and step 16 are all 0; the restart cleared the in-flight data, so all tokens were sampled by the current version.

The sawtooth profile of gradually climbing, being interrupted by a restart, and climbing again is a normal shape (pro climbs from 0.8151 at step 4 to 1.8208 at step 9, after the restart drops to 0.4403 at step 11, climbs again to 1.2125 at step 14, and then resets to zero after another restart).

What to watch out for is “no restart, yet staleness stays pinned at a high level”: flash steps 21~24 go 1.8013→1.9269→2.0337→2.1832, hitting new highs for four consecutive steps with no sign of falling back, indicating that the rollout side cannot keep up with the trainer.
To judge inference engine consistency, look at bucket 0 KL together with it: high staleness with flat bucket 0 KL means the pipeline is merely loose.
items.observed: pro first/last: 0.0000→1.0133, peak 1.8208 at step 9, minimum 0.0000 at steps 1 and 15, overall mean 0.8777. flash first/last: 0.0000→0.3198, peak 2.1832 at step 24, minimum 0.0000 at steps 1 and 16, overall mean 1.3595. Its correlation coefficient with global KL is 0.9300 for pro and 0.9252 for flash, while bucket 0's KL is almost uncorrelated with it (pro -0.1939, flash 0.1965). flash steps 24 to 25 are the cleanest controlled experiment: staleness 2.1832→0.3198 (-85%), global KL 0.010106→0.005971 (-41%), while bucket 0's KL 0.003407→0.003549 (+4%).
traps: The number of buckets differs between the two runs (pro has 8, flash has 10), which determines that the two sides have different achievable upper limits for staleness. flash reaching 2.1832 while pro only reaches 1.8208 does not mean flash's pipeline is worse; rather, its buckets are set deeper. Be careful when comparing this number across runs.
It is a token-weighted average, not an average over the number of rollouts; long sequences will dominate this number.
Returning to zero does not mean training has improved; it only means the restart cleared the in-flight data. pro's step 15 and flash's step 16 are both restart steps.
The first step after a restart is a natural baseline for calibrating global KL: at that point global KL equals bucket 0 KL (pro step 15: 0.002577 vs 0.002580; flash step 16: 0.003267 vs 0.003271).

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: policy versions between sampling and training, on average
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.venue: Notion blog (ByteDance, source of motivation for verl Rollout Correction)
sources.quote: The relentless push for faster inference has created a dangerous "training-inference mismatch" that can silently kill reinforcement learning with LLMs.
sources.topic: Training-inference inconsistency is the direct cause of training collapse
sources.note: We wrote "When you see such metrics deteriorating, look at staleness first, then decide whether to touch the engine or adjust the parallel strategy." The article gives half the answer: it attributes the collapse to engine-side numerical inconsistency (the same batch of in-flight data), showing that the engine axis other than staleness can also independently cause collapse, and the two axes need to be investigated separately.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation
sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: These off-policy gaps can cause training instability and policy collapse.
sources.topic: Official classification of the off-policy problem: engine implementation differences vs temporal lag
sources.note: We wrote "A rise in staleness itself is not necessarily bad; an asynchronous pipeline inherently has one to two versions of latency." The documentation lists temporal lag as one of the normal engineering scenarios requiring IS/RS correction, rather than a fault, corroborating this judgment.

sources.title: Prosperity before Collapse: How Far Can Off-Policy RL Reach with Stale Data on LLMs?
sources.authors: Haizhong Zheng, Jiawei Zhao, Beidi Chen
sources.quote: M2PO sharply reduces the fraction of clipped tokens under high staleness (from 1.22% to 0.06% over training), precisely masking high-variance tokens while maintaining stable optimization.
sources.topic: Order of magnitude of the clipped token fraction under high staleness
sources.note: We wrote 「it is the most easily misread on the whole dashboard... a rise in staleness is not necessarily a bad thing」. That paper's prosperity-before-collapse phenomenon supports 「stale data can be just as informative as on-policy data」, i.e. high staleness in itself does not mean training is getting worse.

sources.title: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: Formulation and Practices
sources.authors: Chujie Zheng, Kai Dang, Bowen Yu, Mingze Li, Huiqiang Jiang, Junrong Lin, Yuqiong Liu, Hao Lin, Chencan Wu, Feng Hu, An Yang, Jingren Zhou, Junyang Lin
sources.quote: through a first-order approximation, we show that this surrogate becomes increasingly valid only when both the training-inference discrepancy and policy staleness are minimized.
sources.topic: TIM and staleness are two independent quantities that must both be pushed down
sources.note: We wrote 「judging engine consistency must be read together with the bucket 0 KL: high staleness with a flat bucket 0 KL means the pipeline is merely loose」. That paper singles out policy staleness as a factor that can independently degrade the effectiveness of the proxy objective, supporting our treating it as one dimension orthogonal to engine difference.

sources.title: Missing Old Logits in Asynchronous Agentic RL: Semantic Mismatch and Repair Methods for Off-Policy Correction
sources.authors: Zhong Guan, Yongjian Guo, Haoran Sun, Wen Huang, Shuai Di, Likang Wu, Xiong Jun Wu, Hongke Zhao
sources.quote: This missing-old-logit problem entangles discrepancy repair with staleness correction, breaks the intended semantics of decoupled correction, and makes clipping and masking thresholds interact undesirably.
sources.topic: The total ratio should be split into two terms: the 'engine difference term' and the 'staleness term'
sources.note: We wrote 「the global KL is approximately Σ(frac_k × KL_k)... the bucket 0 KL is essentially unrelated to avg_staleness」, and on that basis split the global metric into a data-mix term and a bucket-own term. That paper gives the same split from the semantic level of the importance ratio: the total ratio should be decomposed into a 「training-inference difference term on the same behaviour version」 and a 「staleness term from the historical policy to the current policy」, and delayed updates / partial rollout entangle the two — which is exactly why we observe 「the global KL correlates 0.93 with staleness while the bucket 0 KL is unrelated to it」.

sources.title: PipelineRL: Faster On-policy Reinforcement Learning for Long Sequence Generation
sources.authors: Alexandre Piche, Ehsan Kamalloo, Rafael Pardinas, Xiaoyin Chen, Dzmitry Bahdanau
sources.quote: PipelineRL employs concurrent asynchronous data generation and model training, distinguished by the novel in-flight weight updates.
sources.topic: In an asynchronous pipeline, sequences are generated across policy versions.
sources.note: We wrote 「an asynchronous pipeline inherently has one to two versions of built-in delay」 and 「0 means the data was sampled in exactly this step」. That paper's in-flight weight update mechanism is precisely the technique that lets a sequence being generated span policy versions, giving a physical origin for the bucket definition 「behind by k policy versions」; it also explains why freshness must be pursued (otherwise it degenerates into stale off-policy data).

sources.title: Group-Relative REINFORCE Is Secretly an Off-Policy Algorithm: Demystifying Some Myths About GRPO and Its Friends
sources.authors: Chaorui Yao, Yanxi Chen, Yuchang Sun, Yushuo Chen, Wenhao Zhang, Xuchen Pan, Yaliang Li, Bolin Ding
sources.quote: without assuming a specific training data distribution, showing that it admits a native off-policy interpretation. This perspective yields two general principles for adapting REINFORCE to truly off-policy settings: regularizing policy updates, and actively shaping the data distribution.
sources.topic: GRPO-type algorithms themselves have an off-policy interpretation
sources.note: We wrote 「a rise in staleness is not necessarily a bad thing... below 1.0 means the pipeline is very tight, which is a good state」. That paper proves from first principles that group-relative REINFORCE does not depend on the training data distribution and has a natural off-policy interpretation, and that the principle for handling off-policy is to regularize the update and shape the data distribution, rather than pushing staleness to 0.

sources.title: Rethinking the Divergence Regularization in LLM RL
sources.authors: Jiarui Yao, Xiangxin Zhou, Penghui Qi, Wee Sun Lee, Liefeng Bo, Tianyu Pang
sources.quote: In practice, LLM RL is often off-policy because of training-inference mismatch and policy staleness, making trust-region control essential for stable optimization.
sources.topic: the two sources of off-policy, side by side
sources.note: We wrote 「it is the metric most easily misread on the whole dashboard, and the key to explaining the global KL」, treating staleness and engine difference separately. That paper lists training-inference mismatch and policy staleness side by side as the two sources that make LLM RL off-policy, consistent with this two-axis framework.

sources.title: Computed here: global KL is the weighted average of the KL of the freshness buckets
sources.quote: Point-by-point verification: global KL = Σ(bucket token share × bucket KL): pro 19 steps, flash 26 steps, the bucket shares each sum to 1.0000, maximum relative error 0.15%.
sources.topic: CL blended scope
sources.note: Since the global KL is a weighted average and staleness is a weighted sum of bucket indices, the two naturally move in the same direction. Measured correlation pro 0.930 / flash 0.925 —— the high correlation is decided by the definition; it cannot be used as evidence that 「staleness causes the KL to get worse」.

items.name: mean data staleness for code/dataset-yfch
items.what: the staleness of the single dataset dataset-yfch under the code category, defined the same as partial/avg_staleness. It is the stalest dataset on the whole dashboard. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.how: Same algorithm as the global staleness, restricted to this dataset. Bucket-level tags are also present, and the buckets go as deep as the global ones: pro is partial/code/dataset-yfch/0..7 (8 buckets), flash is partial/code/dataset-yfch/0..9 (10 buckets). The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It is one of the answers to the question "which data source is slowing down training". When the global staleness at flash step 24 spiked to a historical peak of 2.1832, this dataset was at 7.2748, more than twice the global value; that is, a dataset whose traffic share is not particularly large pushed the average staleness of the whole batch up a substantial amount. When you see avg_staleness spike, check it first.
read: Its magnitude is an order of magnitude higher than the other datasets in the same run: flash's overall mean is 3.1660, while in the same run general/dataset-epqd is only 0.4867 and chat/dataset-lm3t is only 0.4083. pro's overall mean is 1.6804, while in the same run chat/dataset-lm3t is only 0.3192.
Its bucket depth matches the global one (pro 8, flash 10), meaning it is almost always at the back of the queue, and it is precisely what pushes the global bucket to its deepest.
Its correlation coefficient with global staleness is 0.890 for pro and 0.892 for flash; although not the highest, what it contributes is the absolute level rather than the shape.
A restart resets it to zero, and then it climbs again, so its sawtooth is steeper than the global one (pro step 10 4.5652 to step 11 1.8480, flash step 24 7.2748 to step 25 1.5555).
items.observed: pro first/last 0.0000→1.5929, peak 4.5652 at step 10 (the largest value across all datasets in pro), overall mean 1.6804, minimum 0.0000 at steps 1 and 15. flash first/last 0.0000→1.5555, peak 7.2748 at step 24 (the largest value across all datasets in flash), overall mean 3.1660. The trends of both runs are in sync with the global: pro climbs monotonically from 0.7499 to 4.5652 over steps 4~10, flash climbs monotonically from 0.9449 to 7.2748 over steps 17~24.
traps: It is the staleness of a single dataset and cannot represent the code category as a whole. Other code datasets in the same run (e.g. code/dataset-dnpn, flash mean 0.5082) are much lower.

That it is as high as 7.27 indicates that this dataset's rollout lags severely, but because its token share is not high (flash bucket 9 appeared only 5 times in total, mean 2,780,618 tokens), its effect on the global is to raise the average rather than to fill up the batch. Do not overestimate its absolute impact.
Zeroing at the restart step makes the curve show a deep V; do not take a deep V as this dataset's problem having been fixed.

sources.title: Computed here: split global KL into a "data mix change" part and an "in-bucket change" part
sources.quote: The reconstructed curve that fixes the data mix and plugs in only the true per-step bucket KL correlates with the true global KL at only pro 0.53 / flash 0.55; plugging in only the true data mix and averaging the bucket KL instead gives a reconstruction R² of pro 0.79 / flash 0.90.
sources.topic: Is it the data mix or the buckets that got worse
sources.note: Likewise, for any staleness reading broken down by data source, the first question to ask is: is this category of data really older, or has its share of the batch increased.

items.name: Average data staleness for cyber/dataset-9aui (removed)
items.what: The staleness of the only dataset under the cyber category, defined the same as partial/avg_staleness. This dataset has been officially taken offline on pro. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.how: Same algorithm as global staleness, restricted to this one dataset. The bucket-level tags on pro are partial/cyber/dataset-9aui/0..3 (4 buckets); on flash there are no bucket-level tags at all, only avg_staleness. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It is an observation window onto two different questions. First, it is one of the datasets with the highest staleness on the entire dashboard, indicating that cyber-type tasks have long environment preparation and grading times and severely lagging rollouts; second, its reporting interruption is a direct trace in the data of "the dataset being removed", and from it you can see when a configuration change took effect.
read: Both runs are far above the other datasets in the same run: pro's full-run mean is 1.5335, while pro's general category is generally around 0.35; flash's full-run mean is 1.4290, while general/dataset-1doa in the same run is only 0.5548.

Its value stayed high until it stopped reporting: pro's last bar (step 14) is still 2.0896, and flash's last five bars (steps 16–20) are 0.0000, 0.9015, 1.5095, 2.1223, 1.4910. There is no sign of it "dropping before being removed".
Its correlation coefficient with the global staleness is pro 0.946 and flash 0.825, the highest of all datasets on pro.
On pro it is entirely null from step 15 on, right after the notice in notices that "the cyber dataset is removed from pro's next run".
items.observed: pro reports steps 1~14, peak 2.6476 at step 7, final value (step 14) 2.0896, overall mean 1.5335, null from step 15 on. flash reports steps 1~20, peak 2.8061 at step 6, final value (step 20) 1.4910, overall mean 1.4290, null from step 21 on. pro's bucket-level tags are only 0..3, 4 buckets in total, and they stop being supplied at the same time as avg_staleness; flash has no bucket-level tags at all.
traps: Its supply cut-off is a configuration change, not data loss or a metric failure. Do not treat a null as an anomaly alert.
On flash this dataset has no bucket-level frac / n_tokens, so bucket-level analysis is not possible, nor can it be compared with pro in bucket structure.

Although it is one of the datasets with the highest staleness, be cautious about taking it as evidence that "cyber-type tasks slow down training": it is already retired on pro, and on flash it stopped from step 21 as well.
The two runs' cut-off steps differ (pro step 15, flash step 21), so when aligning pro and flash for comparison there will be an interval where only one side has values.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Maximum absolute log-prob difference
items.what: The largest |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| in this step, i.e. the extreme disagreement on a single token. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.how: Takes the maximum over the same batch of comparison data. The bucket-level version partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/new_infer/diff_abs_max also exists, but bucket 5 in both runs does not have this tag. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It is the only quantity in this group that can show how long the tail is. A log-prob difference of 60 nats means that the probabilities the two engines assign to the same token differ by on the order of e^60; the importance sampling ratio for such tokens will directly blow up, which is the reason the clip and ratio clipping mechanisms must exist. It is also the direct answer to "why you cannot look only at mean": mean is 0.04, max is 90, differing by a factor of 600~2500.
read: It is the only quantity in this group that is not dominated by staleness: its correlation coefficient with the global KL is only pro 0.5123 and flash 0.2119; with diff_abs_mean it is pro 0.5113 and flash 0.2378.
So it is suited to being an anomaly detector rather than a trend indicator. Normally it jumps irregularly between 20–90 nats, and high points can appear whether or not there is a restart.

Bucket 0's max is also on the same order of magnitude (pro 12.13–60.00, flash 15.33–51.37) and cannot be separated from the global pro 20.27–97.97 and flash 27.99–89.38. Extreme tokens are not a problem unique to stale data.
Step-to-step comparison is basically noise; only "a sudden overall jump up by an order of magnitude" is worth investigating.
items.observed: pro first/last 60.0009→49.2879, minimum 20.2746 at step 2, maximum 97.9694 at step 14; flash first/last 38.0661→38.4528, minimum 27.9940 at step 9, maximum 89.3838 at step 21. The first steps of the two runs are 60.0 and 38.1 respectively, which are typical levels. The two largest steps (pro step 14 staleness 1.2125, flash step 21 staleness 1.8013) have nothing special about them, indicating that this quantity is unrelated to freshness.
traps: A single token determines the reading; step-to-step differences are mainly noise. A drop in it does not mean training has become stable.
The magnitude (tens of nats) far exceeds diff_abs_mean (a few hundredths), so do not put them on the same axis to compare absolute values.
Bucket 5 in both runs lacks this tag, so the bucketed curve will have a missing segment.
Its value is heavily affected by the numerical precision of the inference engine and trainer: whether the probability on a token is calculated to 1e-30 or 1e-40 determines whether max is 30 or 90.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: the divergence is most severe for tokens that have a low probability according to the vLLM inference engine. As a token's inference probability approaches zero, the training probability can become orders of magnitude smaller, leading to an infinite PPL and gradient.
sources.topic: Low-probability tokens are where disagreement concentrates.
sources.note: We write "it is the only quantity in this group that can show how long the tail is ... probabilities on a token differ by on the order of e^60". That article gives the mechanism: disagreement sharply amplifies as the inference-side probability approaches zero, and can differ by several orders of magnitude, so mean being 0.04 while max is several tens of nats are two ends of the same phenomenon.

sources.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
sources.quote: we show that its root cause lies in the floating point precision itself. The widely adopted BF16, despite its large dynamic range, introduces large rounding errors that breaks the consistency between training and inference.
sources.topic: Precision source of train-inference mismatch
sources.note: We write "its value is greatly affected by the numerical precision of the inference engine and trainer: whether a probability on a token is computed to 1e-30 or 1e-40 determines whether max is 30 or 90". That article attributes the root cause of the entire TIM to BF16 rounding error, which is precisely the public basis for this "extreme values are determined by precision" claim.

items.name: Mean of the absolute log-prob difference between trainer and inference engine
items.what: On the same batch of tokens, subtract the log-prob computed by the inference engine from the log-prob computed by the trainer, take the absolute value, and then average. It directly answers "how much the two engines differ on average per token". The dashboard does not give an official explanation, and it is not among the 22 official explanations; translated literally from the tag name, it is the mean of the absolute difference.
items.how: It uses the same batch of comparison data as new_infer/kl, only the aggregation method differs: KL is a divergence at the distribution level, while this is the first-order average of per-token absolute differences. A bucket-level version also exists (partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/new_infer/diff_abs_mean), so fresh data can be viewed separately. The dashboard does not provide an official explanation.
items.why: It is easier to read than KL, and its unit is nats; unlike diff_abs_max, it is not dominated by a single anomalous token, making it suitable as a long-term trend line. But it mixes tokens from the entire step together, so it gets raised by stale buckets; therefore its ability to measure "whether the data is old" is far greater than its ability to measure "whether the engine is good".
read: Normal range 0.02~0.05 nats. Its curve is almost identical to global KL (correlation coefficients pro 0.9965, flash 0.9911), so it likewise cannot be used to judge engine consistency.
To judge engine consistency, look at bucket 0: pro bucket 0 is 0.02289~0.02673 throughout, flash 0.02422~0.03236, both with only minor drift.

Its correlation coefficient with avg_staleness is 0.9171 (identical for pro and flash), and it is almost uncorrelated with bucket 0 KL (pro 0.0475, flash 0.4099). Taken together, these two numbers show that it is a freshness thermometer.
The minimum always occurs at steps where staleness is close to 0, which can serve as corroborating evidence that 「the data at this step is brand new」.
It is highly collinear with diff_abs_std (correlation pro 0.9952, flash 0.9849), so do not use these two numbers as two independent pieces of evidence.
items.observed: pro first/last 0.023767→0.041376 (+74%), peak 0.046246 at step 9; flash first/last 0.027036→0.039026 (+44%), peak 0.050068 at step 24. Bucket 0 over the same period only rose from 0.02380 to 0.02646 (pro, +11%), and from 0.02708 to 0.03236 (flash, +19%). The lowest points all fall near the steps where staleness returns to zero: pro step 1 0.023767, step 15 0.026099; flash step 1 0.027036, step 16 0.030576.
traps: Do not conflate it with the train_infer_diff/nll_loss difference (log_probs minus rollout_log_probs). That one is a signed average, only 0.006~0.010 nats; this one takes the absolute value, 0.039~0.050 nats. The two differ by about a factor of 5, indicating that the positive and negative differences per token cancel out 79%~91%.
It is still contaminated by stale data and is not a clean reading of 「the true disagreement between the two engines」.
The dashboard only gives the mean, not the median, so a few extreme tokens can still push it up: the std at the same step is 2.5~3.1 times it.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: The mismatch primarily occurs in non-first-round model outputs, manifested by a larger mean absolute difference in both log-ppl and token probability between FSDP policy and vLLM policy compared to the first-round output
sources.topic: The inconsistency in multi-turn/agentic outputs is more severe.
sources.note: We write 「its correlation with avg_staleness is 0.9171… it is a freshness thermometer」. The article shows that the mean absolute difference is systematically larger on non-first-run (staler, more OOD context) outputs, consistent with our reading of the mean difference as a thermometer of freshness/OOD degree.

items.name: Standard deviation of the absolute log-prob difference
items.what: Standard deviation of the per-token |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob|. The mean only tells you 「how much they differ on average」; the standard deviation tells you 「how uneven the differences are」. The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.how: For the same batch of comparison data, take the standard deviation of the per-token absolute difference. A bucket-level version, partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/new_infer/diff_abs_std, is also available. The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.why: The variance of the importance sampling ratio mainly comes from tokens whose differences are especially extreme, not from how much they differ on average. The ratio of std to mean reflects the shape of this difference distribution: a stable ratio means the degree of heavy tails has not worsened; a sudden increase in the ratio means the disagreement among a few tokens is exploding, which is more worth alerting on than a rise in mean.
read: The std/mean ratio is very stable throughout: pro 2.60~3.13, flash 2.50~3.03. This ratio itself is more informative than the respective levels of the two numbers.

The minimum of the ratio occurs at restart steps (pro step 15: 2.603, flash step 16: 2.495), when the data is brand new and the bucket structure is simplest, indicating that part of the heavy tail is contributed by stale data.
Its correlation coefficients with global KL are pro 0.9957, flash 0.9967, and with diff_abs_mean are 0.9952 / 0.9849. In this run, the three are basically the same signal.
To see the trend, you should likewise look at the bucket 0 version.
items.observed: pro first-to-last 0.063351→0.124422 (+96%), peak 0.141710 at step 9; flash first-to-last 0.072203→0.107227 (+48%), peak 0.142213 at step 24. Bucket 0 over the same period only goes from 0.06339 to 0.06883 (pro, +9%), and from 0.07225 to 0.07930 (flash, +10%). The global std peaks of the two runs are synchronized with the global KL peaks (both at step 9 for pro, both at step 24 for flash).
traps: For a heavy-tailed quantity like |difference|, the sampling noise of the standard deviation is large. A single-step jump (e.g., from 0.095453 at flash step 3 to 0.122288 at step 5) does not mean the distribution shape has changed.
It is collinear with diff_abs_mean to 0.98~0.99; do not treat it as a second independent piece of evidence.
It reflects the consistency of the two engines while also being driven by data freshness, so step-to-step fluctuations cannot be read directly as 「a decline in training stability」.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: the divergence is most severe for tokens that have a low probability according to the vLLM inference engine. As a token's inference probability approaches zero, the training probability can become orders of magnitude smaller, leading to an infinite PPL and gradient.
sources.topic: Low-probability tokens are where disagreement concentrates.
sources.note: We write 「a sudden increase in the ratio means the disagreement among a few tokens is exploding, which is more worth alerting on than a rise in mean」. The article is precisely this mechanism: the disagreement is concentrated on low-probability tokens and can differ by several orders of magnitude, so for a heavy-tailed quantity like |difference|, the standard deviation is mainly driven by a few exploding tokens.

items.name: Proportion of tokens with absolute difference exceeding 1.5 (tau=1.5)
items.what: Among the same batch of tokens, the proportion of tokens whose |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| exceeds 1.5. That is, 「what proportion of tokens are already severely inconsistent」. The dashboard provides no official explanation: among the 22 official explanations there is no F(tau) family, and the meanings of F and tau are not explained; the following is an inference based on the data shape.
items.how: There are three grounds for the inference. First, in the same comparison batch, F decreases monotonically with tau; for tau=1.5/2/3/5/10 we always have F(1.5) > F(2) > F(3) > F(5) > F(10), consistent with 「cumulative tail proportion exceeding the threshold」, not 「proportion less than the threshold」. Second, its correlation with global KL over the entire run is 0.9999 (both pro and flash), and it moves in the same direction as diff_abs_mean (0.9965 / 0.9911), indicating that it and KL are another characterization of the same degree of divergence. Third, the magnitudes are self-consistent: for pro at step 9, F(1.5)=0.024959, and in the same step diff_abs_mean is 0.046246, diff_abs_std is 0.141710, diff_abs_max is 90.02; a very heavy tail is needed for 2.5% of tokens to fall outside 1.5 nats. The above is an inference; the dashboard provides no explanation.
items.why: The mean smooths over the fact that on a small number of tokens the probability difference between the two engines spans several orders of magnitude, and that is exactly what breaks the importance sampling ratio. F(tau) is a quantile-style readout: it directly tells you what fraction of tokens have crossed some divergence threshold. tau=1.5 nats already corresponds to the two engines' probability difference for the same token being e^1.5, about 4.5 times, which is a fairly loose warning threshold.
