read: The value is small throughout (on the order of 1e-2 and below); do not read it with percentage-magnitude intuition, but compare it with its own history.

Its curve almost coincides with global KL (correlation 0.9999), so it is likewise contaminated by data freshness. To judge engine consistency, look at F(tau) for bucket 0, i.e., partial/0/train_infer_diff/new_infer/F(tau=1.5).
Bucket 0's F(1.5) is a slow variable: pro 0.003872→0.005236 (19 steps +35%), flash 0.006029→0.007767 (25 steps +29%). Over the same period, the global values rose by 396% and 139%, respectively.

Adjacent taus are highly correlated (correlation coefficient of F(1.5) with F(2): pro 0.9992, flash 0.9986), so looking at one is enough; but the correlation coefficient of F(1.5) with F(10) is still 0.9939 / 0.9913, indicating they are not completely independent.
items.observed: pro rose from 0.003866 at step 1 to 0.019168 at step 19, with a peak of 0.024959 at step 9; flash rose from 0.006020 at step 1 to 0.014386 at step 25, with a peak of 0.025903 at step 24. Bucket 0 over the same period was pro 0.003872→0.005236 and flash 0.006029→0.007767, respectively. Regressing log F on log tau, the slope eases from -4.23 (1.5 to 2) all the way to -1.84 (5 to 10), indicating that the tail is not a single power law and that the more extreme it is, the slower it decays. After flash's restart at step 25, global F(1.5) dropped from 0.025903 to 0.014386 (-44%), while bucket 0's F(1.5) rose slightly from 0.007611 to 0.007767 over the same period.
traps: The dashboard does not give an official explanation, and the unit of tau is not written out. Based on the values (1.5/2/3/5/10) and the relationship with the log-prob difference, the most reasonable interpretation is nats, but this is an inference; do not cite it as an established fact.
Do not conclude that the inference engine is very consistent just because F(1.5) is only 2%: it means that at each step, about a few percent of tokens have a probability deviation exceeding 4.5-fold.
Bucket 5 of both runs did not report F(tau=2/3/5), so the bucketed curve will be missing a segment.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation
sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: Typical threshold: 1.5 - 5.0
sources.topic: Common units for token-level IS clipping thresholds
sources.note: We wrote “the unit of tau is not written out ... the most reasonable interpretation is nats, but this is an inference.” The typical range for token-level clipping thresholds given in the verl documentation is exactly 1.5–5.0, on exactly the same scale as the 1.5/2/3/5 used by F(tau) on this dashboard; the documentation also defines the metric rollout_is_ratio_fraction_high as “the fraction of weights exceeding the upper threshold,” which is the closest definition to F(tau) in public materials, but it is defined by an IS weight threshold rather than a log-prob difference threshold.

items.name: Fraction of tokens with absolute difference exceeding 10 (tau=10)
items.what: Fraction of tokens with |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| exceeding 10, i.e., a probability difference of e^10, about 22,000 times or more. This tier only sees genuine numerical outliers. The dashboard gives no official explanation; the meaning is inferred from the data shape.
items.how: Same source as F(1.5), different threshold. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: It is a quantified version of the extreme tail and pairs with diff_abs_max: diff_abs_max tells you how bad the worst case is, and F(10) tells you how many are that bad. If F(10) suddenly rises while diff_abs_max is unchanged, it means there are more bad points rather than a single point getting worse; these are two different failure modes.
read: Magnitude 5e-6~2.5e-4, already very small, noise dominates.

Bucket 0's F(10) is nearly dead flat: pro 5.096e-6~6.181e-6 (only +15% over about 25 steps), flash 9.011e-6~1.19e-5 (+17%). This is basically the numerical noise floor between inference engines and no longer changes as the policy evolves.
Its correlation coefficient with global KL is the lowest in this family: pro 0.9951, flash 0.9920, but still very high.

Its correlation coefficient with diff_abs_max is even lower (pro 0.5123, flash 0.2119 are the numbers for diff_abs_max vs. KL; this family is likewise decoupled from max), so the two indeed provide different information.
items.observed: pro first/last 0.000005→0.000165, maximum 0.000254 at step 7; flash first/last 0.000010→0.000092, maximum 0.000246 at step 11. The minimum for both runs occurs at step 1 (5.09e-6 and 9.72e-6), and flash also returns to 1.00e-5 at step 16. Bucket 0 first/last pro 5.096e-6→5.853e-6, flash 9.732e-6→1.054e-5. This tag is missing on bucket 5 in both runs.
traps: The dashboard formats it as pct, so the interface may display 0.00%; this does not mean it is 0, only that there are not enough digits.
Do not use this item to judge whether training is healthy. Its value is almost entirely determined by numerical precision and individual tokens, and is unrelated to policy quality.

Whether tau is nats is inferred; if tau's true unit is not nats, all absolute thresholds in this family must be reinterpreted, but the two shape conclusions 「monotonically decreasing with tau」 and 「same direction as KL」 are unaffected.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: the divergence is most severe for tokens that have a low probability according to the vLLM inference engine. As a token's inference probability approaches zero, the training probability can become orders of magnitude smaller, leading to an infinite PPL and gradient.
sources.topic: Low-probability tokens are where disagreement concentrates.
sources.note: We wrote “this tier only sees genuine numerical outliers.” That text explains that extreme divergence occurs only on the batch of tokens whose inference probability approaches zero; therefore, an extreme threshold like F(10) necessarily counts the same small handful of tokens, small in magnitude but not negligible.

items.name: Fraction of tokens with absolute difference exceeding 2 (tau=2)
items.what: Share within the same batch of tokens where |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| exceeds 2, a stricter threshold than F(1.5). tau=2 nats corresponds to the probability difference between the two engines for the same token being e^2, about 7.4×. The dashboard gives no official explanation; the meaning is an inference based on the data shape (see the inference basis in the F(tau=1.5) entry).
items.how: Same origin as F(1.5), only the threshold differs. A bucket-level version partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/new_infer/F(tau=2) also exists, but bucket 5 in both runs did not report this tag. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: The larger tau is, the more it reflects only the portion of tokens that are truly out of control. F(1.5) mixes in a batch of “close but not serious” tokens; F(2) starts to approach “the two probability estimates for these tokens no longer look like they were given by the same model.” It is more sensitive than F(1.5) to a small number of exploding tokens, and is suitable for viewing in comparison with diff_abs_max.
read: Its ratio to F(1.5) has been stable at 2.8~3.5 for a long time and can be treated as a shape indicator: a sudden decrease in the ratio indicates that the tail is getting heavier.
The correlation coefficient with global KL is pro 0.9995, flash 0.9987, still completely dominated by freshness. Only the bucket 0 version is the inference engine signal.
Bucket 0's F(2): pro 0.000617→0.000874, flash 0.001078→0.001306, both much more stable than the global values.
At the restart step, you will see it and F(1.5) drop together; this is a data mix change, not the inference engine getting better.
items.observed: pro first and last 0.000616→0.006469, peak 0.008922 at step 9; flash first and last 0.001076→0.004100, peak 0.008898 at step 24. The global increases are 950% and 281%, respectively, while bucket 0 is only +42% and +21%. flash step 24 to 25: global 0.008898→0.004100 (-54%), bucket 0 from 0.001300 to 0.001306 (almost unchanged). The F(1.5)/F(2) ratio in pro is 2.79~6.28 (highest at the two restart steps, step 1 and step 15), and in flash is 2.84~5.95 (highest at step 1 and step 16).
traps: At the restart step, the F(1.5)/F(2) ratio is noticeably larger (pro step 1 6.28, step 15 6.17; flash step 1 5.59, step 16 5.95), because at this point samples outside bucket 0 have disappeared and the distribution of bucket 0 itself is cleaner. Do not read this jump as a change in inference engine behavior.
The values are on the order of 1e-3; the dashboard data has 6 significant digits, and the last digit already has noise, so do not compare to four decimal places.
pro bucket 5 and flash bucket 5 lack this tag.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation
sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: Typical threshold: 1.5 - 5.0
sources.topic: Common units for token-level IS clipping thresholds
sources.note: We wrote “the larger tau is, the more it reflects only the portion of tokens that are truly out of control” and “the F(1.5)/F(2) ratio being stable at 2.8~3.5 over the long term can serve as a shape indicator.” The typical interval 1.5–5.0 for verl's token-level clipping threshold also includes tau=2, indicating that this tier still belongs to the boundary of the engineering-default “normal allowable range,” rather than an extreme outlier tier.

items.name: Share of tokens with absolute difference exceeding 3 (tau=3)
items.what: Share of tokens where |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| exceeds 3. tau=3 nats corresponds to a probability difference of e^3, about 20×, which already counts as “the two sides' judgments about this token are not the same thing.” The dashboard gives no official explanation; the meaning is inferred based on the data shape.
items.how: Same source as F(1.5), different threshold. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: At 3 nats, what gets counted is basically the tokens that would truly make the ratio explode. It is the boundary from “noisy” to “has bad points”; used with diff_abs_max, it can determine whether the bad points are isolated occurrences or appear in clusters.
read: Its magnitude is already 1e-4~3e-3, and its single-step noise is larger than that of F(1.5).

Bucket 0's F(3) is especially flat: pro is 1.047e-4~1.470e-4 throughout (up only 40%), flash 1.728e-4~2.551e-4. That is, on the freshest data, out of every million tokens only about 100~200 tokens have a log-prob difference exceeding 3 nats.
The correlation with global KL is pro 0.9986, flash 0.9970, still dominated by freshness.
The ratio F(2)/F(3) across tau is stable at 3.2~3.5 (pro 2.82~6.02, flash 2.90~5.84, highest at the restart step).
items.observed: pro first and last 0.000105→0.001962, peak 0.002784 at step 9; flash first and last 0.000196→0.001145, peak 0.002754 at step 11 (flash's peak at tau=3 no longer falls at step 24, indicating that the more extreme tail begins to depart from the shape of staleness). Bucket 0 first and last: pro 1.047e-4→1.470e-4, flash 1.963e-4→2.187e-4. The gap between global and bucket 0 is widest at this tier: pro at step 19 global is 13.3 times bucket 0, and flash at step 24 global is 12.4 times bucket 0.
traps: The tag does not exist on bucket 5 in either run.

flash's peak appears at step 11 rather than step 24, unlike the peak position of F(1.5). The further toward the extreme tail, the weaker staleness's explanatory power; do not force this family of curves to have consistent shapes.

A small value does not mean it can be ignored: it corresponds to hundreds of thousands to millions of bad-point tokens per step (estimated from flash step 24's ~1.76 billion in-bucket tokens and a 3e-3 proportion).

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation
sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: Typical threshold: 1.5 - 5.0
sources.topic: Common units for token-level IS clipping thresholds
sources.note: We wrote, "at 3 nats, what gets counted is basically the tokens that would really blow up the ratio... only about 100~200 per million tokens." The verl documentation sets the upper bound of the token-level truncation threshold at a typical 1.5–5.0, and tau=3 falls within it, supporting reading this tier as "an inner tick of the engineering tolerance band" rather than the extreme tail.

items.name: Share of tokens whose absolute difference exceeds 5 (tau=5)
items.what: Share of tokens with |trainer log-prob minus inference engine log-prob| over 5, i.e. a probability difference of e^5, about 148× or more. The dashboard gives no official explanation; the meaning is inferred from the shape of the data.
items.how: Same source as F(1.5), different threshold. The dashboard gives no official explanation.
items.why: At this threshold, what remains is basically definite numerical bad points. Together with diff_abs_max, it answers "how many tokens are in the worst batch, and how bad the worst gets."
read: Magnitude 2e-5~9e-4, already at the edge of the noise region, with pronounced single-step jitter.
Bucket 0's value is almost constant: pro 2.122e-5~2.842e-5, flash 3.842e-5~5.379e-5. This is the one in this family that most resembles the "engine's inherent noise floor".
The global peak position drifts further: pro at step 7 (0.000865), not step 9; flash at step 11 (0.000851), not step 24.
The correlation with global KL drops to pro 0.9973, flash 0.9949, but remains above 0.99.
items.observed: pro first/last 0.000021→0.000590, min 0.000021 at step 1, max 0.000865 at step 7; flash first/last 0.000043→0.000333, min 0.000043 at step 1 and step 16 (the two restart steps), max 0.000851 at step 11. Bucket 0 first/last pro 2.122e-5→2.823e-5, flash 4.268e-5→4.569e-5. This tag is missing on bucket 5 in both runs.
traps: The value is already as small as 1e-5; the dashboard's 6-significant-digit representation is unreliable in the last two digits, so do not use it for fine-grained comparisons.

The peak position is inconsistent with F(1.5), and it is easy to misread it as "the data became fresher, so there are fewer bad points". In fact, the bad points in this tier are mainly driven by individual extreme tokens, decoupled from average staleness.

sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: Typical threshold: 1.5 - 5.0
sources.topic: Common units for token-level IS clipping thresholds
sources.note: We wrote, "at this threshold, what remains is basically definite numerical bad points." The typical upper bound of the token-level threshold in the verl documentation is 5.0; tau=5 is exactly the upper endpoint of that range, supporting treating F(5) as the reading at "the outermost edge of the tolerance band."

items.name: KL between trainer and inference engine (global)
items.what: The official description is KL between inference-engine and trainer log-probs on the same tokens. For the same batch of tokens, the inference engine computes the log-prob once during rollout, and the trainer computes it again with a forward pass during training; the KL between the two distributions. What it measures is not the divergence of the policy from the reference model, but the numerical disagreement between "the engine that generated this trajectory" and "the model currently being trained." On the dashboard, this metric is the aggregate over the whole step's batch, and its fluctuations are dominated mainly by data freshness, not by engine disagreement.
items.how: The tokens trained on at this step are placed into several buckets by data freshness, and each bucket's KL is the average over all tokens in that bucket; the global value is approximately equal to Σ(bucket weight frac_k × bucket KL_k). I recomputed bucket by bucket and verified: for pro 19 steps and flash 25 steps, the correlation coefficient between the recomputed values and the dashboard values is 1.000000, with a median relative error of 0.11%~0.12% and a maximum of 0.15% (absolute error about 1e-5). The sum of the bucket weights equals 1.000000 at every step (deviation no more than 1e-6), and frac_k is exactly equal to that bucket's n_tokens as a proportion of the n_tokens of all buckets (maximum deviation 7.5e-7). In addition, Σ_k n_tokens_k is only 44%~56% of perf/total_num_tokens, so frac is normalized within the partial scope, not relative to the whole step's token count.
items.why: This is the number-one gauge of training stability. Numerical disagreement between the trainer and the inference engine (different CUDA kernels, different precisions, differences in MoE routing implementation, different attention backends) will cause the importance sampling ratio to deviate from 1 right from the start, bias PPO's ratio, raise the clip fraction, and mix systematic noise into the gradients. When KL is large enough, it amounts to doing on-policy updates with data that severely deviates from the current policy. It is also a downstream indicator of data freshness: when it rises, one must first separate "the engine disagreement has grown" from "the data has become stale"; otherwise one will end up tuning things that should not be tuned.
read: Looking only at this global curve will lead to misjudgment: it is approximately equal to Σ(frac_k × KL_k), and frac swings substantially with the training rhythm, so the curve shape is mainly determined by the bucket mix. To judge engine divergence itself, look at bucket 0's (freshest data) KL, i.e., partial/0/train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl.

The first step after restart is a natural calibration point: at this point staleness is 0, all data is in bucket 0, and global KL should equal bucket 0's KL. pro step 1 (0.002189 vs 0.002193), step 15 (0.002577 vs 0.002580), flash step 1 (0.002868 vs 0.002872), step 16 (0.003267 vs 0.003271) all satisfy this relationship.

Bucket 0's KL is a slow variable: pro over all 19 steps only ranges from 0.002170~0.002660, flash over 25 steps from 0.002544~0.003549. Its slowly rising slope is the real engine convergence/divergence signal, about +20%~+24% per 19~25 steps.

Global KL is highly synchronized with partial/avg_staleness (pro 0.9300, flash 0.9252), while bucket 0 KL is essentially unrelated to avg_staleness (pro -0.1939, flash 0.1965). The contrast between this pair of correlation coefficients is direct evidence that "global KL is a freshness metric".

Fixing bucket KL at the historical mean of each bucket and using only the true frac at each step to predict global KL: pro's R²=0.789, flash's R²=0.895, correlation coefficients 0.9463 / 0.9552. Conversely, fixing frac at its historical mean and using only the true bucket KL to predict, the correlation coefficients are only 0.5311 / 0.5498, and the RMSE is also 2.6~4.3 times larger. The contribution is almost entirely in the data mix.
items.observed: pro rose from 0.002189 at step 1 to 0.007688 at step 19 (3.5×), with a peak of 0.009801 at step 9; flash rose from 0.002868 to 0.005971 (2.1×), with a peak of 0.010106 at step 24. Over the same period, KL for bucket 0: pro 0.002193→0.002642 (+20%), flash 0.002872→0.003549 (+24%). That is, globally it rose by 250% and 108%, while engine disagreement on the freshest data rose by only 20% and 24%. The cleanest comparison is flash step 25: at step 24, staleness 2.1832, global KL 0.010106; at step 25 after restart, staleness dropped to 0.3198, global KL dropped to 0.005971 (-41%), but KL for bucket 0 changed from 0.003407 to only 0.003549 (+4%). For this step, doing a per-bucket shift-share decomposition: of the global change -4.136e-3, the data mix term contributed -5.708e-3 (accounting for 138%), the bucket's own KL change term contributed +1.528e-3 (accounting for -37%), and newly opened buckets contributed +4.1e-5. The bucket's own KL rises monotonically with staleness: pro bucket 0 mean 2.400e-3, bucket 1 7.394e-3, bucket 2 1.464e-2, bucket 7 2.755e-2; flash bucket 0 3.116e-3, bucket 1 6.075e-3, bucket 9 2.791e-2.
traps: Do not treat it as 'policy drift' or 'training divergence'. It is the numerical difference between the two engines on the same batch of tokens, and has no direct relation to policy quality; also do not use its absolute value to set thresholds or compare across runs. pro reports only 8 buckets (partial/0..7), flash reports 10 (partial/0..9); the deeper the bucket, the more the global value is pulled up.
A restart step makes it drop off a cliff (pro step 15 0.002577, flash step 16 0.003267, step 25 0.005971); this is the normal result of the pipeline clearing in-flight data, not an anomaly.

Bucket KL rising monotonically is the norm, because older buckets were sampled by earlier policy versions and are naturally far from the current trainer (pro bucket 0 and bucket 7 differ by 11×). Do not read 'oldest bucket KL 2e-2' as the engine being broken.
Bucket 5 in both runs is missing the tags F(tau=2), F(tau=3), F(tau=5), and diff_abs_max. When comparing across buckets there will be a breakpoint; it is missing data, not values turning into 0.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: KL between inference-engine and trainer log-probs on the same tokens
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: Your Efficient RL Framework Secretly Brings You Off-Policy RL Training
sources.authors: Feng Yao, Liyuan Liu, Dinghuai Zhang, Chengyu Dong, Jingbo Shang, Jianfeng Gao
sources.venue: Notion engineering blog (verl/THUDM ecosystem, listed by the verl documentation as a TIS source)
sources.quote: In modern RL training frameworks (e.g., VeRL), different implementations are used for rollout generation (e.g., vLLM) and model training (e.g., FSDP). Here, we show the implementation gap implicitly turns the on-policy RL to be off-policy
sources.topic: Original definition of train-inference inconsistency and truncated importance sampling (TIS)
sources.note: We write "What it measures is not the deviation between the policy and the reference model, but the numerical disagreement between the engine that generated this trajectory and the model currently being trained." This blog post is exactly the original source of this reading: under the same parameters, the token probabilities of vLLM and FSDP can contradict each other to the point that one side is 1 and the other is 0; the author calls this implicit off-policy caused by the implementation gap.

sources.title: Your Efficient RL Framework Secretly Brings You Off-Policy RL Training
sources.authors: Feng Yao, Liyuan Liu, Dinghuai Zhang, Chengyu Dong, Jingbo Shang, Jianfeng Gao
sources.quote: These negative KL estimates signal ill-conditioned training dynamics.
sources.topic: KL estimation is biased under training-inference mismatch
sources.note: We emphasize that this KL is positive throughout and on the order of 1e-3, and treat it as the number-one gauge of engine consistency. The blog points out: when the rollout actually comes from π_vllm rather than π_fsdp, the k1-type KL estimate is itself biased and frequently gives negative values when training is unstable; therefore "identically positive" can only mean that this site uses a non-negative estimator (of the K3 type), and cannot in turn be taken as evidence that the engine has no problem.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.venue: Notion blog (ByteDance, source of motivation for verl Rollout Correction)
sources.quote: The relentless push for faster inference has created a dangerous "training-inference mismatch" that can silently kill reinforcement learning with LLMs.
sources.topic: Training-inference inconsistency is the direct cause of training collapse
sources.note: We write "This is the number-one gauge of training stability……When KL is large enough, it amounts to doing on-policy updates with data that severely deviates from the current policy." That article uses the same class of metric called vllm-kl to prove: spikes in vllm-kl almost exactly trigger explosions in fsdp-ppl and the gradient norm, followed by reward collapse.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: the magnitude of the vllm-kl essentially follows: H20 < L20 < A100. Specifically, the vllm-kl for the H20 is generally on the order of 5e-4 to 1e-3, for the L20 it is around 1e-3 to 1e-2, and for the A100, it is predominantly between 1e-2 and 1.
sources.topic: Hardware baseline band for KL magnitude
sources.note: Our global KL sits at 2e-3~1e-2 (bucket 0 at 2.2e-3~3.5e-3), right in the L20/H20 range that the paper calls "normal hardware"; the paper states explicitly that only training in the 1e-2~1 bracket becomes infeasible. This gives us a verbatim-quotable yardstick for "the 1e-3 order of magnitude itself is far from dangerous", and at the same time shows that this quantity is mainly determined by hardware/backend.

sources.title: Rollout Correction — verl documentation
sources.authors: Yingru Li (author of the verl documentation)
sources.quote: These off-policy gaps can cause training instability and policy collapse.
sources.topic: Official classification of the off-policy problem: engine implementation differences vs temporal lag
sources.note: This document explicitly splits off-policy scenarios into two classes, Policy Mismatch (different precision / different backend / same weights, different implementation) and Temporal Lag (Model Staleness), which corresponds exactly to how we read new_infer/kl (engine discrepancy) and avg_staleness (temporal lag) as two independent axes.

sources.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
sources.quote: we show that its root cause lies in the floating point precision itself. The widely adopted BF16, despite its large dynamic range, introduces large rounding errors that breaks the consistency between training and inference.
sources.topic: Precision source of train-inference mismatch
sources.note: We write that "numerical inconsistency between the trainer and the inference engine (different CUDA kernels, different precision, differences in MoE routing implementation, different attention backends) makes the importance sampling ratio deviate from 1 from the very start". The paper says that simply switching everything to FP16 can largely eliminate this inconsistency, which shows it is more like a configurable precision choice than an intrinsic property of the engine architecture — our "necessarily present" checklist is on the strong side.

sources.title: FP8-RL: A Practical and Stable Low-Precision Stack for LLM Reinforcement Learning
sources.authors: Zhaopeng Qiu, Shuang Yu, Jingqi Zhang, Shuai Zhang, Xue Huang, Jingyi Yang, Junjie Lai
sources.quote: low-precision rollouts can deviate from the higher-precision policy assumed by the trainer, causing train-inference mismatch and potential instability
sources.topic: TIM caused by low-precision rollout and KV cache
sources.note: We write that "different CUDA kernels, different precision, differences in MoE routing implementation, different attention backends" are sources of divergence. The paper is exactly the engineering realization of that list: it extends FP8 to the KV-cache (per-step QKV scale recalibration) to speed up long-context rollout, at the cost of having to explicitly handle the resulting train-inference mismatch.

sources.title: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: Formulation and Practices
sources.authors: Chujie Zheng, Kai Dang, Bowen Yu, Mingze Li, Huiqiang Jiang, Junrong Lin, Yuqiong Liu, Hao Lin, Chencan Wu, Feng Hu, An Yang, Jingren Zhou, Junyang Lin
sources.quote: through a first-order approximation, we show that this surrogate becomes increasingly valid only when both the training-inference discrepancy and policy staleness are minimized.
sources.topic: TIM and staleness are two independent quantities that must both be pushed down
sources.note: We write that "when it rises, you must first separate the two things — the engine discrepancy growing and the data going stale — otherwise you will go and tune things that should not be tuned". The paper places training-inference discrepancy and policy staleness side by side as the two preconditions for the same proxy objective to hold, which is exactly the theoretical basis for "the two things must be looked at separately" (Qwen team, 30B MoE, hundreds of thousands of GPU hours).

sources.title: Beyond Precision: Training-Inference Mismatch is an Optimization Problem and Simple LR Scheduling Fixes It
sources.authors: Yaxiang Zhang, Yingru Li, Jiacai Liu, Jiawei Xu, Ziniu Li, Qian Liu, Haoyuan Li
sources.quote: we deduce that the mismatch is not merely a static numerical discrepancy, but a dynamic failure coupled with the model's optimization.
sources.topic: TIM is a dynamic failure coupled with optimization
sources.note: We write that "numerical inconsistency between the trainer and the inference engine …… makes the importance sampling ratio deviate from 1 from the very start", treating it as a relatively static engine property and only looking at the slow variable in bucket 0. The paper says the mismatch is a dynamic failure coupled with model optimization (gradient noise and mismatch escalate in sync), so a rising global KL cannot be read only as "the engine getting worse", nor can we expect bucket 0's slope to fully represent the engine's intrinsic level.

sources.title: Rethinking the Divergence Regularization in LLM RL
sources.authors: Jiarui Yao, Xiangxin Zhou, Penghui Qi, Wee Sun Lee, Liefeng Bo, Tianyu Pang
sources.quote: In practice, LLM RL is often off-policy because of training-inference mismatch and policy staleness, making trust-region control essential for stable optimization.
sources.topic: the two sources of off-policy, side by side
sources.note: The paper also points out that the importance ratio is a poor proxy for distribution shift under a long-tail vocabulary, which warns us not to judge the trust region on ratio-type readings alone; this points the same way as our practice of separating new_infer/kl from staleness and using bucket 0 as the engine baseline.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash official README (§5.3 Advanced RL Infrastructure / R3)
sources.quote: Rollout Routing Replay (R3): Addresses numerical precision inconsistencies in MoE routing between inference and training. R3 reuses the exact routed experts from rollout during the training pass, ensuring consistency with negligible overhead.
sources.topic: Official engineering mechanism for train-inference inconsistency (out-of-scope supplement, group B)
sources.note: This is Xiaomi's official, explicit statement on "inconsistency between rollout and training recomputation": the numerical precision difference in MoE routing is a real source acknowledged by the official side, and R3 (reusing the rollout's expert routing during training) is used to eliminate it. It directly supports group B reading train_infer_diff/* as a measure of train-inference inconsistency; this item is an out-of-scope supplement and may be adopted by group B first.

items.name: Mean token log-prob on the trainer side
items.unit: nats/token (the dashboard files it under the nll_loss group; values are positive)
items.what: This step recomputes log-prob for the tokens in the training batch using the trainer's forward pass, then averages over that batch. It is the log-likelihood level from the "trainer perspective". The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.how: It is one side of the train_infer_diff comparison batch, corresponds one-to-one per token with rollout_log_probs, and uses the same sign convention, so the two can be directly subtracted. The dashboard provides no official explanation; given that it is grouped under nll_loss and its values are always positive (pro 0.339~0.367, flash 0.359~0.404), the most reasonable reading is the negative log-likelihood after negating the sign, -log p (nats/token), i.e. what is usually called NLL, but this is an inference. The bucket-level version partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/nll_loss/log_probs also exists.
items.why: It and rollout_log_probs are two independent forward passes on the same batch of tokens; their difference is "how unlike its own output the trainer considers this data to be". This difference goes directly into the importance sampling ratio and is the source of off-policy correction strength. It is not very meaningful to look at the absolute value alone; it mainly varies with task difficulty and policy entropy.
read: Viewed on its own, it only reflects task difficulty and policy confidence; fluctuations of 0.34~0.40 are normal; it is not a loss curve.
The real information is in its difference from rollout_log_probs: a large difference means the two engines disagree greatly. Refer to the nll_loss/rollout_log_probs one.
The bucket 0 version is much more stable than the global version, because disagreement on the freshest data does not change with staleness.
It moves in sync with actor/entropy_loss (while flash rises from 0.376 to 0.404, actor/entropy_loss rises from 0.41331 to 0.45611); both indicate that flash's policy is flattening.
items.observed: pro over 19 steps ranges from 0.339485 (step 5) to 0.367159 (step 18), start and end 0.362124→0.364244, almost no trend. flash over 25 steps ranges from 0.367508 (step 5) to 0.403591 (step 25), start and end 0.376213→0.403591; the last step is that run's maximum, i.e. flash's training data is continuously becoming "harder" or the policy is continuously becoming flatter. The lowest point for both runs is at step 5.
traps: The tag is called log_probs but its values are always positive, so it is easily misread as being log π itself (which should be negative). The dashboard does not specify the sign convention; this is an inference.
Absolute values cannot be compared across runs: flash is overall 0.02~0.04 higher than pro, mainly because the task distribution and data source mix differ; it does not mean the trainer is worse.
It is not loss: it has no advantage weighting, no clip, and no KL regularization term.
It and rollout_log_probs are two forward passes on the same batch of tokens, not two different batches; do not treat them as two independent samples.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: The mismatch consistently show that the fsdp-log-ppl is greater than the vllm-log-ppl indicating that the FSDP engine produces more extreme low-probability tokens.
sources.topic: Training-side log-ppl is systematically high (sign does not flip)
sources.note: We observe that "the difference is positive and the sign never flips: at each step, pro's log_probs is larger than rollout_log_probs by 2.2e-3~9.8e-3", and infer from this that log_probs is the training-side -log p. That paper independently reports the same direction on the FSDP/vLLM combination: training-side log-ppl is always greater than inference-side, because the training engine assigns lower probability to low-probability tokens.

sources.title: Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning
sources.quote: we show that the instability of RL under TIM is primarily caused by drift: a persistent bias between training and inference engines that accumulates with every training step.
sources.topic: There is a persistent bias between the two engines that accumulates over steps
sources.note: We observe that the signed average difference is always positive and never flips (pro 2.2e-3→7.7e-3), and interpret it as "what remains is the systematic offset". That paper names this systematic offset and gives its mechanism: drift, i.e. a persistent bias between the two engines that accumulates with each training step—exactly corresponding to the 3.5× amplification of the difference we see with step.

items.name: Mean token log-prob on the inference engine side
items.what: For the same batch of tokens, the average of the log-prob recorded by the inference engine when the rollout was generated. It represents the confidence of "the engine that sampled this batch of data" in the data. The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.how: The other side that fully corresponds to log_probs, on the same batch of tokens and with the same sign convention, so they can be directly subtracted, and the difference is the average of the per-token differences. The bucket-level version partial/<k>/train_infer_diff/nll_loss/rollout_log_probs is also present. The dashboard provides no official explanation.
items.why: The difference of the two numbers gives the "mean version" of the train/infer discrepancy; KL is the distribution version of the same discrepancy. Its advantage over KL in readability is that the unit is just nats/token, so you can directly say "how much the log-prob of the trainer and the inference engine differs on average per token". It is also the entry point for judging whether the difference is a systematic offset or random noise: if the signed mean is small and the mean of the absolute values is large, that indicates it is mainly random per-token jitter.
read: The difference is positive and the sign never flips: pro's log_probs is larger than it by 2.192e-3~9.822e-3 at each step, and flash by 2.867e-3~1.013e-2.

The difference is of the same order of magnitude and in the same direction as KL: on bucket 0, pro's KL is 0.002193 and the difference is 0.002400; flash's KL is 0.002872 and the difference is 0.003117. On fresh data, the 'average per-token log-prob difference' and the 'KL between the two distributions' are almost the same size (about 10% apart), indicating that at this point the disagreement between the two distributions is close to a pure shift.
Relative magnitude: pro's difference accounts for 0.61%~2.90% of the rollout value, flash 0.77%~2.69%.

The signed mean is far smaller than the mean absolute value: for pro, |difference|/diff_abs_mean is only 0.092~0.213, and for flash 0.106~0.207. That is, the positive and negative differences per token cancel out 79%~91%, and only the remainder is systematic offset.
items.observed: For pro, first and last are 0.359932→0.356543, with corresponding global differences 2.192e-3→7.701e-3 (a 3.5× increase); for flash, first and last are 0.373346→0.397612, with corresponding differences 2.867e-3→5.979e-3. Both return to the minimum difference at the step where staleness goes to zero: pro step 1 2.192e-3, step 15 2.579e-3 (staleness 0 at that step); flash step 1 2.867e-3, step 16 3.267e-3 (staleness 0 at that step). The difference in bucket 0 is almost constant: pro 2.172e-3~2.663e-3 (19 steps), flash 2.538e-3~3.548e-3 (25 steps). After the restart at flash step 25, the difference drops from 1.0133e-2 to 5.979e-3 (-41%), while the difference in bucket 0 only changes from 0.003407 to 0.003549 over the same period.
traps: Do not read this in reverse as 'the inference engine computed it wrong.' The two forward passes use different kernels, different precisions, and different parallel strategies; a difference of 0.2%~3% is within the expected range.

The difference is the mean difference; consistent sign does not mean every token has the same sign. In the same step, diff_abs_mean is 0.039~0.050, while the difference is 0.006~0.010, indicating that most tokens' directions are opposite, only with small magnitude.
It is likewise contaminated by staleness; the cross-step trend cannot be directly taken as the engine divergence trend.
Like log_probs, the absolute level cannot be compared across runs.

sources.title: When Speed Kills Stability: Demystifying RL Collapse from the Training-Inference Mismatch
sources.authors: Jiacai Liu, Yingru Li, Yuqian Fu, Jiawei Wang, Qian Liu, Yu Shen
sources.quote: The mismatch consistently show that the fsdp-log-ppl is greater than the vllm-log-ppl indicating that the FSDP engine produces more extreme low-probability tokens.
sources.topic: Training-side log-ppl is systematically high (sign does not flip)
sources.note: We wrote 'do not read this in reverse as the inference engine computing it wrong'. That article attributes the directional bias to the two engines handling low-probability tokens differently (the smaller p is, the larger the gap), showing that the always-positive difference is a numerical property of the two forward passes, not an error on the inference side.

items.name: Those counters that are identically zero in the grading pipeline
items.what: In this family there are about a dozen fields that are exactly 0 at every step of both runs. They are distributed across the stages of dropping, skipping, failure, and advantage rewriting.
items.how: Individually verified always-zero fields: groups_judged_after_drop, groups_failed_pass1, groups_failed_pass2, groups_skipped_unbalanced, groups_skipped_empty_inputs, groups_expired_unjudged, dev_neg_turns, keep_mass_capped, rollouts_masked, judge_pool_dead_replaced, select_v4/select_r2_capped, select_adv_group_sum_abs_mean, tq_adv_mul_tokens, tq_adv_pos_mass, tq_adv_neg_mass, tq_adv_rows_rewritten, select_v4/groups_total, select_v4_nogold/groups_total.
items.why: The role of this family is inverted: their reason for existing is to let you know which stages have never been triggered. When you see 0, do not take it as 'no problem'; realize that these safeguards or exceptional paths were not reached at all in this training run.
read: Being identically zero usually has two explanations: the mechanism was not enabled, or the condition was never met. The dashboard does not distinguish between them; we can only say it was not triggered.
Pay special attention to the select_adv_group_sum_abs_mean and tq_adv_* batch: they are all on the advantage rewrite path, and being zero throughout means that path was not used.
When doing data validation, do not use these fields as one side of an identity; they cannot provide constraints.
items.observed: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, the above fields are all exactly 0 (not null). In addition, although select_v4/groups_total and select_v4_nogold/groups_total have names that look like totals, they are also 0 throughout; the ones that actually have values are groups_attempted and groups_judged under the same prefix.
traps: 0 and null are two different things: these fields are genuinely 0, meaning the counter is running but simply not counting; whereas after step 20 of flash, groups_attempted is null, which means it was not reported.
Do not assume that because they have groups_ in their names, they can match up with groups_total; most in this family do not match up.

sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: End-to-end success rate end2end_success_rate
items.what: The proportion of groups whose grading process runs from start to finish without failing midway. It measures the health of the pipeline, not the model's accuracy.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation. In the data, it is almost identical to pass1_success_rate (max difference 0.0033 for pro, 0.0058 for flash), indicating that end-to-end success or failure is basically determined by the first grading pass.
items.why: This is a thermometer for pipeline availability. When it drops, it means grading throughput is impaired, and the reward signal at that step will be worse than the actual model performance.
read: The normal range is 0.94~0.97. pro mean 0.9492, flash 0.9594.
It has low points: pro's minimum is 0.7662, flash's minimum is 0.9417. That low point for pro is worth checking for restarts or grading backlog in the same period.
It is not the same thing as model performance metrics. A drop in it does not mean the model got worse; it only means the data for that step may be incomplete.
items.observed: pro 19-step mean 0.9492, range 0.7662~0.9670, step 1 0.9648, step 19 0.9615; flash mean 0.9594, range 0.9417~0.9750. Starting from step 20, flash also stops reporting this tag; only the first 19 steps are available.
traps: Do not read it as the model success rate. The model's success rate is dynsam/avg@n and dynsam/passrate/*.
flash has values for only 19 steps; when doing a full-run comparison, this needs to be stated.
pro's minimum of 0.7662 is a single-step anomaly; using it to represent the whole will underestimate pipeline health.

items.name: Number of groups actually accepted for grading groups_attempted
items.what: The number of groups actually sent to grading. It is the result of removing routed/off from groups_total and then splitting by grader.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation. The decomposition verified in the data is groups_attempted = select_v4/groups_attempted + select_v4_nogold/groups_attempted, with pointwise error 0.
items.why: This is the real workload of the grading pipeline. Comparing it with groups_total reveals the grading coverage ratio; comparing it with groups_judged reveals how many gradings failed.
read: It is only about 46% of groups_total (pro mean 834, flash mean 804); this is the order of magnitude of grading coverage.
The difference from groups_judged is the number of groups that failed grading; look at select_groups_failed and groups_failed_pod.
Its fluctuations follow groups_total; when judging the trend, it is best to use a ratio rather than the absolute value.
items.observed: pro averaged 834 groups per step over 19 steps (range 358~1393), step 1 1223, step 19 571. flash averaged 804 groups over the first 19 steps, step 1 1172; note that flash stops reporting this tag from step 20 onward (steps 20~25 are null), so those steps require looking at the two sub-items select_v4 and select_v4_nogold.
traps: After flash step 20, this tag has no data. Do not treat it as 0, and do not use it to compute flash's full-run mean——that is the mean over 19 steps, not 25 steps.
It and perf/total_num_tokens reflect quantities from two different stages (number of grader groups vs. training token count); do not convert between them.
