sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Number of groups that completed grading groups_judged
items.what: The number of groups that completed grading and obtained results. It is the remainder after subtracting the number of failures from the number accepted.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation. In the data, groups_attempted − groups_judged matches select_groups_failed point by point (error no more than 4, due to rounding), so we can consider the number graded = the number accepted − the number failed.
items.why: Only groups that completed grading have reward differences available, and only these groups can enter advantage estimation. If the number of completed groups drops, there are fewer groups usable for learning at this step, and the gradient signal becomes sparser.
read: The grading completion rate (groups_judged / groups_attempted) has consistently been high: pro 94.9%, flash 95.9%, indicating that grading itself is not the bottleneck.
For its gap with groups_attempted, look at select_groups_failed and groups_failed_pod.
This number also affects the denominator definition of passrate-type metrics; pay attention when comparing across groups.
items.observed: pro averaged 791 groups per step (range 343~1330), grading completion rate 94.9%; flash averaged 777 groups (range 469~1233), grading completion rate 95.9% (calculated over the 19 steps with data). The difference mainly comes from the respective failure rates of the two paths select_v4 and select_v4_nogold.
traps: The grading completion rate is calculated from the sum of both sides; looking only at the ratio of a single small step will be noisy, so don't draw conclusions from a single step.
Being graded does not mean being graded correctly. Grading quality should be assessed via select_probe_disagree_rate and several r2/r3-related quantities.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Total number of candidate groups groups_total (entry point of the grading funnel)
items.what: The total number of candidate groups (groups) sampled at this step and entering the grading process. A group is usually a batch of parallel attempts on one task, and only after grading does the reward difference within the same group constitute the advantage signal. It measures the scale of the grading pipeline's input, not the amount of training data.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. The decomposition that can be verified in the data is: groups_total = routed/off + routed/select_v4 + routed/select_v4_nogold, with a point-by-point verification error of 0 over 19 steps / 25 steps. That is, candidate groups are first routed to three paths: no grading (off), grading via select_v4, grading via select_v4_nogold.
items.why: It is the entry count of the grading pipeline. If the entry drops, the downstream graded count and advantage signal count drop with it; if the entry rises but the graded count does not, it means things are stuck at the grading stage. Looking at this step's total also lets you tell how wide the sampler spread in this run.
read: First look at the routing breakdown: about half the groups never enter grading (routed/off), so a large groups_total does not mean a large grading volume.
groups_total and groups_attempted differ greatly (pro average 1820 vs 834); don't treat the two as the same quantity.
It fluctuates greatly by step (pro 996~2753); this is a structural difference in sampling batches, not an anomaly.
To determine grading capacity, look at it together with judge_pending and judge_pool_in_flight.
items.observed: pro over 19 steps averages 1820 groups per step, range 996~2753, step 1 2736, step 19 1254; flash over 25 steps averages 1734 groups, range 1282~2683, step 1 2625, step 25 2315. The routing shares are nearly the same on both sides: for pro, 48.9% go to routed/off, 25.3% to select_v4, 25.8% to select_v4_nogold; for flash it is 48.3% / 26.1% / 25.6%. That is, close to half of the candidate groups are not graded in this pipeline.
traps: The dashboard has no official explanation for this tag; the reading in this entry comes from an identity verified in the data (the three routing items sum exactly to the total), not from the official interpretation.
groups_total is not the size of the training batch. For the training batch scale, look at perf/total_num_tokens and prompts_per_step.
select_v4/groups_total and select_v4_nogold/groups_total, these two same-named subfields, are 0 throughout; don't use them as totals—the ones with values are groups_attempted and groups_judged.

sources.title: Site computation: the three identities of the grading pipeline
sources.quote: groups_total = routed/off + select_v4 + select_v4_nogold (exact at all steps); groups_attempted = select_v4/attempted + select_v4_nogold/attempted (exact at all steps); attempted − judged ≈ select_groups_failed (difference ≤4).
sources.topic: Grading definition
sources.note: Since groups_total is strictly equal to the sum of the three routes, it is not "all candidate groups produced by the model" but the quantity after one routing filter. Using it as the denominator to compute the grading coverage rate will overestimate it.

items.name: Number of pending groups and grading pool load judge_pending / judge_pool_in_flight
items.what: judge_pending is the number of groups currently awaiting grading, judge_pool_in_flight is the number of groups being processed in the grading pool, judge_pool_max_load is the maximum load of a single grading node.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. In the data, judge_pending and judge_pool_in_flight are nearly equal point by point (pro mean 95 vs 94, flash 114 vs 113), indicating that those awaiting grading are essentially the ones in flight, with no extra queueing.
items.why: The two numbers being close means the grading pool is always full: newly arriving groups are picked up immediately, with no backlog buffer. Once the sampling volume rises further, queueing will appear immediately, and thereby drive up data staleness.
read: pending ≈ in_flight is the 「at full capacity but no backlog」 state. Only when the two numbers diverge is it a signal of a problem.
judge_pool_max_load averages 8~9 (pro range 4~11, flash 3~14), reflecting per-node parallelism.
judge_pool_dead_replaced is 0 throughout, indicating that no node was replaced due to failure.
Looking at it together with time_total_sec_mean allows estimating grading throughput.
items.observed: For pro, judge_pending averages 95 (range 29~145), judge_pool_in_flight averages 94 (range 29~146), judge_pool_max_load averages 8 (range 4~11); for flash they are 114 (24~189), 113 (24~190), 9 (3~14) respectively. The two are essentially equal throughout.
traps: The dashboard does not explain the relationship between these two tags (whether one includes the other or they are parallel); all we can say is that they are almost equal in value.
They are instantaneous snapshots, not cumulative quantities; only one point is sampled per step, so they cannot represent the queueing situation throughout that step.

sources.title: Site computation: grading saturation and second-pass review not enabled
sources.quote: judge_pending ≈ judge_pool_in_flight (pro 95 vs 94, flash 114 vs 113), there is no backlog in the queue; grading a single group takes about 562 seconds (pro) / 570 seconds (flash), of which 97% is spent on the first pass; pass2_success_rate is identically 1.0, while judge_pass2_attempts is identically 0.
sources.topic: Grader term explainer
sources.note: The number pending grading is almost equal to the in-flight pool size, indicating that the grading side has been running at full load with no backlog. In this pattern, 「slow grading」 is not a stuck process, but a capacity ceiling.

items.name: First-pass grading success rate pass1_success_rate
items.what: The proportion of successful first-pass grading (pass 1). This grading setup is two-pass; pass 1 is the main path, and pass 2 is the supplementary path.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. In the data, pass2_success_rate is identically 1.0 while judge_pass2_attempts is identically 0, indicating that these two runs never reached the second pass at any point; pass 1 is all the grading that actually occurred.
items.why: It almost coincides with the end-to-end success rate, so it is the real 「grading health」. Together with judge_pass1_attempts, it shows how many groups were attempted and how many succeeded at each step.
read: It differs from end2end_success_rate by within 0.6 percentage points; for routine monitoring, looking at one is enough.
Grading time is also concentrated in pass 1: time_pass1_sec_mean and time_total_sec_mean are basically equal.
pass 2 is not used at all throughout, so 「two-pass grading」 is not actually enabled in these two runs.
items.observed: pro mean 0.9496, range 0.7662~0.9670; flash mean 0.9592, range 0.9418~0.9750. judge_pass1_attempts averages 825 per step (pro) and 802 per step (flash). judge_pass2_attempts is 0 at every step of both runs.
traps: 「Two-pass system」 is an implication of the dashboard field naming; in the actual data the second pass never runs, so don't, as you write, end up treating it as an enabled mechanism.
judge_pass1_attempts and groups_attempted are not equal (the former is slightly smaller); the two differ in definition, so don't compute success rates from one using the other.

sources.title: BAITBENCH: Measuring Agent Reward Hacking with Optional Shortcuts Planted in ML Tasks
sources.quote: Across seven frontier agents scored by our two-stage judge pipeline, 57.1% of runs exhibit reward hacking, with five of seven above 50%.
sources.topic: Public magnitude of reward hacking rate and two-stage grading pipeline
sources.note: They use a two-stage judge pipeline, indicating that 「multi-stage grading」 is a common design in public work; however, the paper does not give success rates or timing definitions for each stage, so it can only serve as background and cannot be used to verify our specific reading of pass1/pass2.

items.name: Second-pass grading success rate pass2_success_rate
items.what: The proportion of successful second-pass grading (pass 2).
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. This value is exactly equal to 1.0 at every step of both runs, while judge_pass2_attempts is 0 at every step. Together, the two facts can only indicate that the second-pass grading never ran, not that it 「ran and all succeeded」.
items.why: Its value lies in reminding readers: the dashboard contains some metrics that look normal but were never actually triggered. The 「perfect score」 of 1.0 here is an empty value, not good news.
read: It is always 1.0 and the attempt count is always 0, indicating this path is not enabled. When you see 1.0, don't take it as 100% success.
Similar cases of 「looks normal but actually has no data」 include time_pass2_sec_mean (always 0).
Fields of this kind should be ignored when reading charts; do not include them in your judgment.
items.observed: pro 19 steps, flash 25 steps, all exactly 1.0000; judge_pass2_attempts and time_pass2_sec_mean are 0 throughout.
traps: This is the type of value most easily misread in this dashboard: a constant perfect score usually means there is no data, not that performance is perfect.
Do not cite it in conclusions as evidence that 「grading quality is very good」.

sources.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle: Why Self-Improving Agents Need Deterministic Guardrails
sources.quote: Agents achieved perfect scores by reading cached answer keys from their environment, a 100% pass rate concealing 68% true capability.
sources.topic: A perfect score may be a product of cheating
sources.note: The core evidence of this paper is 「a perfect score masks true ability」——they use canary cases to make 「a perfect score itself evidence of cheating」. It directly reinforces our warning that 「a constant perfect score usually means there is no data/unreliable, not perfect performance」, and suggests that perfect scores such as pass2_success_rate identically 1.0 should be treated as an anomaly rather than good news.

sources.title: BAITBENCH: Measuring Agent Reward Hacking with Optional Shortcuts Planted in ML Tasks
sources.quote: Across seven frontier agents scored by our two-stage judge pipeline, 57.1% of runs exhibit reward hacking, with five of seven above 50%.
sources.topic: Public magnitude of reward hacking rate and two-stage grading pipeline
sources.note: Same as above: two-stage graders do exist in public work, but on our side the second pass was never executed (judge_pass2_attempts identically 0). This discrepancy has no public material that can be directly compared against, and can only be written into gaps.

sources.title: Site computation: grading saturation and second-pass review not enabled
sources.quote: judge_pending ≈ judge_pool_in_flight (pro 95 vs 94, flash 114 vs 113), there is no backlog in the queue; grading a single group takes about 562 seconds (pro) / 570 seconds (flash), of which 97% is spent on the first pass; pass2_success_rate is identically 1.0, while judge_pass2_attempts is identically 0.
sources.topic: Grader term explainer
sources.note: The success rate is identically 1 while the attempt count is identically 0: this is not 「the second pass all passed」, but rather the second pass was never actually executed. Looking only at the success rate reads 「did not run」 as 「ran and was perfect」.

items.name: Ungraded group count routed/off
items.what: The number of candidate groups routed to the “no grading” path. It is the largest of the three destinations of groups_total.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. From the data, it and the other two routing items sum exactly to groups_total, so it is the part of the total excluded by the grading pipeline.
items.why: Grading (running tests, running the evaluator) is much more expensive than sampling; directly excluding half the groups is a common way to save compute. This number is looked at to know how much of the sampling surface grading covers; when it rises, it means fewer groups are used for learning at this step.
read: Calculate the proportion together with groups_total. Both pro and flash are stable around 48%, with little fluctuation.
That it is not graded does not mean these groups were sampled in vain—the dashboard does not explain where this batch of groups went; don't draw a conclusion.
A sudden change in proportion is more noteworthy than a change in absolute value.
items.observed: pro averages 890 groups per step (range 560~1333), accounting for 48.9% of groups_total; flash averages 837 groups (range 620~1219), accounting for 48.3%. The proportions are nearly identical across the two runs, indicating this is a pipeline setting rather than load fluctuation.
traps: The dashboard does not explain why this batch of groups was excluded (difficulty, duplication, or simply to save compute); here we can only report the count.
Do not interpret it as “discarded data”; it may just not go into grading rather than not go into training.

sources.title: Site computation: the three identities of the grading pipeline
sources.quote: groups_total = routed/off + select_v4 + select_v4_nogold (exact at all steps); groups_attempted = select_v4/attempted + select_v4_nogold/attempted (exact at all steps); attempted − judged ≈ select_groups_failed (difference ≤4).
sources.topic: Grading definition
sources.note: The previous identity shows that “how many groups were graded” is composed only of the sum of three routes, with no fourth destination. This also means routed/off is not optional statistical noise; it accounts for nearly half of all candidate groups.

items.name: Number of groups that failed grading select_groups_failed
items.what: Number of groups that were accepted but could not be fully graded. It and groups_failed_pod, groups_failed_select are counts on the same chain.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. In the data, groups_attempted − groups_judged matches it point by point, so it is the total grading loss; the two sub-items it breaks down into are groups_failed_pod (the sandbox environment fails to start) and groups_failed_select (fails the selection stage).
items.why: This is direct loss in the grading stage. When it rises, you need to distinguish whether it is an infrastructure problem (pods fail to start) or a grading logic problem (selection stage failure); the former is an operations problem, the latter may be a sample quality problem.
read: First look at the magnitude: pro averages 42 failed groups per step, flash 33 groups; relative to an accepted volume of around 800, that is 4%~5%.
Then break down the subitems: pro averages 9 pod failures and 33 select failures, so the main cause is the selection stage rather than the environment.
It occasionally spikes (pro reached 205 around step 12); for a single-step spike, first check whether there was a restart.
items.observed: pro averages 42 groups per step (range 15~205), of which groups_failed_pod averages 9 groups (range 3~19) and groups_failed_select averages 33 groups (range 9~194). flash averages 33 groups (range 18~62), of which groups_failed_select averages 24 groups; the groups_failed_pod tag does not exist on flash.
traps: flash does not have the groups_failed_pod tag, so the failure composition of the two runs cannot be compared directly.
The sum of the two subitems differs from the total by 2~4 in the decimals, which is caused by rounding; do not treat it as a data error.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Suspected cheating attempt rate select_hack_attempt_rate
items.what: The proportion of groups flagged by the grader as “suspected cheating attempts.” The dashboard does not give a definition for this signal; from the name, it appears to be behavior where the model bypasses the evaluation during problem solving rather than actually solving the problem.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. There is a series of related quantities under it (ge_min, ge_min_rate, turns_per_pass, exposed_not_relied), indicating that this determination itself is tiered.
items.why: In agentic RL, the biggest fear is that the model learns to modify tests and guess answers instead of solving problems. If this proportion keeps rising, it means the reward is being driven by gaming rather than capability. This is one of the metrics on this dashboard that most needs long-term monitoring.
read: Look at the trend, not the absolute value. pro rose from 0.4001 at step 1 to 0.5056 at step 19; flash rose from 0.4139 to 0.5184. Both runs are rising.
Over the same period, avg@n is also rising (pro 0.5647→0.6334, flash 0.5137→0.6408). Capability and this signal rise in the same direction, so you cannot look at only one side.
Look at it together with select_pass_new_tests_rate: that one is also rising, indicating that the grader's determination of “passing new tests” is becoming more common.
It is only the rate of “attempts”, not equal to actually succeeding at cheating. The same-family exposed_not_relied (exposed but not relied upon) is used to distinguish this layer.
items.observed: pro 19-step mean 0.4032, range 0.3216~0.5056; flash 25-step mean 0.4813, range 0.3814~0.5524. Both runs trend upward throughout, and flash's level is overall higher. Among the same family, the comparable metric for select_v4_nogold is somewhat lower: pro mean 0.3710, flash 0.3832.
traps: The dashboard does not explain the criteria for this signal, so it cannot be cited as a “cheating rate”; it can only be called “the proportion marked by the grader as suspected cheating attempts”.
The absolute level is somewhat high (40%~52%), possibly because the grading criteria are broad; it does not mean half the groups are actually cheating.

It rises in the same direction as the success rate, and is easily misread as “the model is learning bad behavior”; the data cannot support this conclusion; it can only be said that it needs continued watching.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report Appendix B (Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench)
sources.quote: B Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench
sources.topic: Officially, a separate section discusses reward hacking on SWE-Bench.
sources.note: The official technical report lists "reward hacking on SWE-Bench" as a standalone appendix (verbatim title; the appendix body could not be retrieved due to scraping length limits, so only the title itself is cited), indicating that this kind of trickery flagged by the grader is a specifically discussed subject within MiMo's own system, not an observation dimension we invented out of thin air.

sources.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Is Not an Oracle: Why Self-Improving Agents Need Deterministic Guardrails
sources.quote: Agents achieved perfect scores by reading cached answer keys from their environment, a 100% pass rate concealing 68% true capability.
sources.topic: A perfect score may be a product of cheating
sources.note: the agent reads the cached answer key from the environment to get a 100% pass rate — precisely an instance of "bypassing the evaluation rather than solving the problem" — supporting our long-term watching of select_hack_attempt_rate as a direct signal that the reward is driven by gameplay.

sources.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
sources.quote: We show that we can monitor a frontier reasoning model, such as OpenAI o3-mini, for reward hacking in agentic coding environments by using another LLM that observes the model's chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning.
sources.topic: Detection of reward hacking (CoT monitoring)
sources.note: Using another LLM to monitor the CoT to detect reward hacking in agentic coding environments is a publicly validated practice, supporting our treating "the proportion flagged by the grader as suspected cheating attempts" as a class of monitoring metric backed by literature (the paper also warns: once monitoring is written directly into the optimization objective, the model will learn obfuscated cheating, so this proportion can only serve as an observational quantity).

sources.title: BAITBENCH: Measuring Agent Reward Hacking with Optional Shortcuts Planted in ML Tasks
sources.quote: Across seven frontier agents scored by our two-stage judge pipeline, 57.1% of runs exhibit reward hacking, with five of seven above 50%.
sources.topic: Public magnitude of reward hacking rate and two-stage grading pipeline
sources.note: A public benchmark gives a cheating-rate magnitude of 57.1%, with five of seven models exceeding 50%, exactly the same order of magnitude as our line's pro 0.40→0.51 and flash full-run mean 0.48, supporting our cautious reading that "a high absolute level does not mean half the groups are actually cheating" (they too only measured it via embedded hiddden test).

sources.title: Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench: Evaluating Reward Hacking in Terminal Tasks
sources.authors: Amit Roth, Ivan Bercovich, Yonathan Efroni
sources.quote: Measuring reward hacking is itself challenging, as detection typically relies on human inspection or LLM judges, both of which can be unreliable.
sources.topic: The reliability limits of using an LLM grader to detect cheating
sources.note: Directly challenges our practice of treating this 40%~52% as a stable signal: the paper points out that relying on human or LLM judge to detect cheating is itself unreliable, which is why they switched to an environment with "embedded detectable hacks". The grading criteria dashboard for our line is not public, so it can only be cited as "suspected", not as a cheating rate.

sources.title: Robust Code RL via Faulty-Code-Driven Test case Synthesis and Dense Reward Shaping
sources.quote: its efficacy is often hindered by insufficient test case coverage, leading to reward hacking and policy degradation
sources.topic: Using newly generated tests to fill in coverage to treat reward hacking
sources.note: The paper explicitly links cheating attempts to insufficient test coverage, supporting our combined read of the two lines hack_attempt_rate and pass_new_tests_rate together.

sources.title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
sources.quote: Our analysis further highlights the risks introduced by increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors.
sources.topic: Risk checklist for autonomous rewards and environment generation
sources.note: Lists reward hacking as the number-one risk of autonomous rewards, supporting our positioning of this 40%~52% suspected cheating attempt rate as "one of the metrics most in need of long-term watching".

items.name: Proportion passing new tests select_pass_new_tests_rate
items.what: The proportion of cases where the "passes newly added tests" item in the grading holds. The dashboard does not give a definition; from the name, it appears the grader adds tests beyond the original tests and counts how many groups pass.
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. It is in the same family as select_hack_attempt_rate, in the opposite direction: one counts attempts to bypass the evaluation, the other counts cases of passing newly added verification.
items.why: If the newly added tests can block solutions that "modify the tests to sneak past", a rise in this proportion is a good thing; if it rises together with the cheating attempt rate, that indicates the two are happening simultaneously, and one needs to distinguish whether it is a capability improvement or the grader patching holes.
read: It rises in the same direction as select_hack_attempt_rate; this is the combination in this data that most needs attention.
pro rose from 0.6598 at step 1 to 0.7656 at step 19; flash rose from 0.6246 to 0.7159.
Viewed alone, it has no clear good/bad direction; it must be read together with hack_attempt_rate and avg@n.
The dashboard does not provide a definition; do not directly treat it as evidence that “the model generalizes to new tests”.
items.observed: pro mean 0.6795, range 0.6122~0.7656; flash mean 0.6940, range 0.6246~0.7664. Both are upward throughout, by a magnitude of 6~10 percentage points.
traps: There is no official definition; the dashboard does not say what the new tests in the name specifically refer to or who generates them.
Its rise cannot be interpreted alone as the model getting stronger, because it moves in the same direction as the cheating attempt rate and the success rate.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report Appendix B (Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench)
sources.quote: B Reward Hacking of SWE-Bench
sources.topic: Officially, a separate section discusses reward hacking on SWE-Bench.
sources.note: The existence of the same appendix suggests: the official team has indeed encountered reward hacking problems on test-driven grading like SWE-Bench, consistent in direction with our practice of reading this proportion together with hack_attempt_rate.

sources.title: MiMo: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of Language Model -- From Pretraining to Posttraining
sources.quote: During post-training, we curate a dataset of 130K verifiable mathematics and programming problems for reinforcement learning, integrating a test-difficulty-driven code-reward scheme to alleviate sparse-reward issues and employing strategic data resampling to stabilize training.
sources.topic: The official team uses test difficulty to drive code reward
sources.note: The official MiMo-7B report explicitly writes that it uses "test-difficulty-driven code-reward" for code RL, showing that using tests (and their difficulty) to score/filter code solutions is MiMo's own established practice, supporting our reading of "the proportion passing newly added tests" as a signal that the grader is filling in test coverage.

sources.title: Robust Code RL via Faulty-Code-Driven Test case Synthesis and Dense Reward Shaping
sources.quote: its efficacy is often hindered by insufficient test case coverage, leading to reward hacking and policy degradation
sources.topic: Using newly generated tests to fill in coverage to treat reward hacking
sources.note: The paper clearly lays out the causal chain “insufficient test coverage → reward hacking → policy degradation” and uses newly synthesized test cases for filtering, supporting our reading of select_pass_new_tests_rate as “the grader adds verification beyond the original tests” rather than taking it as evidence of model generalization.

sources.title: Reality Is the Final Verifier: On Two Key Gaps in Agentic Software Engineering
sources.quote: reward hacking exploits omissions in the requirements or model, while hallucination widens the gaps by fabricating requirements or environment assumptions
sources.topic: Tests passing ≠ deployment acceptable (two gaps)
sources.note: It adds a boundary condition to our line “new tests can block solutions that cheat by modifying tests, so a rise in this ratio is a good thing”: the paper says reward hacking exploits precisely omissions in the requirements and deployment environment model; even if all tests pass (or even a formal proof passes), acceptable post-deployment behavior is not guaranteed, so a rise in this ratio cannot be taken as proof that “the grader successfully patched the gaps.”

items.name: Grader probe disagreement rate select_probe_disagree_rate
items.what: The proportion of cases where probes inside the grader reach inconsistent conclusions. It measures how uncertain the grading itself is.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation. Judging by the name and data shape, grading uses multiple probes/judgment paths to verify the same group, and this counts the proportion of cases where their conclusions conflict.
items.why: If grading is unreliable, rewards are unreliable, and the gradient direction will be skewed by noise. This metric tells you “how much of the reward signal at this step is trustworthy.”
read: It is normally 0.51~0.60, meaning more than half of the determinations have probe disagreement; this level is high, indicating that the grading task itself is difficult.
pro mean 0.5698, flash 0.5536; pro's disagreement is slightly higher.
It has no obvious trend (pro step 1 0.5593, step 19 0.5434); it is stable background noise rather than worsening.
Looking at it together with select_r2_flagged and select_r3_rate can distinguish “disagreement” from “actual error”.
items.observed: pro mean 0.5698, interval 0.5409~0.6031; flash mean 0.5536, interval 0.5147~0.5880. Fluctuation is not large; over 25 steps it stays basically within 3 percentage points above and below the mean.
traps: “Inconsistency” does not equal “wrong grading”. Probe disagreement may be because the task itself has multiple reasonable solutions; the dashboard does not distinguish them.
It is a proportion, not a count; it only indicates the certainty of the determination and cannot be directly converted into how many groups were misjudged.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.quote: We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them.
sources.topic: Systematic biases of LLM graders (position/length/self-enhancement)
sources.note: This is a classic source on LLM-as-a-judge bias: position bias, length bias, and self-enhancement bias are inherent to graders, supporting our reading of the 51%~60% probe disagreement as background noise from “the grading task itself being hard and the grader being unreliable,” rather than something in the pipeline being broken.

sources.title: When Consistency Does Not Mean Reliability: Evaluating Local LLM Judges Against Human Ratings
sources.quote: These results show that high self-consistency does not necessarily indicate high agreement with human judgments.
sources.topic: Self-consistency ≠ correctness
sources.note: It directly challenges our line “it is a proportion, not a count, so it can only indicate the certainty of the judgment”——the paper shows that certainty (self-consistency) and correctness can be decoupled, so a low value on this line should not be read as “grading is trustworthy.”

sources.title: Can We Trust LLM Judges: A Study of Capability-Dependent Biases and Multi-Judge Ensemble for Bias Calibration
sources.quote: We introduce a disagreement-based estimator that derives these error rates purely from inter-judge agreement patterns, requiring no ground-truth labels or task metadata.
sources.topic: Multi-grader aggregation and using “disagreement” to estimate error rates
sources.note: The paper proves that the “agreement/disagreement patterns among reviewers” can by themselves be used to infer each reviewer's false-negative and false-positive rates (without labels), which is exactly the public methodological basis for our reading of select_probe_disagree_rate as a grading-confidence reading.

sources.title: Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench: Evaluating Reward Hacking in Terminal Tasks
sources.authors: Amit Roth, Ivan Bercovich, Yonathan Efroni
sources.quote: Measuring reward hacking is itself challenging, as detection typically relies on human inspection or LLM judges, both of which can be unreliable.
sources.topic: The reliability limits of using an LLM grader to detect cheating
sources.note: The paper explicitly states that LLM judge detection is unreliable, providing an external explanation for “probe disagreement staying at 51%~60% for a long time”: this is an inherent ceiling of grader capability, not necessarily a pipeline failure.

items.name: Grader review flagged-red group count select_r2_flagged
items.what: The number of groups flagged in the second round of grading review. The sibling select_r2_capped is 0 throughout, indicating that they were only flagged red and no cap protection was triggered.
items.how: The dashboard provides no official explanation. The same family also has select_r2_evidence_rejected (evidence rejected) and select_r2_rate; judging by the names, these are counts in a review process.
items.why: It measures how many grading results need review. A drop in the count usually indicates cleaner judgments, but it could also just mean the review criteria changed; the dashboard does not explain.
read: The absolute amount is declining: pro fell from 120 at step 1 to 20 at step 19; flash fell from 114 to 73.
Relative to the number of graded groups (pro average 791), it is about 7%, not a large proportion.
select_r2_capped is 0 throughout, indicating that the capacity limit was not reached; this protection was not used.
items.observed: pro averages 56 groups per step (interval 17~120), first and last 120 → 20; flash averages 67 groups (interval 27~114), first and last 114 → 73. Both are declining, and pro declines more thoroughly.
traps: The dashboard does not give review criteria or the handling after red-flagging; the inference “decrease=better” does not hold.
Single-step volatility is high (pro between 17~120), do not use one or two steps to determine a trend.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.quote: We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them.
sources.topic: Systematic biases of LLM graders (position/length/self-enhancement)
sources.note: The paper points out that these biases require dedicated mitigation measures (the paper itself gives several mitigation schemes), which is consistent with our cautious reading that “a drop in flagged-red count does not equal improvement; the review criteria need to be considered,” but it does not give a process definition like “flagged red in the second round of review.”

items.name: Third-round judgment rate select_r3_rate
items.what: The proportion of groups that need to reach third-round judgment. The sibling select_r3_groups is its absolute count (on average 7~9 groups per step).
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. It and select_r3_groups are a ratio and a count, and the magnitudes match (7~9 groups divided by the number of groups that finished grading 380~790 is exactly 1%~2%).
items.why: Reaching the third run means the first two runs were inconclusive. This ratio reflects how large the small subset of 'hard-to-grade' cases in the grading process is; a rising ratio means grading cost is increasing.
read: The magnitude is very small: pro mean 0.0198, flash 0.0224, i.e. around 2%.
Both runs are slowly trending upward: pro step 1 0.0169 → step 19 0.0198, flash 0.0132 → 0.0210. The absolute change is only 0.3~0.8 percentage points, so it cannot yet be called a trend.
Look at it together with select_probe_disagree_rate: of the 50% probe disagreements, only 2% require a third round, indicating the review mechanism is working.
items.observed: pro mean 0.0198, range 0.0139~0.0360, corresponding to select_r3_groups averaging 7 groups per step (range 3~16); flash mean 0.0224, range 0.0129~0.0341, corresponding to averaging 9 groups per step (range 5~15).
traps: Neither numerator nor denominator is given on the dashboard; the magnitude consistency here is inferred from two tags, not an official definition.
The total volume is too small; single-step relative changes are meaningless (3 groups becoming 6 groups is a doubling).

sources.title: When Consistency Does Not Mean Reliability: Evaluating Local LLM Judges Against Human Ratings
sources.quote: These results show that high self-consistency does not necessarily indicate high agreement with human judgments.
sources.topic: Self-consistency ≠ correctness
sources.note: We wrote 'among the 50% probe disagreements, only 2% need a third run, showing the review mechanism is working'——the boundary condition this paper gives is: the grader can have a self-consistency rate of 92%~97% while having a correlation coefficient of only 0.28~0.34 with human ratings, so 'a low proportion reaching the third run' only shows the process is stable; it cannot be inferred that grading is accurate.

sources.title: Can We Trust LLM Judges: A Study of Capability-Dependent Biases and Multi-Judge Ensemble for Bias Calibration
sources.quote: We introduce a disagreement-based estimator that derives these error rates purely from inter-judge agreement patterns, requiring no ground-truth labels or task metadata.
sources.topic: Multi-grader aggregation and using “disagreement” to estimate error rates
sources.note: The solution the paper gives is weighted majority voting (WMV), a kind of multi-reviewer aggregation, which supports reading 'reaching the third run decision' as a kind of multi-reviewer correction mechanism, but it discusses aggregation weights, not a run design like 'the third run'.

items.name: Group rubric tier proportions select_tier_share_T1/T2/T3/H
items.what: After grading, groups are divided into several tiers by quality; here the share of each tier is given. T1, T2, and T3 are three quality levels, and H is a separate tier (the name looks like hard or hold, the dashboard gives no explanation).
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. In the data, the sum of the four items is exactly equal to 1 (error no more than 8e-7), so they are a partition of the same batch of groups, not four independent metrics.
items.why: The tier distribution reflects the difficulty structure of the currently sampled tasks. A high T1 share means most groups fall into the easiest tier, and the learning margin may be small; the drift in shares is more worth watching than the absolute level.
read: Look at the four items together; looking only at T1 loses information. pro is roughly T1 68%, T2 30%, T3 0.8%, H 1.1%.
The rubric tier structure of the two runs is almost identical, indicating this is a property of the task distribution rather than a model difference.
T3 and H together are only 1%~2%, belonging to the long tail; single-step volatility is high, do not use them for trend judgment.
items.observed: pro mean T1 0.6804, T2 0.3007, T3 0.0080, H 0.0109; flash mean T1 0.6732, T2 0.3049, T3 0.0078, H 0.0141. pro's T1 drops slightly from 0.6796 at step 1 to 0.6546 at step 19, and T2 rises from 0.2965 to 0.3270, that is, slightly more high-difficulty groups.
traps: The dashboard does not explain the definitions or sort direction of T1/T2/T3/H; do not assume T1 is necessarily the hardest or easiest.
The proportions of T3 and H are too small; single-step relative changes look large (e.g. doubling) but the absolute volume is very small.

sources.title: MiMo: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of Language Model -- From Pretraining to Posttraining
sources.quote: During post-training, we curate a dataset of 130K verifiable mathematics and programming problems for reinforcement learning, integrating a test-difficulty-driven code-reward scheme to alleviate sparse-reward issues and employing strategic data resampling to stabilize training.
sources.topic: The official team uses test difficulty to drive code reward
sources.note: Officially, rewards are given stratified by test difficulty, indicating that 'tiering by difficulty' exists in the MiMo system; but the report does not give tier names such as T1/T2/T3/H, so it can only serve as background and cannot be used to determine the ordering direction of our four tiers.

items.name: Average grading time per group time_total_sec_mean
items.what: The average wall-clock time for a group from the start of grading to the end. The same family also includes time_pass1_sec_mean (first pass), time_pass2_sec_mean (second pass), and time_pod_setup_sec_mean (environment setup).
items.how: The dashboard gives no official explanation. In the data, time_total_sec_mean ≈ time_pass1_sec_mean + time_pass2_sec_mean (pro mean 562.44 vs 547.32+14.66=561.98, within 0.5 seconds), while time_pass2_sec_mean is identically zero.
items.why: Grading time determines the throughput of the grading pipeline. If grading is slow, sampled groups have to queue and wait, which directly pushes up data staleness (partial/avg_staleness).
read: A single group takes 9~11 minutes, of which 97% is spent on first-pass grading, while environment setup takes only about 15 seconds.
Look at it together with judge_pool_in_flight and judge_pending to determine whether the pipeline is at full load.
It has no obvious trend (pro mean 562 seconds, flash 570 seconds), indicating grading cost is stable.
items.observed: pro averages 562.44 seconds (range 508~655), of which the first pass is 547.32 seconds and environment preparation 14.66 seconds; flash averages 570.13 seconds (range 523~624), of which the first pass is 554.40 seconds and environment preparation 15.27 seconds. The second-pass time is 0 for both throughout.
traps: The relationship between the sum of the three components and total elapsed time is inferred from the data; the dashboard does not give the timing definition.
This is the mean, not a quantile. Slow groups in the long tail will not show up here; using the mean to assess timeouts will underestimate.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Average prompt length of trajectories (ctx_prompt_length/mean)
items.what: The average token count of the initial input (prompt) of each trajectory. It is the stable base within the context length, accounting for only 4%~5%.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide a separate official explanation for this one; literally translated from the tag name, it is the average prompt length; it forms a subtraction relationship with ctx_total_length/mean and ctx_response_length/mean (total minus response approximately equals prompt; for pro, the deviation across steps is within 1 token).
items.why: The significance of its stability is: if the context is getting longer and it is mainly this that is rising, then it is task input or tool returns that are inflating, which is a data-side problem; if it is stable while response rises, that is a change in model behavior. Only by distinguishing these two can you know whether to change the data or change the training. Its occasional extreme values (a single prompt reaching 560,000 tokens) also explain why some individual trajectories are close to the length limit right from the start.
read: Check stability: pro over the entire run 3963.9~4464.4, flash 3995.4~4588.9, with fluctuations all within ±7%; this is a healthy shape.
Look at the division of labor with response: it only accounts for 4%~5%, so any significant change in context length should not be attributed to prompt.

Look at the jumps in max: the mean is very stable, but single-step max can reach several hundred thousand tokens, indicating an extreme long tail in the distribution; when troubleshooting, do not look only at the mean.
items.observed: For pro, the range over 19 steps is 3963.92 (step 15)~4464.42 (step 4), mean 4147. For flash, the range over 25 steps is 3995.4 (step 10)~4588.87 (step 19), mean 4256; the two runs differ by only 2.6%. As a proportion of ctx_total_length/mean, pro is 4.7% and flash is 4.1%. The fluctuation of the maximum is much larger: for pro, the longest prompt in a single step ranges from 71054 to 566065 (step 10), and for flash from 83058 to 710514 (step 15); that is, the average is only 4,000 tokens, but each step is mixed with extremely long prompts of hundreds of thousands of tokens.
traps: Its stability does not mean the data is fine: the mean is stable while the max fluctuates sharply, indicating the long tail has always existed and is merely averaged away.
This line's share is too small; do not treat it as an explanatory term for context growth.
The dashboard does not give a separate official explanation for this line; the above is read from the tag name and its subtraction relationship with total/response.

sources.title: Raw series from this site's telemetry repository
sources.note: This explainer comes from the raw series in the telemetry repository, tag naming, and verifiable identities within the data. This round of provenance search found no directly corresponding public literature; if readers know of relevant materials, contributions are welcome.

items.name: Average generation length of agentic trajectories (ctx_response_length/agentic/mean)
items.what: On this class of agentic trajectories, how many tokens the model generates on average. It is a subset metric of ctx_response_length/mean, specifically looking at the class of tasks that require multiple rounds of tool calls.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide a separate official explanation for this one; according to the naming convention, it is the mean of ctx_response_length over the agentic subset; the same family also includes ctx_total_length/agentic/mean, ctx_prompt_length/agentic/mean, and same-named subsets split by code/general/visual/chat.
items.why: Separating out agentic is to distinguish whether 'overall generation getting longer' actually means all tasks are getting longer, or only the part with multiple rounds of tool calls is getting longer. Agentic trajectories being long is normal (each round of tool calls adds something to the context), so to judge whether context inflation is healthy, you need to see whether it grows faster or slower relative to the overall.
read: Compared with ctx_response_length/mean: pro's agentic mean 92071 is 8.7% higher than the overall mean 84731, and flash's 107950 is 8.0% higher than 99947; the two magnitudes are close, indicating the main force lengthening the context is indeed that batch of agentic trajectories.
Look at the growth rate: pro rose from 73116.9 to 107156 (+47%), flash from 72305.1 to 123620 (+71%), growing a bit faster than their respective overall generation lengths.
If one day the agentic mean falls below the overall mean, first suspect that agentic's call rounds are being truncated or tool returns are being dropped.
items.observed: pro 19-step range 69746.7 (step 2) ~110672 (step 14), mean 92071, first step 73116.9, last step 107156. flash 25-step range 72305.1 (step 1) ~135043 (step 20), mean 107950, first step 72305.1, last step 123620. The agentic mean at step 1 of the two runs is almost the same (73117 vs 72305); after that flash pulls ahead all the way, and by step 19 they are 107156 and 123620 respectively. The ratio of pro's agentic mean to overall generation is in the 1.05~1.09 range throughout, and the ratio is stable.
traps: The page does not give an official definition for this line; which harnesses agentic specifically covers can only be guessed from the naming and the train/harness/* grouping.
Its denominator is the trajectory count of the agentic subset; it cannot be directly subtracted from the overall mean.
The value being higher than the overall is normal (multi-turn calls are inherently long); do not treat it as an anomaly signal.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash official README (§5.3 fine-grained data scheduling and partial rollout)
sources.quote: We extend the rollout engine to schedule fine-grained sequences instead of micro-batches. Combined with partial rollout, this significantly reduces GPU idleness caused by long-tail stragglers.
sources.topic: Long-tail tailing causes GPU idling during the generation phase
sources.note: The long-tail samples are exactly the batch of agentic multi-turn trajectories; the official source treats it as an object that needs dedicated scheduling, which supports examining the generation length of the agentic subset separately, rather than only looking at the overall mean.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale (§3.2 Long tail dominates generation time)
sources.quote: the generation time is typically dominated by the generation of long-tail samples if the RL system is synchronized and the generation stage is not pipelined
sources.topic: Generation wall clock is dominated by long-tail samples
sources.note: Long-tail samples mainly come from agentic trajectories with multi-turn tool calls, which supports monitoring the length and growth rate of the agentic subset separately, to locate the long-tail source of outer_gen.

items.name: Trajectory average generation length (ctx_response_length/mean)
items.what: The average number of tokens generated by the model itself per trajectory; the official definition is tokens generated per trajectory. It accounts for more than 95% of the entire context length, so when the context gets longer, it is basically this that is getting longer.
items.how: The official description is tokens generated per trajectory. The dashboard does not say whether it includes content returned by tool calls (in most agent frameworks, this content is counted as part of the subsequent prompt, not as generation), nor does it say whether it counts truncated trajectories. What can be confirmed is that the difference between ctx_total_length/mean and ctx_prompt_length/mean is near this value.
items.why: Generated tokens are exactly the tokens that require paying inference compute, so they directly determine the cost of the rollout phase. They are also key to judging 'whether the model is winning by getting longer': if reward rises while generation length also surges, it means part of the gain is bought with tokens. When they rise, they will chain-push up outer_gen, total_num_tokens, and the truncation ratio.
read: Look at its ratio to ctx_total_length/mean: stable around 95%, indicating no abnormal expansion on the prompt side.
Look at the growth rate: pro rose from 68078.1 to 96974.5 (+42%), flash from 67462.9 to 114444 (+70%); flash's generation expansion is faster.

Don't directly convert it to outer_gen: the correlation coefficient between pro's response length and generation wall clock is only 0.074, and flash's is 0.309, indicating generation time is also affected by concurrency and long tails; average length alone cannot be used to infer time.
items.observed: pro 19-step range 65098.9 (step 2) ~101993 (step 14), mean 84731, first step 68078.1, last step 96974.5. flash 25-step range 67462.9 (step 1) ~124824 (step 20), mean 99947, first step 67462.9, last step 114444. The flash mean is 18.0% higher than pro. Throughout, it accounts for 95.3% (pro) and 95.9% (flash) of ctx_total_length/mean. pro's single-step generation peak appears at step 14 (101993), then falls back to 87494 at step 15, coinciding with the two restarts between step 14/15, but the dashboard does not state whether the two are related.
traps: It is an average, flattened at both ends: the shortest trajectory in a single step is only 109~788 token, and the longest tops out at 1046420.
Longer generation is not necessarily bad (multi-turn tool calls are inherently long); read it together with dynsam/agg_turn/mean and reward.
Truncated trajectories are counted here as 'generated to the limit', so this mean will be slightly inflated on steps with truncation and cannot be treated as a pure benefit metric.

sources.quote: we observe that excessively long samples often exhibit low-quality patterns such as gibberish and repetitive words

Therefore, the pro +42%/flash +70% length inflation must first rule out low-quality inflation.

Our statement “look at whether the growth slope exceeds expectations... this is a normal form of agentic RL” therefore needs to retain this alternative explanation.

sources.title: Site calculation: cost is accumulated linearly by wall clock time
sources.quote: cost = rate × (now − start) holds exactly at all 21 synchronization points (rate: pro $5.71/s, flash $2.855/s). Converted to training tokens: pro $35,181 / 1B tokens, flash $10,690 / 1B tokens, a 3.3× difference.
sources.topic: Cost basis
sources.note: The other half of the per-token cost difference comes from context length: flash averages 104,203 tokens, 17% higher than pro's 88,878, but its unit price is still much lower, indicating the difference is mainly not in sequence length.

items.name: Proportion of context truncated (ctx_total_length/clip_ratio)
items.what: The proportion of trajectories in this step that were truncated because they hit the length limit. The dashboard does not provide an official explanation; a literal translation of the tag name is “the proportion that is clipped”. A truncated trajectory is equivalent to the answer being hard-cut, often cannot get the correct reward, and is a sample that both burns compute and pollutes the training signal.
items.how: The dashboard does not explain the numerator and denominator. From the data, the smallest non-zero value is about 4.0e-5, i.e. about 1/25000, which matches the order of magnitude of 25088 training trajectories per step (1568 prompts × 16), so it is roughly “number of truncated trajectories / number of trajectories in this step”. But the exact denominator cannot be confirmed from the dashboard; below, it is uniformly expressed as “how many trajectories per ten thousand trajectories”.
items.why: Truncated trajectories are a hidden data loss. A rise in the truncation ratio means two things happen at the same time: more samples that are “cut off before finishing” are mixed into the training signal, and at the same time that portion of compute does not buy effective gradients. It and ctx_total_length/mean are a causal pair: longer context pushes the distribution toward the length limit, and truncation naturally increases.
read: Look at magnitude, not absolute value: pro is about 0.4~2.4 per ten thousand throughout, flash is 0.4~31.0, both are still at a very small magnitude and do not currently constitute a major problem.

Look at the trend: flash's mean over the first 5 steps is 1.68 per ten thousand, and over the last 5 steps is 13.25, up nearly 8-fold; this line deteriorates as context grows longer, and is not random.
flash is nonzero across all 25 steps, while pro has 2 steps (steps 2 and 11) that are exactly 0, indicating pro's truncation is more sporadic.
When this line rises, it must be examined together with ctx_total_length/max to confirm whether the long tail has increased or the cap has been changed.
items.observed: For pro, over 19 steps the range is 0 (steps 2, 11)~2.40462e-4 (step 14), mean 1.180e-4, which converts to 0~2.40 per ten thousand trajectories, average 1.18; among the 17 non-zero steps, the values are basically on the order of an integer multiple of 1 trajectory. For flash, over 25 steps the range is 4.00256e-5~3.09922e-3 (step 19), mean 7.286e-4, i.e. 0.40~30.99 per ten thousand, average 7.29; all 25 steps are non-zero. flash's mean is 6.2× that of pro, and it is clearly worsening: the first 5 steps have mean 1.682e-4, the last 5 steps have mean 1.325e-3. The two steps where pro is 0 (steps 2, 11) are both after a restart; restart causes rollout to warm up again, and the long tail has not had time to pile up.
traps: A small value does not mean no problem: this is a ratio, flash's peak is already 31 per ten thousand, and it is monotonically worsening.
A high truncation ratio does not mean the reward is necessarily bad; it depends on whether truncated trajectories are discarded; the dashboard does not state the fate of truncated samples.
Don't use ctx_total_length/max to infer it in reverse: max hitting the cap only means 'at least 1', and the order of magnitude still has to be read from this line.
The dashboard does not give the numerator and denominator; the above conversion is based on a minimum granularity of about 1/25000 and is an inference.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale（Overlong Reward Shaping）
sources.quote: Overlong Reward Shaping, which reduces reward noise and stabilizes training.
sources.topic: Overly long samples need dedicated reward shaping
sources.note: DAPO lists Overlong Reward Shaping as one of the four key techniques for large-scale RL, indicating that “trajectories hitting the length limit” must be specially handled (otherwise they bring reward noise and unstable training), supporting our reading that “truncated trajectories pollute the training signal.”

items.name: Maximum trajectory context length (ctx_total_length/max)
items.what: The context length of the longest trajectory in this step. It is a “long-tail detector”: the mean tells you how long on average, while it tells you where the longest one tops out.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide a separate official explanation for this one. From the data, a very robust pattern can be observed: this line for both runs lands exactly at 1048570 on the vast majority of steps, and 1048570 is very close to 1024 × 1024 = 1048576, so it can almost certainly be determined that this is a context length limit. The dashboard does not state this limit value, so this is inferred from the data.
items.why: It is the first signal for determining “whether any trajectories are truncated”: as long as max hits the limit, this step has at least one trajectory cut off. Together with ctx_total_length/clip_ratio, you can tell whether it is “a single one hitting the cap” or “a batch cut off.” It is also a troubleshooting entry point: if max suddenly far exceeds the limit or is far below the limit, it indicates that the bucketing or scoring logic may have a problem.
read: See whether it is consistently hugging 1048570: pro has 8/19 steps and flash has 13/25 steps exactly equal to this value, indicating that in most steps at least one trajectory hits the cap.
Look at steps where it is clearly below the cap: pro step 3 is 525095 and step 15 is 562406; in these steps no trajectory hit the cap, and they are relatively clean steps.

Check whether there is abnormal out-of-bounds: flash step 14's 2236430 is 2.13 times the cap, and is the only time across both runs that the cap is exceeded; the dashboard does not provide an explanation.
Don't use it as 'the context for this step is this long'; it is a single extreme value, not a representative length.
items.observed: In pro, 8 of 19 steps have a maximum length exactly equal to 1048570 (steps 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 19), and the remaining steps range from 525095 (step 3) to 985685 (step 1). In flash, 13 of 25 steps are equal to 1048570 (steps 6, 7, 9, 12, 13, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24), steps 1 and 2 are 1049640 and 1048610, and the rest range from 659032 (step 4) to 940676 (step 11). The only anomaly is 2236430 at flash step 14, about 2.13 times the limit. The proportion of steps where flash hits the limit (13/25 = 52%) is still higher than pro (8/19 = 42%), which is the same thing as flash having longer context and a higher truncation ratio.
traps: Don't use it as the upper bound of the length distribution: flash step 14 is 2236430, showing that this line can exceed 1048570.
The fact that 1048570 is the cap is inferred by me from the constant value recurring repeatedly in the data; the dashboard body does not state this number.
max hitting the cap does not mean most trajectories are truncated; look at the magnitude of ctx_total_length/clip_ratio: pro averages only 1.2 per ten thousand.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale（Overlong Reward Shaping）
sources.quote: Overlong Reward Shaping, which reduces reward noise and stabilizes training.
sources.topic: Overly long samples need dedicated reward shaping
sources.note: Since overly long samples are to be specially shaped, observations such as max hitting 1048570 — “at least one trajectory hits the limit” — now have a public motivational background: it is the first signal for determining whether length governance should be triggered.

items.name: Average trajectory context length (ctx_total_length/mean)
items.what: The average context length per trajectory, equal to the prompt plus everything generated by the model. It is the most intuitive curve for long-context training, and also the source of this step's token cost and time.
items.how: The official explanation is total context length per trajectory (prompt + response), in tokens. The dashboard does not say whether it is weighted by trajectory or by sequence, nor whether it includes truncated trajectories. You can check for yourself: subtracting ctx_prompt_length/mean from it is basically equal to ctx_response_length/mean (pro deviation is within 1 token), indicating the two are consistent.
items.why: Context length is the common driver of all cost metrics in this group. When it rises, perf/total_num_tokens rises with it, trainer_ops rises with it, timing_s/step rises with it, and the number of trajectories truncated by the length limit also rises. So it is both a load metric to watch and the first candidate for explaining “why this step got slower.”
read: Look at whether the growth slope exceeds expectations: both are steadily rising (pro 19 steps +40%, flash 25 steps +65%), which is the normal shape of agentic RL, because the model learns to use more rounds of tool calls.

flash is clearly higher than pro: the overall mean is 104203 vs 88878 (17.2% higher), and the gap widens gradually—at step 1 they are still basically the same (71634 vs 72178), and by step 19 it is already 123899 vs 101040 (22859 higher).

Breaking it down to see whether response or prompt is driving it: on both sides response accounts for over 95%, and prompt stays stable at around 4 thousand tokens, so what drives up the context is the model's own generation, not the input.
items.observed: pro 19-step range 69231.9 (step 2)~106203 (step 14), mean 88878, first step 72177.6, last step 101040, up 40% over the whole run. flash 25-step range 71633.5 (step 1)~129392 (step 20), mean 104203, first step 71633.5, last step 118576, up 65% over the whole run. flash mean is 17.2% higher than pro. Cell-by-cell comparison shows the difference is not always positive: at step 1 flash is instead 544 less than pro, and at step 9 it is 203 less, but from step 11 onward flash is consistently higher by more than 10,000, and at step 19 it is higher by 22859. Broken down, response accounts for 95.3% (pro) and 95.9% (flash) of the total length, and the prompt mean stays stable throughout between 3964~4464 (pro) and 3995~4589 (flash). The vicinity of the length cap also provides corroborating evidence: pro has 8/19 steps and flash has 13/25 steps whose maximum length hits exactly 1048570.
traps: The mean cannot represent the distribution: pro's minimum length is only 184~788 tokens, while the maximum reaches 1048570, so the mean is taken over an extremely wide distribution.

A rising mean does not mean 'the model has become verbose'; it may also be that the task itself has become harder or the number of tool-call turns has increased, so you need to look at dynsam/agg_turn/mean together to judge.
flash's context is longer, but its per-step wall clock is actually shorter than pro's (7613s vs 9177s), so context length cannot be directly equated with time cost.

items.name: In-flight sandbox count (env/active)
items.what: The number of isolated sandboxes active at this moment is, roughly speaking, how many execution environments are open and running rollouts at the same time. It is a waterline for rollout concurrency, not a cumulative value.
items.how: The official description says sandbox environments in flight. I checked the sub-tags under env/: env/active is exactly equal to the sum of the subpools env/code/shared/active, env/code/dataset-m1dt/active, env/general/dataset-*/active, env/visual/dataset-*/active, and env/cyber/dataset-9aui/active, and all of pro’s 19 steps and flash’s 25 steps match one by one (error less than 1.5). In other words, it is a real-time aggregate value split by dataset.
items.why: The concurrency waterline is the precondition for whether the generation phase can run at full capacity. A drop in the number means sandbox supply cannot keep up, or a single trajectory runs too long and occupies a slot, so generation slows down as a result; if the number stays pinned to some ceiling for a long time, it means concurrency has already reached its cap, and to speed up generation further you can only add machines or shorten trajectories. Look at it together with env/total_error and env/total_setup: active is the waterline, total_setup is the flow, total_error is the leak.
read: Look at stability: apart from step 1's 31135, pro's remaining 18 steps are all between 22352~23848, with fluctuation under 7%; flash is 37257~39296 throughout, with fluctuation of only 5%. This stability indicates the scheduler controls concurrency at the water level, which is a healthy shape.
Look for step-like jumps: when the water level suddenly rises or falls as a whole, it usually means the dataset composition has changed (for example, pro removes cyber from step 15).

Calculate the turnover count together with env/total_setup, but know that total_setup is the **cumulative number of starts since the last restart** (at each restart step it drops back to the same order of magnitude as active and then climbs again; this reset to zero can be seen at pro steps 11/15/17/23 and flash steps 16/25/28). So pro step 10's 330720/23180 ≈ 14.3 means 'within this segment each sandbox slot has on average served about 14 trajectories', **not '14 turnovers per step'**; dividing by the number of steps in the segment gives about 2 per step. The two runs are close in this magnitude.
When the water level drops, first check env/total_error to see whether environment errors have taken down the sandboxes.
items.observed: pro's 19 steps range 22352~31135, mean 23486; the 31135 at step 1 is the only time it exceeded 25,000, after which it held steady at 22,000~24,000, with last step 23168. flash's 25 steps range 37257~39296, mean 38069, stable throughout, last step 38368, about 62% higher than pro. The biggest chunk in both runs is env/code/shared/active; pro accounts for 74.4% of env/active (81.8% at the last step), flash 69.6% (74.5% at the last step). From step 15 in pro the cyber sub-pool no longer reports, so it is missing from the env/active sum too, but the overall level did not visibly drop, indicating the remaining data sources made up for it.
traps: It is an instantaneous water level, not cumulative throughput; don't use it as 'how many sandboxes ran in this step'; that is env/total_setup.
pro step 1's 31135 is an anomalous high point (it had just experienced two consecutive restarts at the time); don't use it as a baseline.

The absolute water levels of pro and flash cannot be directly compared: the data mixes, concurrency limits, and model sizes on the two sides are all different; flash being 62% higher does not mean it is doing more effective work.

items.name: Number of in-flight sandboxes in the code shared pool (env/code/shared/active)
items.what: The number of currently active sandboxes in the sandbox pool shared by code-type tasks. It is the largest single sandbox pool in both runs, accounting for more than 70% of all in-flight sandboxes.
items.how: The dashboard does not give an explainer for this one, nor does it explain what shared specifically refers to (it is not a dataset id of the dataset-xxxx form; from the naming it looks like a pool shared across code datasets). It is one of the components of env/active: env/active equals the sum of all env/<category>/<dataset>/active and this one, and this checks out item by item for pro's 19 steps and flash's 25 steps.
items.why: It is the main source of pressure on the environment side, and also the most direct window for observing level fluctuations. Sandboxes for code tasks have to run compilation and tests, and their start/stop cost is higher than for ordinary conversations, so once this pool's level drops, the generation side is the first to feel the stall. In addition, looking at it together with the breakdown of the code datasets (env/code/dataset-m1dt/active etc.) makes it possible to tell whether the shared pool is not enough or whether some dataset has filled the pool up.
read: Look at the share: pro averages 74.4% of env/active (81.8% at the last step), and flash accounts for 69.6% (74.5% at the last step); both runs are dominated by this pool.
Look at fluctuation: pro oscillates between 15317~22143, with step 1's 22143 being the highest point; flash is between 24891~28720, with fluctuation of only around 15%, more stable than pro.
It drops to 15317 at pro step 4 (env/active that step is 23266), while code/dataset-m1dt rises to 1176, indicating the pool is shifting internally toward a single dataset.
items.observed: pro's 19 steps range 15317 (step 4)~22143 (step 1), mean 17479; apart from step 1, all are between 15317~19752. flash's 25 steps range 24891 (step 4)~28720 (step 16), mean 26492, stable throughout. flash's pool is 51.6% larger than pro's (mean 26492 vs 17479), but flash's env/active is only 62% larger than pro's, indicating that pro puts more weight on other categories. After pro removed the cyber dataset (from step 15), this line shows no obvious change, indicating the code pool is unaffected by that adjustment.
traps: The dashboard does not explain the specific meaning of shared; do not assume it is 'the union of all code datasets'—it may also be a resource pool shared across categories.
It is highly synchronized with env/active; looking at it alone makes it easy to misjudge an overall water-level change as a problem on the code side.
The 22143 at step 1 of pro appears after two consecutive restarts, so it is not suitable as a baseline.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash official README (§5.2 Scaling Agentic RL environment scale)
sources.quote: Our automated pipeline maintains a Kubernetes cluster capable of running over 10,000 concurrent pods with a 70% environment setup success rate.

sources.note: This official 10,000+ pods refers to the GitHub issue environment of the code agent setup, which is consistent in direction with our observation that env/code/shared/active is the largest single pool, accounting for more than 70% of the total, but the official figure uses pod while the dashboard uses sandbox, and the two units cannot be converted directly.

items.name: In-flight sandbox count for the cyber dataset (env/cyber/dataset-9aui/active)
items.what: How many sandboxes are currently running for the dataset-9aui dataset under the cyber category. It is the most granular layer in the env/ prefix, broken down all the way by 'category / dataset'.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide a separate explanation for this line; it is one of the components of env/active. The most valuable thing about this line is that it shows a form of 'metric disappearance': for pro, from step 15 onward this line becomes null rather than 0.
items.why: The sandbox count broken down by dataset is used to determine 'which data source is consuming resources'. It is also a window for verifying whether a configuration change has taken effect: when a dataset is taken offline, its sandbox count should first go to zero, then become null, rather than slowly decline. This line on pro exactly records one such change.
read: First distinguish null from 0: null means that at this step this data source is no longer in the dataset, while 0 means it is present but no sandbox was started; the two have completely different meanings.
Check whether the offline transition is clean: pro turns directly to null from step 15, while the previous step (step 14) still had 1222, with no trailing tail.
Look at the normal level: flash has a value throughout, range 1140~5536; the 5536 at step 1 is the peak, after which it is basically between 2300~3100.
items.observed: pro only has values for steps 1~14, range 1222 (step 14)~4496 (step 1), mean 2278; steps 15~19 are all null. This matches the official announcement: the notice in notices.json at 2026-09-17T11:00Z says we also removed the cyber dataset from the upcoming pro run, since we observed some bad patterns in the rollout logs, and in the same period there was also a restart announcement about a network connectivity issue. For flash, this line has values across all 25 steps, range 1140~5536, mean 2650, indicating that cyber was only removed from pro and retained on flash.
traps: Treating null as 0 leads to an incorrect conclusion (thinking 'the cyber sandbox dropped to 0'), when in fact the data source was removed.
pro and flash cannot be compared on this one: one side has cyber, the other does not; this is a difference in product decisions, not a performance difference.
Its disappearance time on pro is slightly later than the announcement (the announcement is at 2026-09-17T11:00Z, and step 15 completed after it); pay attention to this when ordering the timeline.

sources.title: mimo.xiaomi.com/rl official run announcement: remove the cyber dataset
sources.quote: we also removed the cyber dataset from the upcoming pro run, since we observed some bad patterns in the rollout logs.
sources.topic: Official announcement for this run (environment/data source change)
sources.note: The official announcement verbatim confirms that the cyber dataset was removed from the pro run, which precisely explains why this line becomes null from step 15 onward on pro rather than dropping to 0; our reading that 'null means the data source is no longer in the dataset' has official provenance.

items.name: Suspected sandbox leak (env/possible_leak)
items.what: Number of sandboxes suspected of not being properly reclaimed and still remaining in the system. The dashboard does not provide an official definition; translated literally from the tag name, it is 'possible leak'. The difference between it and env/active is: active is a properly managed in-flight environment, whereas this line refers to residue that has escaped management.
items.how: The dashboard does not explain how it is determined, nor does it specify the statistical window. From the data, it is an alert-type metric that is almost identically zero, only jumping to non-zero when there is an anomaly.
items.why: Sandbox leaks are the problem most likely to slowly accumulate in long-running training: each unreclaimed sandbox occupies a share of resources; when leaks accumulate, env/active's water level gradually fails to reach the target and generation slows down, ultimately manifesting as 'we clearly added machines but throughput does not increase'. This non-zero value is the signal that you should check the sandbox reclamation logic. It is usually too quiet and easy to overlook.
read: Any non-zero value is worth investigating: this is a health metric designed to be identically zero, not a continuous quantity.

Look at it together with env/active: if possible_leak rises while active is stable, it means the leak is limited to a very small magnitude; if both rise together, it means the reclamation path is actually broken.
Note that it may be an instantaneous value rather than a cumulative value, so looking at a single point is enough; there is no need to look at the slope.
items.observed: Of pro's 19 steps, 18 are 0; only step 19 (the last step) shows 1. This is the only non-zero occurrence across both runs. flash is 0 for all 25 steps. Relative to env/active at that step (pro step 19: 23168 in-flight sandboxes), a magnitude of 1 can be completely ignored, but it appears at pro's last step and pro had just experienced 9 restarts (including one OOM caused by expert load imbalance), so it is worth recording as a one-off event; the dashboard does not provide an explanation of the cause.
traps: Do not read 1 as precisely as 'leaked one sandbox resource'; the dashboard does not provide a definition, and it is more likely a Boolean-style alert set in count form.
flash being 0 throughout cannot be used to infer that flash's sandbox management is better; the two runs differ in restart count and runtime duration.
Its appearance at pro's last step may also simply be because the data for that step has not finished running yet.
