sources.note: One of the evaluation targets given in the survey is experience quality (environment/experience quality), which is consistent with our direction of using alerts like env/possible_leak to check whether the environment is out of control, but it likewise has no definition-level support.

sources.title: Computed here: the gradient spike at pro step 19 is isolated within the recorded range
sources.quote: At pro step 19, grad_norm is 0.0335148, which is 5.96 times the median 0.005626 of the other 18 steps; in the same step, pg_loss, entropy_loss, rewards/mean, train_infer_diff/new_infer/kl, avg@n, and passrate/zero are all within the normal fluctuation range; flash has no similar spikes throughout (25-step range 0.004928~0.009054).
sources.topic: Whether the spike is anomalous
sources.note: In the same segment of records, only this step has env/possible_leak equal to 1. Their simultaneous occurrence does not constitute causation, but it is worth recording side by side, because anomalous samples are one of the common sources of spikes.

items.name: Number of sandbox errors (env/total_error)
items.what: The number of errors on the sandbox side. From the data shape, what it counts is the cumulative number of errors "since the process last restarted", not a per-step increment: within the same process lifecycle it increments cell by cell, and resets to zero after a restart.
items.how: The official team did not provide an explanation for this one. The basis for judging its semantics is its reset points: pro is 0 at steps 1, 2, 3, 11, 15, 17, exactly the steps after 9 restarts; flash is 0 or very small at steps 1, 3, 16, 25 (step 16 is 14), also exactly corresponding to 4 restarts. The intermediate steps in the same segment are monotonically increasing.
items.why: Sandbox errors directly equal sample loss: the trajectory that errors either gets retried (burning double compute) or becomes an infra error and is discarded (contaminating dynsam's statistics). This line staying persistently high indicates the environment is unstable, and the effective output of training data will be discounted. Upward, it can explain dynsam/infra_error/seq_rate; downward, it can explain env/active dropping.
read: First segment by restart, then look: do not look at absolute values, look at 'how fast errors rise within this segment'. pro rises from 52 to 158 from steps 4~10 (7 steps +106), flash rises from 162 to 215 from steps 17~24.
Convert to error rate: divide by env/total_setup of the same step to get parts per million; pro is 264~732 ppm, flash is 200~1126 ppm, both are below one-thousandth.
Returning to zero after a restart does not mean the errors have been fixed; it only means the counter starts over. You need to see whether the slope changes over the next few steps.
Compare with pro after step 15: after pro removes the cyber dataset, the error increments for steps 17~19 are 24, 43.
items.observed: pro over 19 steps ranges from 0~158 (highest at step 10), final step 43; the steps with value 0 are steps 1, 2, 3, 11, 15, 17, all immediately after a restart, so this is a cumulative quantity zeroed by restart rather than a per-step error count. flash over 25 steps ranges from 0~215 (highest at step 24), final step 0 (two restarts just before step 25). Converted to the ratio of errors/setup, pro is 264~732 ppm (highest 731.5 at step 16), flash is 200~1126 ppm (highest 1126 at step 17). pro steps 1, 2, 3 are all 0, indicating that errors did not appear immediately after three consecutive restarts.
traps: It is a cumulative value, not a per-step value; do not read it as 'this step had 158 errors'; it is actually the total over this process's lifetime.
The absolute values of the two runs cannot be directly compared because the process lifetimes differ (pro ran continuously up to 330720 setups before restarting, flash reached 538096).
Returning to zero after a restart will be misread as 'the errors disappeared'; in fact it is just the counter resetting.
The dashboard does not give an official definition for this one; the above interpretation is inferred from reset points and monotonicity.

items.name: Total sandbox creations (env/total_setup)
items.what: How many sandboxes have been cumulatively created within this step, likewise a cumulative quantity 「since the last restart」 rather than a per-step increment. It measures environment-side throughput: how many isolated environments were started in total to run through these rollouts.
items.how: There is no official explanation. I checked timeline.jsonl: in each sync point, totals.sandboxes_step and the env/total_setup for the same step in series are exactly equal (pro step 14 178352, step 19 147904; flash step 25 38368), so it is the dashboard's own sandboxes_step field. The reset pattern is the same as env/total_error: the first step after restart equals env/active at that time, then it accumulates step by step.
items.why: Dividing it by env/active gives the sandbox turnover count, i.e., on average how many trajectories have successively run in one sandbox slot. A low turnover rate means sandboxes are occupied by long trajectories for a long time (generation is held back by the long tail); a high turnover rate means sandboxes are frequently created and destroyed, and the share of environment startup overhead rises. It is also a direct reading for estimating the pressure on the sandbox orchestration system: by step 15, flash has already cumulatively launched 538096 sandboxes.
read: Compare the ratio with env/active: pro is stable at about 14x per step, flash is also around 14x; the sandbox turnover rhythm of the two runs is close.

Look at restarts: a restart resets the cumulative count back to the level of env/active (pro step 15 22415 = the env/active of that step 22415), so the series will show sawtooth; do not mistake the sawtooth for a sudden drop in throughput.
The increment within a single segment is the true throughput: pro rises from 90400 to 330720 from steps 4~10, with about 3.8~4.4 ten-thousand added per step.
items.observed: pro 19-step range 22352~330720, maximum at step 10 (before restart), then at step 11 it falls to 22629. flash 25-step range 38272~538096, maximum at step 15. Because it is a cumulative quantity, the peaks of the two runs are not comparable (pro ran 10 consecutive steps before restarting, up to step 10; flash ran 15 consecutive steps, up to step 15). Calculating the per-step increment within each segment, pro is about 38,000~44,000/step, flash about 39,000~42,000/step, consistent in magnitude. The ratio to env/active is around 14 times for both runs, indicating that sandbox lifetime and trajectory length match relatively stably.
traps: It is only meaningful when viewed together with env/active: looking at this number alone would make you think flash's environment pressure is much higher than pro's, but it is actually just that flash ran longer and restarted less.
The regression caused by restarts is not a throughput drop; it is a sawtooth caused by counter semantics.
The dashboard does not give a definition; the cumulative basis is inferred back from the reset point.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash official README (§5.2 Scaling Agentic RL environment scale)
sources.quote: Our automated pipeline maintains a Kubernetes cluster capable of running over 10,000 concurrent pods with a 70% environment setup success rate.
sources.topic: Official sandbox environment scale and environment setup success rate
sources.note: The officially stated environment setup success rate is only 70%, whereas what we calculate with env/total_error ÷ env/total_setup is a few hundred parts per million (below one thousandth). The two differ by three orders of magnitude, indicating that env/total_setup is not the 「number of environment setup attempts」 and env/total_error is not the 「number of setup failures」; our statement that 「the error rate is below one thousandth」 cannot be used as the official success rate.

items.name: Training token count for this step (perf/total_num_tokens)
items.what: The total number of tokens that actually participate in training in this step, equal to the sum of the context lengths of all trajectories sampled in this step. It determines how many forward and backward passes the trainer has to compute, and therefore basically determines the training time and compute bill for this step.
items.how: The official description is tokens trained on this step. The dashboard doesn't say whether it includes truncated parts, nor does it give a detailed formula; however, timeline.jsonl gives prompts_per_step = 1568 and trained_step = 25088 (unchanged throughout both runs), 25088 = 1568 × 16, i.e. each step has 1568 prompts each sampled into 16 trajectories. Multiplying it by ctx_total_length/mean reproduces this number.
items.why: It is that "quantity" in the cost model. As token count rises, training time rises and the compute bill rises—this is the most direct cost of long context. At the same time, it is also the ruler for validating other metrics: if it doesn't rise while training time rises sharply, the problem is on the system side, not the load side; if it rises while reward doesn't rise, then the extra tokens are burned for nothing.
read: See whether it is in sync with ctx_total_length/mean; the two are almost the same thing (the number of trajectories in a batch is fixed at 25088), and lack of sync indicates that truncation or a data source change is at play.
Look at the growth slope: pro goes from 1.80B to 2.52B and flash from 1.79B to 3.22B, both nearly doubling; this is the main cause of the increase in training time.
When it is below expectations, look at ctx_total_length/clip_ratio; truncated trajectories contribute fewer tokens.
items.observed: pro 19-step range 1.73064B (step 2) ~ 2.64995B (step 14), mean 2.220B, first step 1.80052B, last step 2.52233B. flash 25-step range 1.78967B (step 1) ~ 3.21691B (step 20), mean 2.594B, last step 2.95026B; flash's per-step mean is 16.8% higher than pro's, almost the same as the context length difference between the two runs (17.2%). Formula check: predicted value = 1568 × 16 × ctx_total_length/mean, pro's 19-step deviation is -0.18% ~ -1.19% (mean absolute deviation 0.46%), flash is -0.29% ~ -2.69% (mean 0.76%, the three cells with the largest deviation are exactly steps 16, 17, 18). The predicted value is systematically slightly higher than the actual value by 0.5%~0.8%, with consistent direction; the dashboard does not explain where this gap comes from.
traps: It is not equal to 'how many tokens were generated': the total generated volume also has to include trajectories that were not adopted and trajectories that were retried; this line is only the part that enters training.
Don't treat it as a throughput metric: more tokens does not mean better training; it is more driven by context length.

The formula deviation for flash at steps 16~18 is clearly larger than at other steps (-2.01% ~ -2.69%); these three steps exactly cover the redo interval and should be looked at separately when reconciling cell by cell.

sources.title: Calculation on this site: training token count per step = 1568 × 16 × context length
sources.quote: perf/total_num_tokens ≈ 1568×16×ctx_total_length/mean, pro's maximum relative error over 19 steps is 1.2%, flash's maximum is 2.7%. From this, each prompt is inferred to be sampled 16 times.
sources.topic: How the sampling count is derived
sources.note: This identity shows that the training token count is entirely determined by "prompt count × sample count × context length", with no extra repeated training. Once context length changes, token count changes proportionally; the two cannot be treated as independent evidence for each other.

sources.title: Site calculation: cost is accumulated linearly by wall clock time
sources.quote: cost = rate × (now − start) holds exactly at all 21 synchronization points (rate: pro $5.71/s, flash $2.855/s). Converted to training tokens: pro $35,181 / 1B tokens, flash $10,690 / 1B tokens, a 3.3× difference.
sources.topic: Cost basis
sources.note: Cost follows wall clock, and 30% of wall clock is restart waiting. When converted to tokens, runs with more restarts have their unit price significantly raised — part of pro's 3.3-fold gap is not a compute efficiency difference, but waiting time.

items.name: Generation (rollout) phase elapsed time (timing_s/outer_gen)
items.what: The wall clock time spent on rollout generation in one step, that is, the time spent letting the policy model (including various agent harnesses) sample 16 trajectories for each of 1568 prompts. It is one of the two largest blocks of step time, and together with trainer_ops it accounts for over 97%.
items.how: The official description is wall-clock of rollout generation; the dashboard does not say whether it includes evaluation, grading, and sandbox scheduling. Measured, it satisfies outer_gen + trainer_ops ≤ timing_s/step (all 44 steps without exception). gen_frac in status.json is outer_gen divided by timing_s/step: pro step 19 4266.6/11831.2 = 0.3606, flash step 25 6487.44/10866.8 = 0.5970, exactly matching the dashboard's 0.360623 and 0.596996, so it can be used as a definition check.
items.why: This line determines 'whether generation is the bottleneck.' A high generation share means throughput is stuck on the inference side; what should be changed is inference concurrency, sandbox supply, and the sequence length cap. A low generation share with a high training share means it is stuck on the training side; what should be changed is the parallelism strategy and batch organization. It is also the direct basis for adding machines: the generation wall clock basically follows concurrency and the token count of a single trajectory.
read: Look at the proportion rather than the absolute value: pro accounts for 52.8% of the step (36.1%~69.1%), and flash accounts for 49.7% (40.6%~68.5%); both sides are roughly 'half generation, half training'.

Look at the trend in the proportion: at step 1, generation accounts for about 68% on both sides, then it declines all the way to 36.1% for pro (step 19) and 59.7% for flash (step 25), indicating that the training side takes up more and more time as context grows longer.

It is not proportional to ctx_response_length/mean (pro correlation coefficient is only 0.074, flash 0.309), indicating that generation wall clock is also affected by concurrency scheduling and long-tail trajectories, and cannot be extrapolated solely from average length.
The generation time for the first step after a restart is on the high side (pro step 1 6513.95s, step 15 8900.15s), because that step is mixed with environment re-warming.
items.observed: pro per-step 3132.2s (0.87h, step 6) to 8900.15s (2.47h, step 15), mean 4854s, 19 steps totaling 25.62h, accounting for 52.9% of Σtiming_s/step. flash per-step 2442.04s (0.68h, step 5) to 6916.98s (1.92h, step 16), mean 3811s, 25 steps totaling 26.47h, accounting for 50.1%. Interestingly, flash ran 25 steps while pro ran only 19, yet the absolute total generation time is about the same (26.47h vs 25.62h), indicating that flash's per-step generation is faster than pro's (mean 3811s vs 4854s), even though flash's context is longer.
traps: It is wall clock, not compute: with high concurrency, the wall clock for the same token count can be shortened, so it cannot be used as a measure of 'inference cost'.
You cannot add outer_gen and trainer_ops together as the step time; there is a gap of about 2% between them (pro average 197s, flash average 219s).
When sequences are truncated by length, generation ends early, making outer_gen look better; in this case, look at ctx_total_length/clip_ratio, and do not assume generation efficiency has improved.

items.name: Per-step wall clock time (timing_s/step)
items.what: How long the training pipeline actually takes to complete one step, i.e. the line on the dashboard for "how long each step takes". The official definition is wall-clock of the whole step, but from the data it only covers the execution time of that step itself; the wait for restart after a process crash, requeuing, and reloading weights are all excluded. So it is "effective working time", not "calendar time".
items.how: The official description has only one sentence: wall-clock of the whole step. Subtracting the per-step values in series from the intervals between adjacent step completion timestamps in events.json reveals the actual definition: for steps without a restart the two are almost equal (within 20 seconds), while for steps that have been restarted they differ by several hours. The current step's since and expected in status.json use the same timing.
items.why: It is the only basis for judging "how many steps training can push per day", and also the cost multiplier (cost = per-step seconds × $5.71 or $2.855). In engineering, watching it mainly means looking at two things: first, whether the per-step time keeps getting longer as training progresses (longer context and a heavier training side both push it up), and second, whether there are sudden spikes. But it only counts the time while the process is alive, so looking at this line alone cannot answer "how long this run actually ran"; you must look at it together with the restart events in events.json.
read: Look at the long-term trend rather than a single point: pro climbs from 6850.61s (step 4) to 23186.7s (step 30), and flash from 4898.82s (step 2) to 12433.3s (step 30); their rank correlations with step number are +0.908 / +0.898; both are trending upward, which is an inevitable result of longer contexts, not an anomaly.

Look at spike attribution: when a single step suddenly doubles, first check events.json for whether there was a restart in the same period. But note the direction — most of the time a restart eats is not in that step's reading but in the gap between the previous step and this one; the timing_s/step reported for a restart step actually looks quite normal (see traps).
Subtract the restart in events.json from this line; the difference is the true downtime. If you do not look at restart, you will think training has been running at full load the whole time.
Comparing speed across runs is meaningless: pro averages 11412.9s per step and flash 8118.4s, but the model scale and parallelism strategy differ, and pro also took 14 more restarts.
items.observed: pro 30 steps, per-step 6850.61s (1.90h, step 4) to 23186.7s (6.44h, step 30), mean 11412.9s (3.17h), first step 9569.79s, last step 23186.7s. flash 30 steps, per-step 4898.82s (1.36h, step 2) to 12433.3s (3.45h, step 30), mean 8118.4s (2.26h), first step 6482.77s, last step 12433.3s. Both are strongly correlated with step number (rank correlation +0.908 / +0.898), and both maxima fall on the final step. Summing gives pro 342387s＝95.11h, flash 243552s＝67.65h, but the wall clock is longer: pro start 2026-09-15T10:32:19Z, last step completion 2026-09-20T17:46:48Z, wall clock 127.24h; flash start 2026-09-15T15:16:29Z, last step completion 2026-09-19T01:04:30Z, wall clock 81.80h. That is, pro has 32.13h (25.3% of the true step time, 25.2% of the total bill) completely not recorded into the step, equivalent to about $660,548 at $5.71/s; flash has 14.15h (17.3%, 17.0%), equivalent to about $145,403 at $2.855/s. Locating the gaps step by step: pro's all fall on step 1 4.16h, step 2 1.83h, step 3 3.06h, step 11 2.97h, step 15 4.73h, step 17 5.88h, step 23 3.50h, step 26 1.99h, step 28 2.50h, step 30 1.49h, and the differences for the remaining 20 steps are at most 16.2 seconds, exactly corresponding to 14 restart events; flash's fall on step 3 1.94h, step 16 5.63h, step 25 4.49h, step 28 2.02h, corresponding to 5 restarts (step 1 has an additional 158-second startup difference unrelated to restarts). pro's largest single item is step 17's 5.88h (about $120,897), sandwiched between the 2026-09-17T20:20Z restart and that step's completion; the reason written in the announcement is GPU OOM (expert load imbalance). flash's largest single item is step 16's 5.63h, but 3.96h of that is steps 16 and 17 completing and then being discarded by a redo (series stores the rerun values), so the actual recovery wait is only 5.5 minutes; in terms of pure recovery waiting, the largest item is step 25's 4.49h (about $46,196), corresponding to two consecutive restarts on 2026-09-18. There is also a very stable overhead between recovery and the step timer starting: 740~800 seconds per occurrence for pro, 328~367 seconds for flash.
traps: Using it to estimate the training duration or total cost will clearly underestimate: pro underreports the true step time by 25.3% (25.2% of the total bill), flash by 17.3% (17.0%). This is the most common mistake with this line.

The timing_s/step of the step right after a restart looks completely normal (pro's 10 restart steps are 9569.79s, 7225.21s, 8494.54s, 9422.84s, 12881.6s, 12807.7s, 14180.2s, 15651.5s, 16311.3s, 23186.7s respectively), because the wait was counted into the previous step's interval; looking only at this line, you cannot tell that it just restarted.
The official wording is vague (the whole step); do not assume it is calendar time; it is in-process timing.

Steps 16 and 17 of flash appear twice in events.json and redo=true; series stores the value after the rerun, which does not match the timestamp of the first completion; when reconciling step by step, these two cells will show a negative gap.

items.name: Trainer time (timing_s/trainer_ops)
items.what: The wall clock time spent on the trainer within a step, that is, the segment where the trajectories sampled for this step are fed in for forward pass, backward pass, and parameter updates. It is another large chunk of step time, and together with generation accounts for more than 97%.
items.how: The official description is wall-clock of the trainer, without breaking down how much forward pass, backward pass, communication, and optimizer each account for. It is the main part after subtracting outer_gen from timing_s/step (the remaining ~2% is something else). In status.json, phase switches between training and rollout on this line, and can be used to determine which segment is currently active.
items.why: It is a direct reading of “training throughput”. Longer context, more tokens in the batch, and changed parallelism strategy (for example, pro adjusted training parallelism because of expert load imbalance) will all be directly reflected on this line. Its continuous climb means the tokens to compute per step keep increasing, and the optimizer stage has become the new bottleneck; if it suddenly drops, first suspect whether the data was truncated or the batch got smaller.
read: Compare with perf/total_num_tokens: for flash the correlation coefficient between the two is 0.983, almost fully synchronized, indicating that flash's training time is determined by token count; pro is only 0.725, indicating that pro's training time is also affected by other factors such as parallelism strategy, and the rise in steps 15~19 is especially obvious.
Look at the long-term climb rate: pro rose from 2889.26s at step 1 to 7332.5s at step 19 (+154%), flash from 1884.41s to 4118.92s (+119%); both are getting heavier at a doubling scale.
Compute the gen/train ratio to determine bottleneck migration: pro drops from 2.25 at step 1 to 0.58 at step 19, flash from 2.36 to 1.58; the training side is becoming the main time consumer.
items.observed: pro per-step from 2889.26s (0.80h, step 1) to 7332.5s (2.04h, step 19), mean 4125s, totaling 21.77h over 19 steps, accounting for 45.0% of Σtiming_s/step (per-step share 29.3%~62.0%). flash per-step from 1884.41s to 4954.26s (step 20), mean 3583s, totaling 24.88h over 25 steps, accounting for 47.1% (per-step share 29.1%~56.4%). A full check confirms outer_gen + trainer_ops ≤ timing_s/step, holding for all 44 steps; the average combined share is pro 97.8%, flash 97.1%, and the dashboard does not label what the remaining 2%~3% (pro average 197s, flash average 219s) is; in magnitude it looks like data preparation, weight synchronization, evaluation, and similar minor remainders not listed separately.
traps: It and outer_gen are not mutually exclusive partitions: adding the two does not equal step time, there is a gap of about 2%; do not use it to infer generation time backwards.
Its increase does not mean "training got slower": in this run, the longer training time is mainly due to longer context and more tokens per step, which is expected load growth.
The dashboard does not state whether it includes communication/checkpoint overhead beyond the optimizer, so do not use it to compute FLOPs utilization for training.

sources.title: Official dashboard metric description
sources.quote: wall-clock of the trainer
sources.note: The description the original site wrote for this metric itself. It is the definition baseline: if our explainer conflicts with it, the official one prevails.

sources.title: MiMo-V2-Flash Technical Report
sources.quote: where the rollout phase consistently emerges as the dominant bottleneck due to the inference and decoding costs
sources.topic: RL system: two stages of generation and training
sources.note: The same passage explicitly divides RL training into two stages, rollout and training, supporting our reading outer_gen and trainer_ops as the two blocks of “half generation, half training”, rather than converting between them.

sources.title: HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework
sources.quote: We further design a 3D-HybridEngine for efficient actor model resharding between training and generation phases, with zero memory redundancy and significantly reduced communication overhead.
sources.topic: Generation/training two-stage split in a hybrid-controller RL system
sources.note: Same as above: the training stage is a separately measurable stage in the public system, supporting our treating trainer_ops as a direct reading of training throughput (the 1.53x~20.57x throughput improvement reported in that paper also comes from work between these two stages).

sources.title: verl docs: Performance Tuning Guide (GPU memory/batch trade-offs for long-sequence training)
sources.quote: To train long sequence (>32k), users may need to decrease the `*micro_batch_size_per_gpu` and `*max_token_len_per_gpu` to avoid OOM.
sources.topic: How lengthening context drives up training time
sources.note: The official documentation explicitly says that long-sequence training must lower the per-GPU batch/token limit to avoid OOM, meaning that the longer the context, the more time and GPU memory the training side consumes; this supports attributing the continuous climb of trainer_ops to more tokens per step, rather than to training getting slower.

sources.title: This site's calculation: the sum of reported per-step durations is a quarter less than the wall clock, and the gap sits on the restart steps.
sources.quote: pro wall clock 127.24h, Σtiming_s/step only 95.11h, gap 32.13h (25.3% of the true step time) equivalent to about $661,000; the gap sits on 10 restart steps, the largest single item being step 17 at 5.88h; flash's gap is 14.15h (17.3%), about $145,000. For non-restart steps, the reported value differs from wall clock by less than 20 seconds.
sources.topic: Where did the under-reported time go?
sources.note: Similarly, the trainer time share (pro once reached 62%) is calculated using 「reported steps」 as the denominator. The denominator itself omits restart waiting, so the share will be systematically inflated; do not use it for a strict machine-time comparison with the generation share.

items.name: Optimizer updates per step (training/actor_optimizer_steps)
items.what: How many times the actor's optimizer is called within one global step, i.e. how many rounds of parameter updates. It defines the algorithmic granularity of 「one step」: when this value equals 1, one step is one round of updates.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide an official explanation for this entry. In the data, it is a constant sequence in the series: pro is 1 for all 19 steps, flash is 1 for all 25 steps. This can be corroborated by trained_step = 25088, also from the timeline — the number of trajectories trained per step is also fixed, indicating that this step is not split into multiple mini-batches for multiple updates.
items.why: It determines how all metrics reported in units of 「step」 should be read. If it is 1, then actor/entropy_loss, actor/pg_loss, critic/rewards/mean are statistics over 「the batch of data corresponding to one update」; if it is greater than 1, there will be multiple updates within the same global step, the physical meaning of those 「per-step」 metrics changes, and the horizontal axis is no longer equivalent. When troubleshooting training anomalies, it is the first definition item to confirm.
read: Being identically 1 means one update per step; all per-step metrics on the dashboard can be directly aligned and compared by step.
Once a step greater than 1 appears, first confirm whether gradient accumulation changed or the data was chunked, then explain the changes in reward and loss.
It and training/global_step are a pair: global_step counts steps, while it counts the number of updates.
items.observed: pro 19 steps and flash 25 steps are all 1, with not a single cell different. Together with prompts_per_step = 1568 and trained_step = 25088, which remain constant throughout timeline.jsonl, it can be confirmed that both runs follow the stable rhythm of 「one step = a batch of 25088 trajectories = one parameter update」, with no gradient accumulation or multiple updates within one step.
traps: Don't assume it is necessarily equal to 1: this is not a constant physical quantity, it just happens to be 1 in this run.
It does not equal the total number of updates; the total number of updates is obtained by multiplying it by training/global_step.
The dashboard does not give the definition of this line; the above is inferred from the constant value and trained_step.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
sources.quote: Whereas standard policy gradient methods perform one gradient update per data sample, we propose a novel objective function that enables multiple epochs of minibatch updates.
sources.topic: PPO clipped surrogate objective and single-epoch/multi-epoch updates
sources.note: We read actor_optimizer_steps being identically 1 as “one global step performs only one parameter update”; the paper builds its argument precisely by contrasting “one update per sample” with “multiple rounds of updates”, which can serve as background for this reading.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) — verl documentation（ppo_epochs）
sources.quote: `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_epochs`: Number of epochs for PPO updates on one set of sampled trajectories for actor
sources.topic: Configuration implications of single-epoch updates
sources.note: The official documentation defines ppo_epochs as “how many rounds of updates to perform on the same batch of collected trajectories”; in this run the value is 1, consistent with our reading of “one global step performs only one parameter update”.

items.name: Global step number (training/global_step)
items.what: Which step training has progressed to; it is the horizontal axis of all curves on the dashboard. It is also the anchor for judging whether a run is stuck, has skipped steps, or has re-run.
items.how: The dashboard does not provide an official explanation for this entry; in the data it is simply an integer increasing by one starting from 1, pro up to 19, flash up to 25. In series.json, the subscript of every metric array is this minus one, so it also serves as an index table.
items.why: All per-step metrics rely on it to align time. In engineering, it is needed most when troubleshooting: if a metric's array length does not match it, or step numbers are duplicated, it indicates that a rerun or data backfill anomaly occurred in between. flash happened to have exactly this situation — in events.json, steps 16 and 17 each appear twice and the second time is marked redo, while global_step has only 25 values, so the counts on the two sides do not match.
read: First check whether it matches the number of step events in events.json: if not, it means there is a redo or a skipped step.
Check whether the advancement speed has slowed: pro took 72.18h wall clock to reach step 19, flash took 67.44h to reach step 25; converted, flash advances faster.
Looking at it together with benchmarks.json reveals evaluation lag: offline evaluation for pro only goes up to step 15, and flash only up to step 21, both lagging behind the current step number.
items.observed: pro's global_step is 1~19 (19 values), flash's is 1~25 (25 values), both consecutive with no skipped numbers. But flash's events.json has 27 step events: step 16 appears once at 1789597499 and once at 1789621327, and step 17 appears once at 1789605123 and once at 1789629325, with the second occurrence of each marked redo=true—this is the re-run caused by what the official announcement says: 'we restarted the flash run from step 15'; so flash actually computed 27 steps, and only 25 entered global_step. There is no redo at all in pro's events.
traps: Consecutive step numbers do not mean there were no reruns; go to events.json to check the redo flag.
Its value equals the series array index plus one; when reading the array, don't be off by one.
Step numbers of the two runs cannot be directly compared horizontally: the definition of a step differs in model size and batch size; flash reaching step 25 does not mean it has done more than pro.

sources.title: mimo.xiaomi.com/rl official run announcement: flash reruns from step 15
sources.quote: we restarted the flash run from step 15. reason: a type of infra error on one of datasets was not correctly detected over the past ~3 hours.
sources.topic: Official announcement for this run (rerun and infra error)
sources.note: The official announcement states verbatim that flash restarted from step 15, which exactly matches our inference that 'in events.json, steps 16 and 17 each appear twice and the second occurrence has redo=true, while global_step has only 25 values': consecutive step numbers do not mean there was no restart.

items.name: AutomationBench v1.0.6 (offline evaluation leaderboard)
items.what: Leaderboard score for automation-type tasks, avg@3. The lowest-scoring one among the three leaderboards, indicating that this group of tasks is harder overall.
items.how: Also comes from the benchmarks API. The dashboard gives the leaderboard name, version number, and avg@3, but not the task composition or grading details.
items.why: It measures an ability skewed toward 'operation/execution', which is not exactly the same direction as what the two coding leaderboards assess. Only by looking at the three leaderboards together can you determine whether the progress is general or only on one type of task.
read: pro rose from 46.2 to 50.7 (+4.50), and flash rose from 43.3 to 49.9 (+6.60).
It had a drop around step 7 (pro 47.5 → 45.4), indicating that this type of task is relatively sensitive to the training stage.
flash is the only one of the three leaderboards that is continuous through step 21 (1~21 with no missing steps), so its trend line is the most complete.
The absolute level is more than 10 points lower than the coding leaderboard, so when comparing across leaderboards, do not use the same 「passing line」.
items.observed: pro steps 1~15 are consecutive, 46.2 → 50.7, with step 7 falling back to 45.4 in between. flash steps 1~21 are consecutive with no missing steps, 43.3 → step 15's 51.2 is the highest, then falling back to 49.9 at step 21; the final segment is a plateau with a slight decline.
traps: After flash surges to 51.2 at step 15, it stays between 49.3~50.8 for 6 consecutive steps; this stretch is a plateau, do not read it as 「stopped improving」.
The three leaderboards differ in difficulty; when using 「how many points it rose」 to compare two runs across leaderboards, different baselines will magnify the difference.

items.name: DeepSWE v1.1 (offline evaluation leaderboard)
items.what: Score from running an offline evaluation with mini-swe-agent on DeepSWE v1.1. Measured once per training step, taking the average of 3 samples each time (avg@3). It is a score on a fixed test set, which is not the same thing as online metrics on the training distribution.
items.how: Data comes from the site's benchmarks API, organized by training step number. The dashboard only gives the score, not the number of tasks, sampling parameters, or grading details.
items.why: This is the only external reference besides the online dynsam/avg@n. The online metric measures the pass rate on the training distribution and drifts as the data recipe changes; the offline leaderboard is fixed, so it can answer 'has the model really become stronger?'
read: Look at the trend, not individual points. pro rose from 58.41 at step 1 to 63.42 at step 15 (+5.01); flash rose from 48.67 to 59.59 (+10.92).
Single steps can drop; pro had a drop from 65.97 → 63.27, and flash fluctuates more (after 60.18 at step 10 it falls to 54.13 and then rises back).
Its coverage lags behind the training progress: pro only goes up to step 15, and flash only up to step 21.

flash starts lower and has a larger gain, and its gap with pro is narrowing: at the same step 15, pro is 63.42 and flash is 60.77, a difference of 2.65 points; at step 1 the difference is 9.74 points.
items.observed: Steps recorded for pro: 1~8, 10~15, missing step 9; the last point is 63.42 at step 15, and the highest overall is 65.97 at step 12. Steps recorded for flash: 1~6, 8, 10~21, missing steps 7 and 9; the last point is 59.59 at step 21, and the highest overall is 64.01 at step 18.
traps: The 3 samples of avg@3 mean that a single step has roughly a few points of sampling noise; the rise or fall of two adjacent steps cannot be taken as a trend.
Missing steps and lag are the norm, not a data error. The official announcement said that offline evaluation scores are backfilled gradually.
It and dynsam/avg@n are similar in units but different in meaning (fixed test set vs training distribution); do not add them together or convert between them.

sources.title: Reality Is the Final Verifier: On Two Key Gaps in Agentic Software Engineering
sources.quote: reward hacking exploits omissions in the requirements or model, while hallucination widens the gaps by fabricating requirements or environment assumptions
sources.topic: Tests passing ≠ deployment acceptable (two gaps)
sources.note: The paper's conclusion is 'predeployment evaluations remain proxies', directly challenging our treating the offline leaderboard as decisive evidence of 'whether the model has really become stronger'—it is only a proxy metric.

sources.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
sources.quote: Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning
sources.topic: Execution environment + long context are inherent requirements of this kind of evaluation.
sources.note: SWE-bench defined the execution-style evaluation paradigm of 'given a codebase + issue, modify the code to make the tests pass' (leaderboards like DeepSWE are derivatives of it), supporting our reading of benchmark/deepswe as an external reference on a fixed test set rather than an online metric on the training distribution.

items.name: In-house Coding Bench (offline evaluation leaderboard)
items.what: Score on the internal coding evaluation leaderboard, avg@3. The tasks are not public; it is an in-house coding task set.
items.how: Like DeepSWE, it comes from the benchmarks API, organized by step number. The dashboard gives the leaderboard title and sampling method (avg@3), but not the task composition.
items.why: It and DeepSWE are references from two different sources. When both leaderboards move in the same direction, conclusions are more reliable; when only one moves, suspect that that leaderboard's tasks are closer to the current training data.
read: The increase is smaller than DeepSWE: pro from 57.54 to 62.26 (+4.72), flash from 53.83 to 61.33 (+7.50).
It is the only one of the three leaderboards where pro has no missing steps throughout (steps 1~15 continuous).
The curve is smoother than DeepSWE, rising stepwise, with no obvious drops, indicating that this leaderboard's task difficulty distribution is more uniform.
flash is catching up closely: at the same step 15, pro is 62.26 and flash is 58.96.
items.observed: For pro, steps 1~15 are continuous, rising from 57.54 to 62.26, with the highest being 62.54 at steps 13 and 14. For flash, the recorded steps are 1~6, 8, and 10~21, missing steps 7 and 9, rising from 53.83 to 61.33 at step 21, and the highest, 61.28 at step 20, is essentially level with step 21.
traps: The tasks on the internal leaderboard are not public, so it cannot be determined whether they overlap with the training data; keep this in mind when scores are on the high side.
It is also avg@3; the single-step noise is not small, and pro has three consecutive points at steps 13~15 that are almost identical (62.54, 62.54, 62.26); this is a plateau period, not exact values.

items.name: Offline evaluation lags training by 5~8 steps, and the two runs differ
items.what: The coverage of all three offline leaderboards stops before the training progress; this is the most easily overlooked structural issue on this dashboard.
items.how: Just compare the set of step numbers in benchmarks with the current training step number. Offline evaluation has to run the full agent pipeline and grade it, which is much slower than online metrics; official notices have also said that scores are backfilled over time.
items.why: It determines how strong a conclusion you can draw about the most recent steps. The last few steps have no independent evaluation backing; you can only use the online metric dynsam/avg@n, and online metrics are on the training distribution and cannot replace external validation. The gap is also not a fixed value: it changes with the pace of evaluation backfilling; for pro, it was 4 steps at the previous observation round, and it has now widened to 6~8 steps.
read: pro: training has reached step 24, DeepSWE and In-house Coding both stop at step 18 (missing 6 steps), AutomationBench stops at step 16 (missing 8 steps).
flash: training ends after 30 steps, and all three leaderboards stop at step 25, missing 5 steps.

The gap is not a fixed delay: it is determined by the pace of official backfilling; for pro, the previous run was 4 steps, and this run is 6~8 steps. The announcement's 「backfilling flash step 12 and pro step 8」 also shows that the nominal step number does not equal when this score can actually be seen —— pro's step 8 score only became readable 5.27 hours after it completed, and flash's step 12 was 3.75 hours.
So the judgment that 「the last few steps are still rising」 has only one source: the online metric (flash step 29 at 0.6623 is the highest throughout, and step 30 falls back to 0.6435).
items.observed: pro has 24 training steps; DeepSWE and In-house Coding reach step 18, AutomationBench reaches step 16, with gaps of 6, 6, and 8 steps respectively; flash has 30 training steps (finished), all three leaderboards reach step 25, a gap of 5 steps. The gaps for the two runs are not the same, so this is not a fixed evaluation cycle but a backfill cadence — this number will keep changing with official backfills, so look at the current value before reading it.
traps: Do not use 「the leaderboard didn't rise」 to judge that the last few steps made no progress —— the leaderboard simply did not test those steps.
Also do not use avg@n's increase to fill in the leaderboard's blank; the two are not measuring the same thing.
When replaying historical slices, the earlier the slice, the larger the leaderboard gap; don't read "at that moment there was no score yet" as "at that moment the score was 0".

items.name: Notices: all 5 are incident reports, with no training conclusions
items.what: The notices section at the bottom of the dashboard. As of now there are 5 items in total, all are stability notices plus one dataset adjustment, and none of them discuss training effectiveness.
items.how: The data comes from the site's notices API and is sorted in reverse chronological order. Each entry has an id, timestamp, English body, and a run field.
items.why: It explains the things in the data that look strange: why a certain step gets rerun, why a dataset's count suddenly breaks off. Reading the notices before the timeline saves a lot of guessing.
read: Read these 5 entries in chronological order; they line up with several breakpoints in the data (annotated in the original text below).
The run field is null for all 5 entries, indicating they are all global announcements and are not differentiated by run.
The announcements explain only 4 of the 13 restarts (pro 3, flash 1); the rest have no separate announcement.
The announcement board is positioned as a fault log, not a progress report—don't expect to read "how much the score rose" from it.
items.observed:
In chronological order, the original text is as follows.

1）2026-09-16 17:58Z (Beijing 09-17 01:58)
"we have updated the latest deepswe results for flash step 12 & pro step 8. we will keep posting as the offline evaluation results come out."
This explains why the results for pro step 8 and flash step 12 on the DeepSWE leaderboard were added later.

2）2026-09-16 20:08Z (Beijing 09-17 04:08)
"the mimo-v2.6-pro run is restarting due to a vram issue on one node."

3）2026-09-17 02:27Z (Beijing 09-17 10:27)
"we restarted the flash run from step 15. reason: a type of infra error on one of datasets was not correctly detected over the past ~3 hours."
This matches flash steps 16 and 17 each appearing twice in the event stream——the direct result of “restarting from step 15.”

4）2026-09-17 12:20Z (Beijing 09-17 20:20)
"there was a network connectivity issue between the pro training cluster and the grader deployment. we have restarted the run. we also removed the cyber dataset from the upcoming pro run, since we observed some bad patterns in the rollout logs."
This matches pro's partial/cyber/**/n_tokens being all null from step 15 onward.

5）2026-09-18 03:49Z (Beijing 09-18 11:49)
"the pro run restarted at step 17 due to a GPU OOM issue caused by expert load imbalance. we have adjusted the training parallelism strategy."
This is the last one, immediately adjacent in time to pro steps 18 and 19.
traps: The run fields of the announcements are all null, so don't assume they relate to only one run; the 3rd entry is about flash, and the 4th and 5th entries are about pro.
"Remove the cyber dataset" refers to "the next run", but in the data the cyber count stops at step 15; you need to align the two in time yourself.
The other 9 restarts have no announcement, which doesn't mean they didn't happen—the number of restarts must be counted from the event stream, not from the number of announcements.
